Docker Sandboxes vs. Containers: Choosing the Right Isolation for AI Agents

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3015 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Docker

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you’ve used Docker for a while, “Docker Sandboxes” might read as “a container with an AI agent inside.” Containers have been the unit of nearly everything Docker ships for over a decade, and a sandbox might sound like one more way to package a workload.
  • They’re actually different technologies.
  • In his WeAreDevelopers keynote, Docker President Mark Cavage mentioned containers are doing exactly the job they were designed to do, but we’re asking them to do a different job.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you’ve used Docker for a while, “Docker Sandboxes” might read as “a container with an AI agent inside.” Containers have been the unit of nearly everything Docker ships for over a decade, and a sandbox might sound like one more way to package a workload.

They’re actually different technologies. A container is an isolated process that shares the host kernel with everything else on the machine. Docker Sandboxes are dedicated microVMs with their own Linux kernel, filesystem, network, and Docker Engine, built for autonomous coding agents that need a whole development machine to work in. A sandbox can run containers, which is part of why the two are easy to conflate.

In his WeAreDevelopers keynote, Docker President Mark Cavage mentioned containers are doing exactly the job they were designed to do, but we’re asking them to do a different job.

Containers were built to isolate applications, which they still do well. But a coding agent is an actor: it makes decisions and operates on your systems the way a developer uses a laptop. It clones repositories, installs packages, starts databases, builds images, and tries again for hours. It can also act on instructions from files, web pages, and tool output that nobody reviewed.

Recent findings suggest that that different job needs a different boundary, and where that boundary sits determines how far an agent’s mistake can travel. This post covers how Docker Sandboxes and containers isolate workloads, what changes beyond the kernel, what a sandbox costs you in setup, and how to pick.

A container is a process, or a group of processes, running on the host with its own view of the filesystem, process tree, and network. Linux namespaces provide that view, and cgroups meter CPU, memory, and I/O. Every container on the machine also shares the host kernel, which is why containers start promptly, pack densely, and carry so little overhead.

Industry observers note that this design has more than a decade of tooling behind it. Compose, Kubernetes, OCI registries, image scanners, and nearly every CI system treat the container as the common primitive. If the job is to run a service, execute a code snippet, process one request, or run an evaluation and disappear, a container is usually the obvious pick, and it will stay that way.

ⓘ Containers share one kernel, even inside a VM. On macOS and Windows, Docker Desktop runs your Linux containers inside a virtual machine, which keeps them off your host operating system. Every container in that VM still shares its single kernel, so the isolation between one container and the next is unchanged.

In a recent development, docker Sandboxes run an AI coding agent inside a microVM that has its own Linux kernel, its own filesystem and network stack, and a private Docker Engine. The agent gets sudo inside the isolated environment. It can install packages, run services, build images, and bring up an entire Compose application without reaching the host Docker daemon, the host filesystem outside its workspace, or other sandboxes on the same machine.

Getting one running takes a single command, using sbx, the Docker Sandboxes CLI:.

In a recent development, that creates the sandbox and starts the agent. You can stop it, resume it, and come back to everything the agent installed until you remove the sandbox.

Industry observers note that coding agents need a full machine because their sessions build up state over hours and they act on unvetted instructions. A container is built for a process with a known set of dependencies, and an agent’s work doesn’t fit that shape.

Industry observers note that an agent needs the authority of a whole machine and a boundary designed for one. The capabilities that make an agent useful, such as running code, installing packages, and reaching the network, are the same ones that wear at the walls around it. An agent probes the edges of its environment because the job requires changing that environment.

A coding agent’s session looks like a developer’s afternoon. It clones a repository, installs packages, starts PostgreSQL, runs migrations, builds images, launches the app with Compose, reads the logs, changes the code, and tries again. That loop can run for hours, and each step depends on what the previous one left behind.

Recent findings suggest that A container is designed to be rebuilt from an image and a few explicit volumes. The packages, databases, and build output an agent creates outside those volumes are lost when the container is recreated. That’s less than ideal for a session where every step builds on the last.

Box by ASCII describes this distinction neatly: “It uses the sandbox the way a developer uses a laptop, so the sandbox has to behave like one.”.

The program deciding which command to run is probabilistic, and it can read instructions from many places at once, including source files, issue descriptions, web pages, package metadata, and MCP tool output. Some of that input is untrusted, and a malicious instruction planted in a README or a tool description can steer the agent on purpose. The code it generates may also be wrong or actively hostile.

We’ve already seen an agent that deleted a production database after misreading its task. Once the agent is running unattended in YOLO mode, there’s no permission prompt left to catch it. A workload with that much authority and that little predictability needs a boundary designed for it.

Put these facts together and you get the reason why we built Docker Sandboxes. An autonomous coding agent needs machine-shaped capabilities without access to everything on the developer’s machine, which comes down to four things:.

The next sections show what each looks like, starting with containment.

It has been revealed that the short version is that a container’s boundary is the host kernel it shares, and Docker Sandboxes have a hypervisor boundary around a kernel the agent has to itself. That one difference decides how far a compromise can travel, and it also settles the awkward question of how an agent could get access to Docker.

This is where containers and containment part ways. A container can be part of containment, and often should be, but containment covers the whole environment around the agent. It starts with a boundary the model can’t rewrite, which is why Docker uses a microVM with its own kernel for autonomous agents.

It has been revealed that A container’s boundary is enforced by the kernel it shares, so escaping it requires a kernel exploit or a side-channel attack. Those aren’t everyday finds. Past that bar, though, sits the entire host kernel, every other process on the machine, and any credentials mounted alongside them.

ⓘ This scenario is specific to Linux environments. On Docker Desktop (macOS and Windows), the shared kernel is the Docker Desktop VM’s kernel, not the host kernel, so an escape would land in that VM rather than the operating system.

Industry observers note that docker Sandboxes give the agent its own kernel behind a hypervisor boundary. If an agent escapes its container, it lands in a disposable microVM, and the host stays out of reach. And you can delete the sandbox and start another. Each agent also gets its own microVM, so two agents running on the same machine can’t reach each other’s sandboxes either. However, the agent can still reach whatever you chose to share with it, including the workspace, allowed network destinations, MCP servers, and skills.

In a recent development, mounting /var/run/docker.sock into a container is the long-standing way to give it Docker access, and it turns up in Compose setups, CI pipelines, and observability tools. It also hands the container control of the host Docker daemon, which Docker limits to trusted owners because it can mount host paths and start privileged containers.

An agent doesn’t need an exploit to use that. Put one in a container started with the socket mounted, and it probes its surroundings, works out that it’s in a container, and finds the hole in the configuration. In Mark’s keynote demo, that was enough for an agent to reach a secrets file on the host with no zero-day involved.

The socket is one hole among several, and agents find them because probing their environment is part of the work. Docker-in-Docker, mounted credentials, and broad host mounts are others. Containers were built to isolate an application that behaves as configured. But an agent keeps testing that configuration, so if there’s a gap, it’s likely to find it.

Recent findings suggest that docker Sandboxes put the missing boundary in the right place. The agent talks to a private Docker Engine inside the guest. It can build images, run Testcontainers, and start a whole Compose stack, and the host daemon and its socket stay outside the microVM the entire time. Containers keep doing what they do best, inside a boundary the agent can’t widen.

Let’s say you ask an agent running inside Docker Sandboxes to find a secrets file on the host. It’ll find a Docker socket, try to use it to mount host paths and start privileged containers, but won’t reach the host. A microVM can give it a much stronger trust boundary than a container. The architecture behind Docker Sandboxes goes deeper on why a microVM was the right shape for this.

Recent findings suggest that containment draws the boundary. Control is what you can see and stop inside it: what the agent is allowed to reach, and the ability to block it when it heads somewhere it shouldn’t. In a sandbox, those controls are enforced by the host, outside the agent’s reach, so the agent can’t switch them off or reason its way around them. Outbound traffic, credentials, and organization-wide policy all work this way. Control also means knowing what the agent can still touch, because a microVM can’t hide what you choose to share with it.

Runs its own Linux kernel in a microVM.

Needs the host socket or a nested daemon.

Uses a private Docker Engine inside the microVM.

Uses a direct read-write mount or an in-VM private clone.

Uses the container network and whatever controls its operator supplies.

Sends outbound traffic through a host proxy with deny-by-default policy.

Commonly receives environment variables, files, or mounted sockets.

Uses host-side credential injection for supported HTTP services.

Usually rebuilt from an image and explicit volumes.

Keeps packages, images, containers, and agent history until sbx rm.

Fits Compose, Kubernetes, and most CI systems.

Uses the sbx lifecycle and experimental environment files.

These controls hold because they run outside the agent process. A rule the agent can reach is a rule it can work around, so the rules that matter live on the host. Outbound traffic goes through a host-side proxy with a deny-by-default policy, which means a destination the agent wants stays blocked until someone adds it to the list. Credentials follow the same logic. For supported HTTP services, the proxy injects them into outbound requests, so the agent can use a credential without the raw value ever entering the VM.

When one developer’s setup needs to become a team standard, Docker AI Governance can move network, filesystem, and MCP policy into organization-wide controls.

A microVM can’t hide what you choose to share with it, so the shared parts deserve the most attention.

Industry observers note that the workspace is the largest of them. It’s mounted read-write by default, so the agent can edit or delete files in your project. Clone mode gives the agent a private in-VM clone to work in, which protects the host working tree, though the original repository stays readable inside the sandbox.

It has been revealed that MCP servers and skills are shared too. A local stdio MCP server runs on the host and shared agent skills use a host-side store, so the agent’s reach extends to both.

So whichever mode you pick, be sure to read the diff before you run modified code.

Recent findings suggest that docker Sandboxes may cost some configuration and a supported hypervisor. But Kits and environment files account for the configuration, and they’re also where you get choice over agents and tools and the capacity to reproduce a setup across a team.

Sources indicate that kits make setup repeatable by packaging tools, files, commands, network rules, credentials, and agent instructions. They’re published for different agents, tools, and IDEs, so you can swap what runs inside the sandbox without rebuilding the environment around it. An sbxenv.yaml file records one project’s sandbox configuration, and committing it to the repo lets a teammate recreate the same sandbox with one command, so every developer works from the same setup. (Kits are in early access and environment files are experimental, so blueprint for changes to both.).

The host-enforced controls take some setup too. Network policy requires someone to decide which destinations belong in the workflow, credential mediation adds service bindings and approved domains, and clone mode adds a fetch step before changes land in the host repository.

In a recent development, running a sandbox takes more from your machine than running a container does. It needs a supported hypervisor, which today means Apple silicon on macOS 14 or later, Windows Hypervisor Platform, or KVM on supported Ubuntu systems, and running inside another VM requires nested virtualization. The separate kernel and Docker Engine also consume more memory and disk than one additional container would.

Industry observers note that if your machine is the limiting factor, Docker Cloud Sandboxes run the same microVM isolation on Docker-managed compute, and one command moves a sandbox between your laptop and the cloud. Local and cloud sandboxes keep separate secrets and network policies.

Choose a container when you control the code and its dependencies, and choose Docker Sandboxes when the workload generates or fetches code at runtime and needs its own boundary.

Reach for Docker Sandboxes when.

You control the code and its dependencies.

The workload generates or fetches code at runtime.

Execution is short-lived and rebuilt from an image.

The session accumulates state for hours.

The workload doesn’t need Docker, or runs in CI that already provides it.

The workload needs its own Docker Engine with no path to the host socket.

You want maximum density and a fit with Compose or Kubernetes.

You need host-enforced network and credential policy the workload can’t switch off.

The kernel boundary is enough for the code you’re running.

You want a hypervisor between the workload and your kernel.

If any of the signals below apply to your project, you should start with Docker Sandboxes.

According to recent reports, start with sbx run claude. Add clone mode, kits, network policy, credential mediation, and organization governance as your workflow grows.

Recent findings suggest that containers aren’t going anywhere. For services, CI jobs, and anything you package to ship, they draw the right boundary, and the ecosystem around them is the reason they’ll keep doing that work. A coding agent needs more than a container to be trusted with real work. It needs containment, meaning a boundary the model can’t rewrite, controls it can’t reason its way around, and the freedom to choose its tools and scale its setup.

Docker Sandboxes provide that containment in a microVM that can still run your containers. The boundary is also what lets the agent move faster. With it in place, you can stop approving every command and let the agent get to work. Once one developer’s setup needs to become a team standard, Docker AI Governance extends the same controls across your organization.

Industry observers note that give it a try and get a sandbox running with one command. Start with sbx run claude and the Docker Sandboxes quickstart. According to recent reports, no. A container is an isolated process that shares the host kernel. Docker Sandboxes are microVMs with their own kernel, filesystem, network, and Docker Engine. A sandbox can run containers, which is why the two are easy to confuse.

It has been revealed that yes. Each sandbox has a private Docker Engine, so the agent can build images, run Testcontainers, and start Compose applications without the host socket or Docker-in-Docker.

Industry observers note that no. Containers remain the right tool for packaged applications, CI jobs, and short-lived execution. Sandboxes add a stronger boundary for autonomous agents, and containers keep running inside them.

Recent findings suggest that A container isolates a workload. Containment involves the whole environment around an agent: the boundary it runs in, what it can reach, which tools it uses, and how you reproduce it. A container can be part of containment, and Docker Sandboxes add the microVM boundary an autonomous agent needs.

Docker describes four requirements: containment (a boundary the model can’t rewrite), control (visibility into what the agent is doing and the ability to stop it), choice (swapping models, agents, and tools without rebuilding), and capacity (a setup other developers can reproduce and scale past one machine).

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Next OS release will bundle modern successor, giving admins a compatibility checklist to work through.
  • Microsoft has confirmed that, at long last, PowerShell 7 will come bundled with Windows, while the venerable PowerShell 5.1 begins its long retirement.
  • According to recent reports, it has been a long time coming, although PowerShell 5.1 isn't going away immediately.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Next OS release will bundle modern successor, giving admins a compatibility checklist to work through.

Microsoft has confirmed that, at long last, PowerShell 7 will come bundled with Windows, while the venerable PowerShell 5.1 begins its long retirement.

According to recent reports, it has been a long time coming, although PowerShell 5.1 isn't going away immediately. It will, however, "be removed from a future version of Windows," and Windows Server 2025 and Windows 11 26H2 are the last versions to include PowerShell 5.1 enabled by default.

After that, PowerShell 5.1 will be available as a Feature On Demand (FOD) before eventually shuffling off into the sunset, while PowerShell 7 takes over automation duties.

PowerShell 5.1 is now more than ten years old and runs on the .NET Framework. PowerShell 7 is its cross-platform, open source successor, but compatibility isn't seamless.

PowerShell was the brainchild of Jeffrey Snover, who sought to bring script automation to Windows at a time when graphical user interfaces were king. He recalled executives telling him "admins don't want command line interfaces," and "exactly what part of effing Windows is confusing you?" but eventually won the argument, and we reckon countless Windows administrators owe him a debt of gratitude.

Industry observers note that powerShell 5.1 hasn't had many new features for years. "PowerShell 7 is the modern PowerShell: the one we develop in the open, across platforms, and where new features go," wrote Jason Helmick, a senior product manager on Microsoft's PowerShell team. But compatibility niggles remain.

In a recent development, the two can run side by side, so existing scripts won't have to move immediately. Finding and testing everything scattered across an enterprise estate, however, could keep administrators occupied for some time.

According to recent reports, microsoft also has unfinished work on the bundled version's MSIX packaging, including support for running as SYSTEM, DISM cmdlets, and machine-wide settings. Those gaps matter for scheduled tasks, services, and management scripts.

Despite the deprecation, PowerShell 5.1 will continue to receive updates based on the lifecycle of the Windows version on which it runs. It will eventually be removed based on usage data and "communicated in advance," according to Microsoft.

Administrators have time to prepare, but checking which scripts run unchanged, which need work, and which still depend on 5.1 won't happen by itself.

"Including PowerShell 7 in Windows is a milestone we've been working toward since PowerShell went cross-platform," Helmick wrote, although the bundled release is still ahead.

Microsoft notes PowerShell 7 will arrive with the next Windows release, but hasn't named it. 27H2, anyone? ®.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that some numbers are hard to picture until you sit with them for a moment. Last week we published the Prime Day 2026 metrics, and the one that stuck with me is 2.3 quadrillion: the daily requests Amazon ElastiCache peaked at during the event. Prime Day ran back in June, so this post always lands as a retrospective, and that gap is part of what makes it worth reading. By the time the numbers reach you, the only evidence that any of it happened is that nothing went wrong.

It has been revealed that the rest of the week pulled in a different direction: smaller, cheaper, and more constrained. Claude Haiku 5.5 arrived on Amazon Bedrock at roughly 75 percent less than Haiku 4.5, Amazon Nova 2.5 Sonic made voice agents quicker on their feet, and Strands Box showed up to put real boundaries around what an agent is allowed to do. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news….

HeadlinesAll the numbers: Amazon Prime Day 2026 powered by AWS is the latest entry in a tradition that goes back to 2016, and the scale is still difficult to hold in your head. Over the four days of Prime Day, Amazon DynamoDB processed more than 59 trillion requests while peaking at 192 million requests per second, and kept single-digit millisecond responses throughout. AWS Lambda handled over 2.3 trillion invocations per day. Amazon EBS peaked above 24.8 trillion I/O operations, moving more than an exabyte of data daily. Amazon ECS released an average of 158.3 million tasks per day on AWS Fargate, a 47.7 percent jump over last year, and AWS Graviton powered up to 49 percent of the Amazon EC2 compute that Amazon.com used.

The number I keep coming back to, though, isn’t a throughput record. The team ran more than 44,000 AWS Fault Injection Service experiments ahead of the event, more than six times what they ran in 2025. Those are deliberate failures injected on purpose, months in advance, so that the trillions of requests above turn into an ordinary shopping afternoon. If you’re preparing for your own peak moment, AWS Countdown Premium is built for exactly that kind of planning.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A coding agent in Docker Sandboxes runs inside an isolated VM, the sandbox controls which hosts it can reach, and credentials stay on the host behind a proxy. The same controls keep the agent from opening a docs page, reading a changelog, or looking up an API that shipped after its training cutoff, so it writes code against the version it remembers. The usual fix is to widen the allowlist until the agent can fetch anything, which hands back most of what the sandbox took away.

The Firecrawl kit gives the agent web search, page scraping, and site crawling through one added host, api.firecrawl.dev, and every page comes back as clean markdown.

The Firecrawl kit is a mixin (kind: mixin): it extends whichever workload you already run rather than defining a new sandbox. Its descriptor, firecrawl/firecrawl.yaml, declares four typed capabilities:.

It has been revealed that the kit adds to the sandbox’s allowlist and does not narrow it, so everything else is set by your global sbx policy. Docker’s balanced preset allows package registries, GitHub, and a curated list of vendor domains, and returns a 403 for general websites, including most documentation sites, so Firecrawl is the agent’s route to those. Under deny-all, it is the agent’s only web host.

Kits are experimental and in Early Access, so the kit format and sbx commands may change. The steps below are current for October 2026; the repository README carries the latest.

Kit: docker.io/firecrawl/sbx-kit-firecrawl:1.0.0 on Docker Hub, for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64. Source: github.com/firecrawl/firecrawl-docker-sandbox.

According to recent reports, 1. Store the key once on the host. The command prompts for the key. Service secrets are global by default, so every sandbox that requests the firecrawl service can use it once you approve. The kit never sees the value; the proxy injects it at request time.

2. Start a sandbox with the kit. The kit is an ordinary OCI image with its descriptor in the manifest, so a version tag is all you need. Each --kit adds a mixin to the workload, and the trailing . mounts your project directory.

On the first run, sbx asks you to approve sending the firecrawl credential to api.firecrawl.dev. Accept the defaults. The credential is required: with no secret stored, sbx refuses to create the sandbox instead of letting the agent hit a 401 mid-task. A detached or CI run cannot answer the approval prompt, so approve interactively once or write the binding to ~/.config/sbx/credentials.yaml first.

Industry observers note that 3. Give the agent a task that needs the live web. Documentation sites are blocked under balanced, so this one has to go through Firecrawl.

Recent findings suggest that the kit’s instructions tell the agent to scrape blocked hosts through Firecrawl, so it calls fc.scrape(...) unprompted. Its response, trimmed:.

4. Verify each layer. In the same session, ! runs shell commands inside the sandbox.

It has been revealed that expected: FIRECRAWL_API_KEY=proxy-managed. A real fc-... value here means the key came from somewhere other than the kit.

Sources indicate that expected: the page as markdown, starting with # Changelog and the latest version heading. The same URL returns a 403 to curl from inside the sandbox, so output here proves the SDK, the credential, and the network rule at once.

Industry observers note that the kit also describes itself inside the sandbox. This prints the published descriptor, and the agent instructions sit next to it as firecrawl-context.md:.

Recent findings suggest that running from source. To review or modify the kit before you run it, clone the repository and point --kit at the firecrawl/ directory; sbx builds source kits on demand:.

With the kit installed, the agent can look things up on the web while it works. The sandbox only needs to talk to one newly introduced address, api.firecrawl.dev, and Firecrawl fetches the pages for it. This matters because the default balanced policy blocks most documentation sites. Without the kit, you’d have to allow each site one by one, and every new site you allow makes the sandbox a little less locked down.

In a recent development, without the kit, you had a choice to make. The default balanced policy blocks most documentation sites, so you could either leave the agent working from what it remembered, or allow sites one by one and loosen the sandbox a little each time. The kit avoids that choice. Your Firecrawl API key stays on your machine, behind the proxy, and the agent still reads the web as it is today.

The result is fewer made-up APIs, fewer failed upgrades, and less time spent correcting an agent that was confidently out of date.

In a recent development, the kit is published under the firecrawl organization on Docker Hub as firecrawl/sbx-kit-firecrawl, with source, changelog, and CI on GitHub under Apache-2.0. The SDK pin is verified against PyPI’s package hashes at install time, and every release passes Docker’s kit-tck conformance suite in CI. Review the descriptor and allowlist before running it, as with any kit.

According to recent reports, pull the kit from Docker Hub: hub.docker.com/r/firecrawl/sbx-kit-firecrawl. Challenges and feature requests go to the GitHub repository.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that reinforcement learning (RL) for large language models is notoriously sensitive to numerical instability: even tiny discrepancies between rollout generation and gradient updates can destabilize training or stall convergence.
  • Industry observers note that in practice, production RL stacks run sampling and training through separate, specialized execution paths.
  • Our zero train–inference mismatch (Zero-TIM) implementation, developed in Tunix and verified at multi-host scale across 64 TPU v5p chips (DP8×TP8), closes this numerical gap.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that reinforcement learning (RL) for large language models is notoriously sensitive to numerical instability: even tiny discrepancies between rollout generation and gradient updates can destabilize training or stall convergence. In LLM RL, the model serves as the policy, π(action | previous tokens), and true on-policy learning requires every action in an patch to be generated and evaluated by that exact same policy. While a synchronous loop ensures each rollout batch is scored using the same weights that generated it, a critical numerical requirement remains: the sampler and trainer must evaluate that policy identically.

Industry observers note that in practice, production RL stacks run sampling and training through separate, specialized execution paths. The sampler chooses each action token during incremental decoding and records its behavior logprob. The trainer evaluates the same token in batched forward-backward passes to compute its current logprob and gradients. Under the same weights, these differing execution paths can still assign different logprobs to the same token and context. The training schedule is on-policy, but the numerical execution has introduced a hidden off-policy gap that compounds over multi-turn trajectories.

Our zero train–inference mismatch (Zero-TIM) implementation, developed in Tunix and verified at multi-host scale across 64 TPU v5p chips (DP8×TP8), closes this numerical gap. At the same weights, the sampler and trainer assign bitwise-identical logprobs to the same action and token history—bringing state-of-the-art, true on-policy stability to TPU RL training.

A reduction is a tree of floating-point additions. Floating-point addition is not associative, so changing the tree changes where rounding occurs. The effect is easier to expose in bfloat16, which retains less precision than float32.

  • TL;DR: Granite 4.2 is our first family of dense, decoder-only reasoning LLMs, released in three sizes: 3B, 8B, and 30B.
  • Granite 4.2 is the reasoning-focused release of the Granite language-model family.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A technical walkthrough of how we built the Granite 4.2 reasoning model family.

TL;DR: Granite 4.2 is our first family of dense, decoder-only reasoning LLMs, released in three sizes: 3B, 8B, and 30B. These models are post-trained from Granite-4.1 base models. Granite-4.1 base models were pre-trained from scratch on roughly 15T tokens with a five-phase strategy that extends the context window to 512K tokens, supervised fine-tuned on chain-of-thought, reasoning, and agentic-trajectory data, then post-trained with a multi-stage reinforcement learning pipeline. That pipeline includes agentic RL, where the 8B and 30B models learn to act with tools inside real sandboxed environments. Every model has a thinking / non-thinking switch, a low-effort thinking mode that spends a short reasoning budget on easy questions, and native tool calling. All Granite 4.2 models are released under the Apache 2.0 license.

Granite 4.2 is the reasoning-focused release of the Granite language-model family. Earlier Granite releases were strong instruction-following assistants; Granite 4.2 adds explicit reasoning. Every model can produce a chain of thought before its answer and can run in thinking or non-thinking mode depending on how much deliberation a task needs. A low-effort mode falls between the two, spending a short reasoning budget on easy questions.

The three sizes (3B, 8B, and 30B) share the same architectural design and follow the same training pipeline (base model, SFT, then multi-stage RL), each at its own scale. All three are strong reasoners and instruction followers. The clearest capability split indicates up in post-training. The 8B and 30B models additionally go through an agentic RL block that teaches them to operate as agents: calling tools, editing and running code, driving a terminal, and searching the web inside real environments. Every model supports native tool calling. Served through an OpenAI-compatible endpoint (for example, with vLLM), it emits tool calls in the OpenAI function-calling format and plugs into agentic harnesses without extra glue. Granite 4.2 is also supported in SGLang, see the SGLang cookbook for a ready-to-serve recipe.

The rest of this post walks through the build: architecture, pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, the multi-stage RL pipeline, and results.

Granite 4.2 models are built on a decoder-only dense transformer architecture with the following core components:.

Granite 4.2 models are post-trained from Granite-4.1 base models. Granite-4.1 base models were trained from scratch on approximately 15 trillion tokens using a five-phase training strategy. Phases 1–2 focus on foundational pre-training, phases 3–4 perform mid-training with progressively higher-quality data annealing, and phase 5 introduces long-context training, extending the context window to 512K tokens. Each phase uses a distinct data mixture and learning-rate schedule, gradually shifting from broad web-scale data toward more curated, high-quality sources.

The pre-training recipe closely follows the previous generation; for a detailed treatment of the data blend, phase schedule, and long-context extension, see the Granite 4.1 blog.

Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) turns the base model into a reliable instruction-following, reasoning, and tool-using assistant. The SFT data mixture combines agentic (31.6%) and non-agentic (68.4%) data, totaling approximately 7.2 million samples, or roughly 100B tokens, of which about 65B are trainable.

The agentic corpus covers a broad range of domains, including software engineering (SWE, 69%), tool calling (12.1%), terminal use (8.0%), math (3.5%), search (0.8%), and action (0.2%). These samples and trajectories are generated using a diverse set of agent scaffolds and harnesses, including OpenHands, OpenCode, Terminus-2, SWE-agent, OpenResearcher, MiniSWE, OpenSeeker, EnvScaler, Gemini CLI, Hermes, Codex, and Goose. The agentic data combines samples from both open-source datasets and our own synthetically generated RL environments, spanning a variety of agent–harness combinations.

The non-agentic corpus consists of several major categories: instruction following (18.8%), coding (18.8%), math (14.6%), multilingual (7.0%), science (5.4%), reasoning (3.0%), and safety (0.8%).

Recent findings suggest that we apply multiple stages of quality control before a sample enters the final SFT mixture. First, data from different sources is normalized and reformatted into a consistent OpenAI Chat format, making the conversation structure and tool interactions uniform across datasets and scaffolds.

Sources indicate that we then use GPT-OSS-120B and Gemma 4 as LLM-based judges to assess sample quality. Low-scoring samples are removed, as are samples containing hallucinated or fabricated information, invalid tool interactions, or tool calls to functions that are not defined in the corresponding tool list. Several targeted, dataset-specific heuristic rules are also applied where appropriate to further improve quality and remove known sources of noise.

Finally, we perform both local and global deduplication. Deduplication is based on SHA-256 hashes computed over the combination of the tools and messages fields, removing duplicate samples both within individual data sources and across the overall SFT mixture.

According to recent reports, the complete corpus is first globally shuffled to reduce ordering effects and ensure that samples from different domains are well mixed during training. The shuffled corpus is then partitioned into equally sized .parquet shards, which are tokenized using the model's tokenizer and chat template and prepared for large-scale distributed training.

Before launching the final large-scale runs, we tune hyperparameters on representative configurations, sweeping learning-rate schedules, initial learning rates, and warm-up ratios to find settings that train stably across model sizes. The final training configuration is summarized below:.

For the 30B model, we additionally perform a second phase of SFT focused specifically on agentic coding. In this phase, agentic, SWE, and coding data are upsampled to increase their effective contribution to the training distribution, while approximately 16% of the mixture is retained as replay data from the original SFT corpus.

The 30B model is then fine-tuned for roughly one additional epoch at a lower learning rate of 3.0e-6. This targeted second phase increases the model's exposure to agentic coding trajectories without discarding the capabilities acquired during the initial SFT phase.

Recent findings suggest that after SFT, we apply a multi-stage, multi-environment reinforcement learning pipeline. Rather than a single RL pass, we run a chain of focused stages spanning many environments: math, code, science, instruction following, tool use, and structured output, then software engineering, terminal use, and web search. Each stage is an independent RL run that targets one capability and warm-starts from the previous stage's checkpoint.

Figure 1. The staged RL curriculum. Foundational RL (verifiable rewards + skill boosters) runs for all sizes; the agentic RL block (SWE → Terminal → Search) runs for 8B and 30B only. Every model finishes with RLHF. Each stage is a separate GRPO run that warm-starts from the previous checkpoint.

Every stage trains with asynchronous GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization), so the generator and trainer halves of the loop never block on each other. A pool of generation workers keeps sampling responses and dropping the finished trajectories into a shared buffer; once the buffer holds a full step's worth, the trainer pulls that batch, takes an optimizer step, and streams the updated parameters back to the generator workers without pausing them. A refresh can land partway through a rollout, leaving a single trajectory stitched together from two adjacent policy versions. We allow this instead of paying to prevent it: the workers reuse their existing KV cache rather than rebuilding it after each refresh, and the one guardrail is a limit that keeps them from drifting more than a single upgrade behind the trainer, which bounds how off-policy any sample can get. Whatever mismatch survives that limit is handled in the objective by truncated importance sampling, which clamps the train-versus-generation log-probability ratio to a fixed ceiling so a handful of stale tokens cannot dominate an update.

It has been revealed that advantages are group-relative with a leave-one-out baseline: each response is judged against the mean reward of the other samples drawn for the same prompt, which removes the need for a separate value network. To make this concrete, take RLVR, the first and longest-running stage: each step pairs 256 prompts with 16 sampled responses apiece for a 4,096-example batch, which the trainer consumes in a single optimizer step before the next rollout begins. Later stages keep this machinery unchanged and adjust only the per-stage shape, shown next.

Industry observers note that the pipeline keeps a common backbone of hyperparameters across every stage, which makes the curriculum easier to run and compare. A handful of knobs are fixed everywhere:.

What changes from stage to stage is the shape of each run: how many prompts and generations per step, how long the context is, whether the agent loop runs, and how hard we pull back toward the reference policy. The table below gives the exact settings for the 30B chain, stage by stage:.

Parameters shown for the 30B model. Global batch size = prompts/step × generations/prompt (e.g. 256 × 16 = 4096 for RLVR). The 3B and 8B models use the same recipe and hyperparameters with fewer stages (see How the Three Sizes Differ); the stage list is what changes, not the knobs.

According to recent reports, the KL schedule follows the reward type: explore freely where the reward is objective and verifiable (RLVR and SWE 2 run at KL 0), and stay close to the reference where the objective is preference, safety, or a narrow skill graft (RLHF and the code booster use KL 0.05). The rollout-turns column counts the environment interactions GRPO itself sees per rollout. In every case the model is trained on complete, real-environment trajectories.

Each stage is a separate RL run with a single objective and its own reward signal. When it finishes, its policy is exported to Hugging Face format and becomes the base model for the next stage, so the pipeline is a sequence of warm-starts:.

It has been revealed that the 8B and 30B models follow the full ladder. The 3B model takes a shortened path: foundational RL and alignment, without the agentic block.

A stage is defined mostly by how it is rewarded. Across the pipeline there are three reward types, and a single stage can use more than one:.

It has been revealed that verifiable rewards are objective and hard to game, so the pipeline front-loads them. Judge- and preference-based rewards handle open-ended qualities that no checker can express. Agentic-outcome rewards are the sparsest: often a single bit at the end of a long tool-use trajectory.

RLVR is the foundational stage and the broadest data mix in the pipeline: a single blended dataset spanning many verifiable domains.

Each task type carries its own verifier, so the reward is grounded per example. RLVR runs for two rounds on 3B and 8B, and three on 30B. Each round is a fresh warm-started run on a re-weighted mix of public and internally curated RL data.

After RLVR, a few short booster stages sharpen specific capabilities that benefit from concentrated training focusing on the following domains:.

Boosters are small, focused runs. A light KL penalty keeps the model close to its current behavior while nudging one skill.

It has been revealed that in the agentic stages the model learns to act: call tools, observe results, and iterate inside a real environment, rewarded on whether the task was actually solved. These stages share the same shape: multi-turn tool use, real (not simulated) environments, sparse outcome rewards, and GRPO, warm-started from the coding-boosted checkpoint. They run in order: SWE → Terminal → Search.

Sources indicate that figure 2. The three agentic-RL environments. Each pairs a real harness with a real environment and a sparse, outcome-based reward. The 3B model runs none of these.

The final stage of every model is RLHF for human preference and safety. It optimizes against a generative reward model (GenRM) for preference, plus a safety reward covering jailbreak resistance and appropriate refusals. This stage uses the highest KL penalty in the pipeline, aligning tone and safety without eroding the capabilities the earlier stages built. In addition to human preference and safety alignment, this stage also applies a reasoning-length penalty to discourage overly verbose reasoning behavior acquired during earlier stages.

Same method and infrastructure; the difference is how far up the ladder each model goes.

3B is a strong foundational-RL model; 8B and 30B add the agentic-RL block on top, learning to act with tools in real environments.

It has been revealed that reinforcement learning at this scale needs infrastructure that can drive a training loop and a fleet of live environments at the same time. This matters most in the agentic stages, where every training example is a multi-turn rollout that edits code, runs commands, or browses the web. Granite 4.2's RL runs on two open components: NeMo-RL on the training side and NeMo-Gym on the rollout side.

Figure 3. The RL system. NeMo-RL drives the GRPO loop (Megatron-Core training backend, vLLM generation, and Megatron-Bridge for HF⇄Megatron weight conversion). NeMo-Gym orchestrates rollouts and hosts the tools, sandboxes, and reward/verifier calls as pluggable Resources.

That uniformity is what makes the staged curriculum above practical: a booster's rule-based checker and a full SWE sandbox present the same interface to GRPO.

This split is also what makes the asynchronous training loop described above physically possible: generation and policy updates live on separate GPU pools, so the expensive generation fleet — including the live agentic environments — stays busy instead of idling through optimizer steps.

Granite 4.2 was evaluated across agentic coding, general agentic and tool use, reasoning, chat and instruction following, and long context. The full benchmark table is below, followed by charts that break out the headline results by model size.

Supported languages: English, German, Spanish, French, Japanese, Portuguese, Arabic, Czech, Italian, Korean, Dutch, and Chinese.

The charts below break these results out by capability area.

It has been revealed that figure 4. Reasoning (pass@1). Scores rise consistently with model size across math (AIME25, HMMT), science (GPQA), and code reasoning (LiveCodeBench, SciCode).

According to recent reports, figure 5. Agentic coding resolve rates. The agentic-RL block is trained only for 8B and 30B; the 30B model leads across SWE-Bench variants and Terminal-Bench.

Figure 6. General agentic and tool-use benchmarks, reported for all three sizes.

Recent findings suggest that we also released four quantized variants of the Granite 4.2 models for inference with vLLM. The models are converted to FP8, NVFP4, and MXFP4 using LLM Compressor, and to the GGUF format using the llama.cpp framework for reduced-memory deployment.

The FP8 version is quantized with dynamic per-channel weights and per-token activations. No calibration is used.

The NVFP4 and MXFP4 versions are quantized using GPTQ calibrated on 2K samples drawn from the SFT dataset. Max context length is 2K during calibration.

Conversion of the Granite 4.2 models to GGUF is done with the canonical llama.cpp tool as described in https://github.com/IBM/gguf#gguf-conversion--quantization.

Several GGUF formats are provided:.

We trained the Granite 4.2 language models on an NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 cluster hosted by CoreWeave, featuring:.

This infrastructure delivers the high-bandwidth, low-latency communication required for efficient large-scale distributed training.

According to recent reports, the training software stack is packaged into .sqsh container images, each giving a run a reproducible, portable environment with its SBSA-compatible CUDA targets, Linux aarch64 Python wheels, and GPU-specific binaries pinned. The large-scale SFT runs build on an NGC PyTorch base image (Ubuntu 22.04, CUDA 12.8, Python 3.12); the RL stack runs in its own NeMo-RL container.

Sources indicate that granite models support tool calling with integrated reasoning: the model reasons about which tool to call and why before calling it. Tools are defined with the OpenAI function definition schema.

Granite models can serve as the backbone for agentic coding tools. Because they support reasoning and tool calling through the OpenAI-compatible API, they integrate with popular agentic harnesses without extra adapters. Start the vLLM server, then follow the harness-specific instructions below.

OpenCode is an AI coding agent that runs in your terminal.

Configure ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json:.

For full documentation, see opencode.ai/docs.

Pi is a minimal agent harness for AI-powered coding that runs in your terminal. It supports custom providers via a models.json configuration file.

Configure ~/.pi/agent/models.json:.

Then select the granite-4.2-30b model with /model or Ctrl+L in the interactive session.

For full documentation, see pi.dev/docs.

OpenHands is an AI software engineer that can plan, write code, and execute commands.

Install and launch OpenHands following the official installation guide.

Configure the LLM in the OpenHands settings with:.

Note: The openai/ prefix is required when connecting to OpenAI-compatible endpoints like vLLM. Refer to the OpenHands local LLM documentation for detailed setup instructions, troubleshooting, and alternative installation methods.

Tech Report: Cyber insurers now want proof you can actually recover

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (863 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • PARTNER CONTENT: As carriers tighten underwriting, a backup job marked green is no longer enough.
  • It has been revealed that cyber insurance pricing has cooled.
  • Part of the reason rates are lowering is because carriers are imposing stricter requirements that determine if you will qualify at all.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

PARTNER CONTENT: As carriers tighten underwriting, a backup job marked green is no longer enough. Here’s the evidence underwriters expect.

It has been revealed that cyber insurance pricing has cooled. Marsh’s Global Insurance Market Index reveals global cyber rates falling for a 13th consecutive quarter, with US rates recently stabilizing after the ransomware-driven spikes of 2020 and 2021.

Part of the reason rates are lowering is because carriers are imposing stricter requirements that determine if you will qualify at all. A major global carrier recently stopped writing law firms altogether because of claims volume, and brokers expect healthcare and managed service providers (MSPs) to be next.

The newest requirement is the one many MSPs are least ready for: proof that you can actually recover. This is what insurers really want to see, and meeting the bar is harder than it sounds.

In a recent webinar with cyber insurance provider Beltex, the familiar list of requirements came up first:.

Multifactor authentication (MFA) on external access and privileged accounts.

Endpoint detection and response (EDR) on every endpoint.

A staffed 24/7 team where managed detection and response (MDR) is required, and timely patching.

According to recent reports, backup is now joining that list, and for good reason. For years it was assumed that having backups and a green job status was good enough. Claims have shown otherwise.

It has been revealed that now, attackers go after backup infrastructure to make their ransomware more effective, and an untested restore can re-infect the production network. Beltex described an MSP that restored a client directly from backup without involving the insurer. The attackers were still in the environment, and the ransom reportedly doubled.

So, carriers are asking for proof. Some want evidence of a successful restore within the last six months, and some insurance applications must be signed by a C-level executive rather than the IT director to put ownership behind it.

Being able to recover is only half the question, because time is where claim costs balloon. Insurers, it turns out, don’t object to paying claims. They object to paying major ones.

According to recent reports, beltex’s favorite example involved an 85-person firm hit through a zero-day firewall flaw. Their MDR solution contained the intrusion in about 20 minutes, forensics confirmed two servers were touched, and clean backups had the firm fully functional within 36 hours. The claim came in at around $85,000.

Sources indicate that compare that with downtime and business interruption: a firm billing $10,000 a day that is offline for a week loses $70,000 in income before recovery costs and claim submission. Yet large servers can take four to 24 hours to restore. That is why underwriters care how fast you can come back and how successfully.

It has been revealed that speed raises a second problem: where do you restore to? Breach counsel treats the first 72 hours as the most critical window, and incident response (IR) teams need to isolate and investigate infected systems during it.

It has been revealed that restoring into production too early risks reintroducing the threat and disturbing the evidence investigators need. Waiting for a safe place has the clock running. Recovery that is fast but not safe doesn’t satisfy anyone.

Put the pieces together and the bar is high:.

Backups you have actually tested.

Recovery times you can state and meet.

And a clean, separate place to recover to.

Underwriters want to know whether you exercised reasonable care, so a row of green checkmarks won’t do. Run a test restore. Confirm you’re protecting everything that matters, including the server someone labeled “not in production.” Have the business owner, not just IT, confirm the right systems came back within agreed recovery time objectives (RTO) and recovery point objectives (RPO), and keep the logs, screenshots and sign-off in your ticketing system. It doesn’t need to resemble a government audit; Beltex noted that this alone puts you ahead of most organizations.

Cloud-native disaster recovery changes the equation. Cove’s DRaaS solution lets teams stage a pre-recovered VM in the N-able cloud that can be failed over to in about 15 minutes, off the production network. That answers the speed question and the location question together. Forensic investigators can validate and hunt in the sandbox while the business keeps moving, with rollback to earlier points in time. Once everyone agrees the recovery point is clean, workloads can run from the cloud over VPN, and failback uses recovery agents to bring changes home.

According to recent reports, insurance is a financial failsafe, not a substitute for a bad data protection posture. Start by listing what the business couldn’t lose for 72 hours, set recovery targets, test them and document the results. Check the policy itself: a standalone cyber policy rather than a small add-on to a general one, with a limit of at least $1 million, and $2 million as the business scales. And if an incident does hit, disconnect affected machines from the network rather than powering them off, so forensic data survives.

N-able Cove Data Protection, recognized as a Champion in the Infotech 2026 Enterprise Backup Data Quadrant, provides cloud-native data protection for organizations. Learn more at n-able.com/products/cove-data-protection.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that developers building web and AI applications on Vercel can now add Amazon S3 storage resources directly from the Vercel Marketplace and v0, combining the durability, scalability, and performance of S3 with the convenience of Vercel’s provisioning workflow. Starting today, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), including Amazon S3 Tables and Amazon S3 Vectors, is natively available on the Vercel Marketplace and v0 by Vercel, covering three distinct workloads: everyday storage, analytics, and AI.

Industry observers note that why this matters Millions of developers build, deploy, and scale web and AI applications on Vercel. Storage is essential to performant applications, but provisioning it previously required navigating to the AWS Management Console to configure policies and credentials. Now, S3 storage integrates directly into the Vercel developer experience, with resource provisioning and connection configuration handled automatically. Together with existing integrations for Amazon Aurora, Amazon DynamoDB, and Amazon OpenSearch Serverless, you get a complete application stack inside Vercel (from your database layer through to object, vector, and open table storage), all on one AWS account with one bill.

Figure 1 – The AWS page on the Vercel Marketplace.

Industry observers note that getting started From the Vercel dashboard, go to the Storage tab and choose Create. Select AWS, pick your S3 bucket type, choose a Region, and create the bucket. Provisioning takes a few seconds.

Figure 2 – Creating an Amazon S3 general purpose bucket in Vercel by choosing a Region and a name.

Connect the bucket to a project, then pull the environment variables with the Vercel CLI:.

Sources indicate that the integration injects AWS_REGION, AWS_ROLE_ARN, AWS_RESOURCE_ARN, and a bucket name such as S3_BUCKET_NAME, S3_TABLE_BUCKET_NAME, or S3_VECTOR_BUCKET_NAME. At runtime, the awsCredentialsProvider from @vercel/functions/oidc exchanges a short-lived OIDC token with AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) for temporary credentials scoped to your resource. No static keys are stored anywhere.

Object storage with S3 This Next.js route uploads a file to a general purpose bucket:.

Use ListObjectsV2Command and GetObjectCommand with the same client to list and read objects.

In a recent development, analytics with S3 Tables S3 Tables offer S3 storage purpose-built for analytics and are designed to automatically optimize query performance as data volumes grow. They provide fully managed Apache Iceberg tables with automated table maintenance and compaction, and they work with any Apache Iceberg REST Catalog-compliant engine. You can use DuckDB inside a Vercel Function for lightweight queries. This example attaches the table bucket by its ARN and runs an aggregate query:.

If you run DuckDB inside a Next.js route, add @duckdb/node-api to serverExternalPackages in next.config.mjs so the native bindings are not bundled.

In a recent development, vector search with S3 Vectors S3 Vectors deliver purpose-built, cost-optimized vector storage for AI agents, AI inference, and semantic search of your content stored in Amazon S3. S3 Vectors provides native support for storing and querying vectors without a separate vector database, but it does not generate them. Create the embeddings with your model of choice, then query the index for the closest matches:.

Building with v0 by Vercel From v0, describe what you want to build and it provisions the right resource. Ask for “a photo gallery where consumers upload images using AWS” to get a general purpose bucket, “a support bot that answers questions from my PDFs” to get S3 Vectors, or “an analytics dashboard for my clickstream data” to get S3 Tables. v0 then configures the connection and generates working code.

Figure 3 – v0 generating a PDF support bot from a natural language prompt, with Amazon S3 Vectors connected and the application in the Preview panel.

According to recent reports, combining S3 with AWS databases Every AWS service on Vercel shares the same account and authentication model, so you can combine them with no extra setup. For example, store file metadata in Aurora with the files in S3, or store document text in DynamoDB with embeddings in S3 Vectors for RAG retrieval.

According to recent reports, using Vercel with your AWS account You can create a new AWS account through the integration, which supports S3 features for building and testing. You can also link an existing AWS account to use your full set of S3 and AWS capabilities and keep your current billing. If you link an existing AWS account, Vercel works only with new buckets that you create through the platform. Because every S3 resource lives in your own AWS account, you keep AWS-native tooling and a single place to manage storage.

Recent findings suggest that pricing and availability There is no charge for the integration, and you pay standard Amazon S3 pricing for the resources you use. New AWS accounts created through Vercel receive $100 in credits valid for six months. Amazon S3, including S3 Tables and S3 Vectors, is available from v0 and the Vercel Marketplace in all commercial AWS Regions supported by Vercel. To get started, visit v0 or the AWS page on the Vercel Marketplace.

Recent findings suggest that join the conversation If you want to call APIs, search documentation, find regional availability, and check troubleshooting about this upcoming feature, try using the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI tool. 💡 Key Takeaways
