GitHub availability report: October 2026

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2045 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Github

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We continue to share monthly updates on the work behind GitHub’s availability and reliability.
  • Industry observers note that the short version of October: we added substantial independently scalable Azure capacity and removed several ways that failures could escalate.
  • As of November 9, 140 of 151 production services and 32 of 50 MySQL primaries were running in Azure Central US.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We continue to share monthly updates on the work behind GitHub’s availability and reliability.

Industry observers note that the short version of October: we added substantial independently scalable Azure capacity and removed several ways that failures could escalate. However, write outages, monitoring gaps during data migrations, and a regional network disruption reinforced the need for capacity growth to be paired with safer operations, stronger isolation, and validated regional recovery.

As of November 9, 140 of 151 production services and 32 of 50 MySQL primaries were running in Azure Central US. Azure served 63% of migrated-service reads, 66% of monolith reads, and 52% of Git reads. We also completed a compute expansion across all nine Central US Kubernetes clusters, more than doubling capacity.

Sources indicate that that capacity is already carrying real growth. Migrated-service traffic has increased 82% since March, with Central US absorbing the growth beyond the highest weekly-average load previously served from our existing datacenter. This gives GitHub more room to grow without pushing the original environment beyond its prior operating range.

Recent findings suggest that we also made several targeted reliability improvements. Actions changes increased capacity for critical Azure control-plane requests. A separate NAT-gateway mitigation reduced usage by 85%; four production jobs failed during the change, compared with approximately 800 expected without the mitigation. Connection limits and other client improvements now also reduce the chance that a dependency interruption becomes a broader reconnect storm.

We removed concentrated sources of database load as well. A high-traffic GitHub Actions endpoint handling more than 250 million requests per day moved to a more efficient service path, reducing peak database reads by 85%. Requiring at least three characters before searching repository topics reduced slow or terminated queries for that pattern by approximately 98%.

In a recent development, reliability was still not where it needed to be. The October 7 write outages exposed an unsafe interaction between database orchestration and production routing. An October 29 Azure network disruption affected all three Central US availability zones and at least 34,128 signed-in people. More details on these and other incidents follow.

The East US 3 buildout is about one week behind blueprint. The next phase starts with its first validated traffic ramp in the first week of December, while we continue hardening migration safety, dependency isolation, and regional recovery.

The principle remains the same: availability, then capacity, then features.

Duration: approximately 3 hours and 45 minutes.

Customers may have seen GitHub Actions jobs on GitHub-hosted runners stay queued much longer than usual, and some workflow runs failed to start. During the worst stretch, which lasted about 90 minutes, most jobs on GitHub-hosted runners did not start within five minutes. Impact eased as we failed over to healthy regions and added capacity. Self-hosted runners were not affected. GitHub Pages sites that build with actions were slow to enhancement, though existing sites continued to serve normally. Some customers also saw errors in repository lists, licensing and billing pages, and some Copilot features.

Sources indicate that actions jobs stayed queued or failed to start because the service that assigns jobs to GitHub-hosted runners stopped working reliably. A partial networking failure on our cloud provider’s side disrupted some of the connections between one of our datacenter regions and the cloud-hosted databases that service depends on. Instead of failing fast, the service waited for those calls to time out. The waiting calls piled up until the service ran out of memory and restarted.

According to recent reports, jobs then shifted to the same service in a healthy region, which did not have enough capacity for the extra demand and began failing too. At the same time, runners that went several minutes without receiving a job shut down and were slow to be replaced, so fewer runners were available to pick up jobs.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 6 minutes of failed or slow requests across github.com, followed by approximately 3 hours and 30 minutes during which enterprise migrations were paused.

Customers may have seen server errors or slow responses when signing in, working with repositories and pull requests, calling the API, or using GitHub Codespaces. Retrying a short time later would have succeeded, and delayed webhook deliveries caught up soon after. At the peak, about 1.3% of all requests failed or timed out, and about 6.4K organizations saw at least one failed or slow request.

Migrations were paused for customers using GitHub Enterprise Importer, and were resumed once a fix was deployed.

A surge in migration activity caused GitHub Enterprise Importer to send a burst of very large queries to a shared database. These queries took much longer than usual and, together with normal traffic, used all of the database’s available connections, preventing other github.com features relying on the same database from completing their requests.

It has been revealed that the importer did not reduce its load when the database became overloaded. The impact ended within minutes, once the importer finished its queued queries and the database’s connections were released.

To prevent a recurrence, we paused migrations until we deployed a mitigation that runs these queries in smaller batches.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: two separate write outages lasted approximately 10 minutes and 9 minutes, totaling about 19 minutes. The second was a recurrence of the first, with the same cause.

Sources indicate that customers may have seen errors when pushing code, signing in, updating pull requests or challenges, or making changes through the API. Webhooks, GitHub Apps and OAuth, actions, code scanning, codespaces, and Copilot were also affected. Viewing content was largely unaffected. Data that was already saved was not lost, and actions that failed during the outages succeeded when retried after recovery.

It has been revealed that web and API request failures peaked at 8.9% in the first outage and 9.3% in the second, affecting more than 12,000 and more than 11,000 organizations, respectively. Some organizations may have been affected by both outages.

During regular maintenance, we replaced machines that manage where database writes are sent. One upcoming machine started with outdated records that still listed retired database servers. Once it was automatically elected leader, it published routing settings that sent writes for several core databases to those retired servers. Incorrect settings passed our existing validation and took effect immediately. Later, an automated maintenance task did not honor a pause on maintenance and triggered another election, and because the new machine had not yet been removed, it became leader again.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 1 hour and 28 minutes.

Customers may have seen delays in GitHub Actions workflow status updates, logs, and checks. About 5% of jobs on GitHub-hosted runners experienced delayed starts, a very small share of workflow runs failed, and some requests to the actions jobs REST API returned errors. GitHub Pages deployments and workflow and check webhook events generated by actions runs were also delayed. For part of this time, live updates on github.com and code search were degraded.

An internal actions service that stores workflow logs and run status lost connections to some of its cache servers in one cloud region. Every server running that service then retried those connections at the same time. Together, those retries saturated the network connections between GitHub’s data center and that region, disrupting other services that use the same link.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 6 hours and 46 minutes.

In a recent development, customers may have seen delays in pull request updates, GitHub Actions workflow status updates, and webhook deliveries. After a push, latest commits were slow to appear on pull requests. Workflows triggered by the push started late. Status checks from actions workflows could look stuck on pull requests, which held up merges that require those checks to pass. These features recovered within about 2 to 3.5 hours.

Industry observers note that audit log events were affected the longest. Recent activity took longer to appear when customers searched their audit logs, with delays of up to 1 hour and 50 minutes. Audit log events were fully caught up after about 6 hours and 46 minutes.

Some webhook deliveries from this period may be missing from webhook delivery history, though the webhooks themselves were delivered.

Some servers in our event streaming platform were close to their memory limits, and memory use on these servers grows with the number of client connections. When requests to these servers failed, new connections were opened immediately, which increased the number of connections and the memory they used. The increase in memory use slowed down and overloaded the servers.

We took the overloaded servers out of service, and their traffic moved to other servers. Those servers then became overloaded too, and the problem spread to more servers over the following hour. We began rebalancing overloaded partitions onto brokers that had available capacity and this mitigated the concern.

Audit logs took the longest to recover. The service that writes audit log events kept restarting on errors from the platform for more than two hours and fell further behind. Once stabilized, it could only write events at a limited rate, so the backlog took several more hours to clear.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 1 hour and 32 minutes.

Customers may have seen errors when using several GPT-family models in Copilot. Requests using these models in Copilot Chat in IDEs and on github.com, the Copilot CLI, Copilot code review, and the Copilot coding agent returned errors or did not complete. About one in 10 requests to the affected models failed. Other models continued to work, and choosing another model avoided the errors. Auto model selection reduced the errors by sending some requests to an unaffected model.

Code scanning autofix and code quality, which are built on one specific model without an alternative model to switch to, were affected more heavily.

Recent findings suggest that copilot reaches these models through an upstream model provider and uses a credential to authenticate with that provider. That credential became invalid, the provider began rejecting our requests as unauthenticated, and our service returned those rejections to clients as authentication errors. Copilot features that use these models send their requests through that provider, so they began failing at the same time.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 9 minutes.

Customers may have seen some requests to github.com hang for up to about 10 seconds and then fail with a server error. Pull request merges and Git operations over SSH and Git LFS were hit hardest. At the worst point, about 43% of merge attempts failed, compared with about 3.5% of API calls. Complications, GitHub Pages, notifications, and sign-in for GitHub Apps and OAuth apps also saw intermittent errors.

According to recent reports, A database connection pool used by many github.com services reached its limit, and for several minutes no connections were available. Latest requests that needed a connection waited until the connection timeout expired and then failed.

Sources indicate that the pool was already running near capacity when some upgrade requests started holding their connections far longer than expected. Each one began writing a change, then ran a separate lookup that could take several seconds, keeping its connection reserved but unused the whole time. With little headroom, those held connections helped tip the pool over.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

In a recent development, follow our status page for real-time updates on status changes and post-incident recaps. To learn more about what we’re working on, check out the engineering section on the GitHub Blog.

Latest Update: GTA VI didn't break the internet, thanks to 'stupid DNS tricks'

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Multiple CDNs and routing users to nearby download sites kept traffic flowing for everyone.
  • Grand Theft Auto VI may put a dent in global productivity today but the game didn’t break the internet.
  • For those unfamiliar, GTA VI is the first fresh instalment of the mega-hit game in 13 years and it is nearly impossible to understate the excitement surrounding its release.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Multiple CDNs and routing users to nearby download sites kept traffic flowing for everyone.

Grand Theft Auto VI may put a dent in global productivity today but the game didn’t break the internet.

For those unfamiliar, GTA VI is the first fresh instalment of the mega-hit game in 13 years and it is nearly impossible to understate the excitement surrounding its release. Anecdotal evidence suggests fans of the game may today report they suddenly feel unfit to perform paid work.

Developer Rockstar Games allowed Xbox and PlayStation owners to pay for and download the 200GB-plus game on November 10, before play commenced on the 19th.

Millions took advantage of the chance to download the game, creating just the sort of internet traffic event that regional internet registry the Réseaux IP Européens Network Coordination Centre (RIPE NCC) can observe with its RIPE Atlas internet measurement network.

RIPE data scientist Emile Aben, with help from staffers Alun Davies and James Cowie, went looking for GTA-related traffic and found some interesting patterns.

Aben observed that traffic to PlayStations mostly came from content delivery networks operated by AWS and Fastly. Microsoft relied on Fastly for over half of traffic flowing to Xboxes and used Akamai too, but eschewed AWS's CloudFront.

The data scientist observed heavy use of “GeoDNS,” a technique that returns different IP addresses for a single domain request, depending on a user’s location. DNS’s designers didn’t intend that. Indeed, the RIPE trio point out that Paul Vixie, the computer scientist who earned his place in the Internet Hall of Fame for massive contributions to the DNS system, regarded things like GeoDNS as “stupid DNS tricks.”.

Whatever you think of GeoDNS, the RIPE researchers found that folks who were likely downloading GTA VI from Los Angeles, Tokyo, and Istanbul were each directed to different sites.

Their probe of a network in Shanghai, China, found “a very distinct long lookup-chain with a hostname that is associated with the Alibaba Cloud in the end that maps to six different IP addresses.”.

“This hints at specialised treatment for some countries/regions,” Aben wrote.

He also noted that Internet Exchange Points, the interconnect facilities that network operators use to exchange traffic and shorten paths, had to cope with record traffic during the download period – and seem to have handled the load.

Aben thinks the GTA VI download program offers a useful lesson.

According to recent reports, “DNS helps steer each player towards a download server, while multiple CDNs share the work of delivering the files,” he wrote. “That distribution matters beyond gaming. On the open Internet, game downloads share routers and link capacity with all kinds of other traffic, including critical services.”.

“Keeping downloads local helps leave capacity on long-distance links free for other uses, making that enormous demand manageable.” ®.

#46463. Tech Report: tokenizers v1: encode, decode and scaling, measured

📅 21 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1567 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: tokenizers v1: encode, decode and scaling, measured

📅 21 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1567 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the tokenizer has not historically been the bottleneck within ML workflows.
  • In a recent development, as models become faster and workloads scale, that balance begins to shift.
  • This is why we have chosen to heavily focus on performance for the upcoming version 1 of tokenizers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the tokenizer has not historically been the bottleneck within ML workflows. Compute-wise, tokenization is light compared to the heavy modeling happening in the rest of the pipeline. Yet, in some cases, it has rapidly become key to accelerating (or slowing down) your machine learning work.

In a recent development, as models become faster and workloads scale, that balance begins to shift. Training on massive datasets, serving many concurrent requests, or repeatedly processing long inputs can put enough pressure on the tokenizer that it starves the model of data.

This is why we have chosen to heavily focus on performance for the upcoming version 1 of tokenizers. Tokenization should be light and should scale with your workflow. Your GPUs should never sit idle waiting for the CPU to complete its tokenization.

In this article, we look at what makes v1 faster than v0.23, often by tens of times.

This work was entirely possible thanks to the rest of the ecosystem. Tokenization is a very active area of open source work, and libraries such as gigatoken, tiktoken, kitoken, tokie, fastokens, wordchipper and ai-tokenizer, as well as many others, have each pushed on what a fast tokenizer can be. We read that work, and several of the ideas below reached us because another project revealed they were worth trying.

Before this refactor, tokenizers was nowhere near the performance it could have had, so contributing to it may not have seemed worth it. With this refactor, we hope to make clear that we intend tokenizers to be a library worth contributing to.

We also thank IBM, NVIDIA, and the ExecuTorch team for contributing patches and helping us test across a wide range of hardware to broaden platform support.

We showcase results for the release candidate of tokenizers v1 against other widely used alternatives. We go over single-threaded, multi-threaded, scaling across threads, per-model comparison, per-language comparison, latency, decoding throughput, memory heap, as well as crate size.

We run this from the tokbench repository, and add a command to rerun the benchmarks on your hardware if you would like to do so.

v1 will produce the same token IDs as v0.23. The goal was to preserve the output, the API, the vocabulary and the merge ranks, and improve everything that can be improved. That includes breadth. The library stays general across tokenizer families rather than specialising on BPE, so v1 loads everything v0.23 loaded.

Recent findings suggest that A tokenizer converts text into the list of integers a model reads. tokenizers runs that conversion in four stages. Normalization applies operations such as lowercasing or Unicode normalization to the raw text. Pre-tokenization splits the text into smaller pieces called pre-tokens. The model turns each pre-token into tokens and maps them to IDs in its vocabulary. Post-processing adds any special tokens the model expects.

The model stage is where most of the work described here happens. Eight of the ten model families measured in this article use byte pair encoding, or BPE. BPE starts from the bytes of a pre-token and repeatedly joins the highest ranked adjacent pair until no ranked pair remains. The ranking is learned when the tokenizer is trained and ships with it, so the same text always produces the same IDs. A merge never crosses a pre-token boundary. The other two families use WordPiece and Unigram, the two other model types the library supports.

The tokenization pipeline page documents the four stages. Tokenization algorithms documents BPE, WordPiece and Unigram.

Sources indicate that each stage was worked on. These are the changes that mattered:.

Industry observers note that BPE models use a regular expression to split the input text into smaller, easier to process chunks called pre-tokens. Merges happen inside a pre-token and never across the boundary between two of them, so this split decides what the rest of the pipeline sees.

That regular expression is a fixed parameter of the model. It ships with the tokenizer and never changes at runtime, so there is no need for a general-purpose regex engine to interpret it on every encode. An equivalent splitting function can be written by hand, once, for the pattern a given model actually uses.

According to recent reports, A hand-written function can then use the SIMD instructions (single instruction, multiple data) of a modern CPU, which apply one operation to many bytes at once and suit UTF-8 text well. bitcannon views the input's bytes as parallel streams of bits, so boundaries fall out of boolean operations across whole registers instead of a scan that advances one character at a time. It decides 64 bytes per register operation. The same idea drives Parabix for text processing and simdjson for JSON.

This depends on recognising the pattern. A handful of grammars cover most byte-level BPE models, and a tokenizer whose pattern is not among them keeps the regex path and none of this speed-up. That is why the gains above vary as much as they do.

Real text contains many repeated words. Because BPE always produces the same token IDs for a given pre-token, v1 can save the result after processing it once. A thread-local cache maps each pre-token's bytes to its token IDs, allowing later occurrences to skip the merge process.

Recent findings suggest that naturally, as the input grows, the number of unique words can grow more slowly than the total number of words. Repeated words then account for an increasing share of the input. Fresh words still appear, which accounts for the occasional misses in the animation below.

Reproduce the shared-prefix result with:.

Caching works best when the input contains repeated pre-tokens. Input with few repeated pre-tokens can pay for lookups without receiving many hits.

Sources indicate that the next major cost comes from the BPE merge loop. For each pre-token, the loop repeatedly finds the highest-priority adjacent pair and merges it. The previous implementation allocated fresh memory for every call and built a new priority queue for every pre-token.

Industry observers note that v1 reuses a scratch buffer owned by the caller, removing those repeated allocations. It stores symbols in a flat array and links adjacent symbols by their positions in that array, which makes updates during merging cheaper. It also processes a batch of pre-tokens in a single model call.

Each candidate pair is also packed into a single 64-bit value, with the merge rank in the high bits. Comparing two candidates is then just comparing two integers, and "no merge here" is the largest possible value, so the loop finds its next merge without a branch.

It has been revealed that small differences in benchmark design can produce large differences in tokenizer performance. We used the following rules to keep the comparison consistent across engines.

Repeatedly encoding one document can be faster than encoding a stream of distinct documents on the same build. The first approach measures performance when the entire document is already represented in the cache. The second measures performance on new input while allowing previously seen pre-tokens to remain cached.

Industry observers note that both conditions are sometimes described as "warm," even though they measure different workloads. Our headline results use distinct documents, and the complete corpus is too large to fit in the cache. Tokenizer benchmarks should identify which workload they use because the choice can dominate the result.

According to recent reports, across the ten model families v1's encode path covers, it encodes text 3 to 30 times faster than v0.23 with one thread on an Apple M4 Max. The low end is t5-base, the high end gpt2. It scales at 76% of linear across eight workers. Throughout these changes, v1 produces exactly the same token IDs as the released library.

The overall improvement comes from several changes working together: a hand-written splitter in place of a regex engine, a cache that answers a repeated word without merging it again, a merge loop that never touches the allocator, and one model call per batch of pre-tokens instead of one per pre-token. Each reduces the work done at a different point in the pipeline.

In a recent development, the next priority is support for more model families. We will move additional models onto the new merge loop before 1.0.0. Once the release candidates stabilize, the next step will be bringing about the improvements within the transformers library and the rest of the ecosystem which depend on the tokenizers library.

This post is generated from tokbench results and will be updated as support expands.

A release candidate for v1 is on crates.io. The API you call is the one you already call, so the only thing that changes is which build you install.

Sources indicate that training is behind a default-on feature that pulls a C++ dependency with it. If you only need to encode, turn it off to exclude the training implementation:.

Encoding is unchanged: same call, same ids.

Every figure in this post was measured against this crate. The Python bindings wrap the same code and are built from bindings/python, but they add per-call overhead that none of these measurements include.

The benchmarks in this post cover the completed release-candidate work listed first. The remaining sections show what is still required for 1.0.0 and what we strategy to explore afterward.

This work is in the Rust pre-release on crates.io:.

Datadog Brings Production Experimentation to AI Agent Observability

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (737 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News Datadog Brings Production Experimentation to AI Agent Observability.
  • Nov 17, 2026 3 min read.
  • Datadog is extending its Agent Observability platform with Online Experiments, allowing engineering teams to compare AI agent versions against real production traffic rather than relying exclusively on predefined evaluation datasets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Datadog Brings Production Experimentation to AI Agent Observability.

Nov 17, 2026 3 min read.

Datadog is extending its Agent Observability platform with Online Experiments, allowing engineering teams to compare AI agent versions against real production traffic rather than relying exclusively on predefined evaluation datasets. The capability combines agent evaluation scores with operational measurements such as latency, token consumption, execution cost, and errors, helping teams establish whether changes to models, prompts, retrieval strategies, or tools actually improve an agent.

Sources indicate that the announcement addresses a growing challenge in agent development: a change that performs better in a controlled test may behave very differently when exposed to unpredictable user requests. Datadog's approach brings controlled experimentation, production telemetry, and execution traces together, giving teams evidence of both the outcome and the behaviour behind it.

Industry observers note that offline evaluations remain an notable part of agent development. Teams can run different versions against predefined datasets, assess responses and identify known regressions before deployment.

In a recent development, however, these evaluations are only as representative as the datasets and scoring criteria behind them. New user workflows, unexpected requests, and changing tool responses can expose weaknesses that existing test cases never anticipated.

Online experiments address this limitation by evaluating agent behaviour against real user interactions. Teams can compare a control version with a modified variant by randomly distributing production traffic between them, reducing the influence of differences in user requests.

This provides a more realistic view of how an agent performs under actual workloads, while also helping teams identify fresh scenarios that should eventually become part of their offline regression datasets.

Datadog integrates its Agent Observability evaluators with its Experiments capability, allowing evaluation scores to be compared alongside conventional operational metrics.

Teams can measure response quality, accuracy, and completeness while tracking execution duration, token consumption, estimated cost, and workflow errors. Feature Flags manage traffic allocation, letting engineers expose a change to a small percentage of users before rolling it out more widely.

This is important because improvements rarely come without trade-offs. A cheaper model might require more retries, while a revised retrieval strategy could improve evidence quality but increase execution time.

According to recent reports, datadog also connects experiment results to individual agent traces. Engineers can inspect tool calls, supplied arguments, and returned results to understand why a particular variant behaved differently.

According to the article, the experiment compared GPT-5.6 Luna against GPT-6 Luna, splitting traffic evenly between the two. An LLM-based evaluator scored investigation quality from one to five, considering accuracy, completeness, and whether conclusions were supported by available evidence.

They claim the results showed a 44.3% reduction in estimated cost for the newer model, with quality scores remaining close at 3.84 and 3.86, respectively.

Industry observers note that however, the operational results revealed potential concerns. The newer model showed estimated increases in execution duration and workflow errors, although the confidence intervals were too broad to establish definitive regressions.

In a recent development, inspecting the traces revealed that the newer model also supplied invalid tool parameters more frequently, usually recovering after retries. This behaviour was not sufficiently visible in the overall quality score.

Sources indicate that datadog used that finding to improve tool handling before proceeding with the model change. The failed calls also provided candidates for additional offline regression tests.

Industry observers note that datadog is not alone in trying to solve this challenge. Tools such as LangSmith and Langfuse provide agent tracing and evaluation capabilities, while experimentation platforms such as LaunchDarkly support controlled feature rollouts. Datadog's approach connects these concerns within its existing observability ecosystem, linking evaluation results directly to production experiments and execution evidence.

Datadog's broader proposition is that online experiments can create a feedback loop between production behaviour and development testing. Unexpected failures become latest regression cases, while subsequent experiments establish whether changes actually resolve them.

The important shift is from asking whether an agent passes a predefined evaluation to establishing whether it performs better under real conditions. For agent engineering, production experimentation may become as important as traditional software testing.

Jun Kim, oMLX creator and maintainer, joins Hugging Face to support the MLX community

📅 22 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (507 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We are super excited to welcome Jun as our newest team member 🔥.
  • Recent findings suggest that MLX is Apple's framework for local AI, especially optimized for Apple Silicon.
  • It has been revealed that stability, and hopefully faster development!
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We are super excited to welcome Jun as our newest team member 🔥. We are completely invested in local AI, and MLX is a central piece of the ecosystem. We are delighted that Jun chose us to set up home and continue contributing to MLX.

Recent findings suggest that MLX is Apple's framework for local AI, especially optimized for Apple Silicon. We are big MLX supporters since it was the Christmas present from Awni and Angelos in 2023, and proud that Hugging Face is the Hub where people find MLX models and contribute their own. Usage of open, local AI is accelerating, and we believe in a healthy ecosystem where people can find the tools that work for them.

It has been revealed that stability, and hopefully faster development! Graduating from a side job to a fully maintained and funded project will allow Jun to better guide the contributors and build for the long-term. oMLX stays Apache 2.0, and Jun keeps leading it as before.

In a recent development, our end goal is to unblock the community to run local AI in any shape or form, and provide the tools and building blocks to make that happen. We expect oMLX to serve as a testbed for latest ideas, while leveraging the foundational work of the dependencies it already relies upon, such as mlx-lm or mlx-vlm. We believe that strong modeling and inference libraries help the community, so we'd love to upstream work to wherever it makes sense. We have been collaborating with many projects mlx-lm, mlx-vlm, LMStudio, and we hope we can strengthen the relationship with Cheng, Prince, Yagil, and their teams to better serve the community together.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that which model to choose? It's elementary but not obvious.

Google periodically tables newly introduced AI models named after elements, and its latest offering has the noble name "Neon.".

"Engineered for long-running agent workflows, Neon sustains performance through complex, tool-heavy tasks end-to-end — whether running standalone or acting as a fast, high-judgment Orchestrator directing parallel Hydrogen subagents in Google Antigravity," explained Koray Kavukcuoglu, SVP at Google DeepMind and chief AI architect at Google, in a blog post.

Neon emerged after Google last week emitted Hydrogen, after delivering Carbon two weeks earlier and wafting Argon out the door in late September.

Unlike OpenAI's celestial more intuitive model naming scheme – Astra, Sol, Luna, and Terra – which maps celestial position to capability, Google's chemical soup doesn't suggest a specific hierarchy.

To judge by price, Carbon or Argon would be Google's top tier model, based on non-discounted price that takes effect next month, each priced at $4/M input tokens, $20/M output.

The Chocolate Factory refers to Carbon as "Our most capable reasoning model" while Argon is "Our efficient Gemini 4 frontier reasoning model … with faster responses and lower token spend per turn compared to Gemini 4 Carbon across complex coding, agentic, math, and science tasks.".

Recent findings suggest that yet Neon, the latest element in the mix, surpasses both in Artificial Analysis' Intelligence Index, scoring 61 compared to Carbon at 60, Hydrogen at 54, and Argon at 50. At the same time, Neon costs less, at $3/M input tokens and $15/M output.

That favorable pricing is all the more surprising in light of Google's willingness, as of two days ago, to let users of its Gemini services opt out of generative AI model training without losing their chat histories.

Kavukcuoglu evidently recognizes the need to clarify its model rankings, an issue addressed in a blog post section titled "Where Neon sits in the Gemini 4 family.".

"While Carbon tackles your hardest, long-horizon projects and Hydrogen handles fast everyday execution, Neon balances depth and efficiency," he explains. "Neon delivers frontier-level reasoning for complex, high-frequency workflows faster and more cost efficiently.".

That may not really clarify which model is appropriate for which task and frankly Google is fine with that.

Sources indicate that as noted, Google Antigravity comes with an Orchestrator that decides how to spend your money for you by swapping models on the fly. As the company describes it, a developer might start a task using Carbon, which would write a plan, and hand the task off to Hydrogen to benefit from its token thrift.

Antigravity does support model pinning, for those who know what they want. But Google, like other companies exploring model routing and orchestration, is fine with developers delegating decisions that affect billing to their trustworthy service provider. ®.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Our normal load testing did not detect the latent concern because [of] the traffic mix and SKUs used in our labs.
  • Recent findings suggest that thereâs a lot going on in this report (as there is in any report for a complex system), but I wanted to zoom in on this one matter: traffic mix.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The preliminary report on last weekâs M365 outage contains one statement that really caught my eye:.

Our normal load testing did not detect the latent concern because [of] the traffic mix and SKUs used in our labs.

Recent findings suggest that thereâs a lot going on in this report (as there is in any report for a complex system), but I wanted to zoom in on this one matter: traffic mix. Itâs crucial, because its the one thing that makes the difference between a great load test and a complete waste of time.

The performance of computer systems is extremely sensitive to workload mix.

Recent findings suggest that letâs start with a simple simulator, looking at a system with a table of locks. Requests arrive with a key, hold the lock for their key for some period of time, and then free the lock and complete. This isnât an unreasonable mental model of a relational database, where each transaction takes a lock during its execution.

Each request takes one of 16 worker threads, waits in a FIFO queue for the lock on its key, holds the lock for an exponentially distributed time (mean 1 ms), then releases it and frees its thread. Keys are drawn from a Zipf distribution over N keys; a coefficient of 0 is uniform.

It has been revealed that as we may expect, the more skewed the distribution, the less throughput you get out of the system. A small number of keys are highly contended, leading to under utilization of the rest of the resources of the machine, driven by the global concurrency limit.

It has been revealed that now, letâs consider a different mental model of a relational database (at least a single-system one like Postgres). A fast, local, in-memory cache containing some of the accessed data backed by a slower store containing the rest of the data.

Keys (N):    Cache size: % of keys    Cache is × faster than storage    Simulate.

According to recent reports, each request takes one of the same 16 worker threads and reads its key. A hit is served from an LRU cache; a miss goes to storage (exponentially distributed, mean 1 ms) and the key is added to the cache. Keys are drawn from a Zipf distribution over N keys; a coefficient of 0 is uniform. Note the log scale on the throughput axis.

According to recent reports, this curve goes the other way! The more skewed the distribution, the better the performance, over something of a broad range. This is what makes it so notable that workload mix in load tests and benchmarks matches real production traffic: throughput can vary by multiple orders of magnitude, in both directions, depending on things as subtle as key skew in the benchmark workload. This is especially true in relational database-shaped things, but applies to systems of all kinds.

In a recent development, aside: This is also a reason I like optimistic concurrency control, and architectures with a single cost/latency mode. Aurora DSQL reflects this thinking on how to make things less workload sensitive: all reads go to a single fast storage layer, and nobody is holding resources waiting on locks.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, we're adding support for running GGUF models efficiently in transformers, so you can use checkpoints sized for your laptop's memory through the familiar transformers APIs.
  • Running AI models on your laptop has become much easier, and llama.cpp has been a significant part of that.
  • Sources indicate that this is where we are right now.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, we're adding support for running GGUF models efficiently in transformers, so you can use checkpoints sized for your laptop's memory through the familiar transformers APIs. Pick a GGUF from the Hub, load it with from_pretrained, and start generating on your own machine.

Running AI models on your laptop has become much easier, and llama.cpp has been a significant part of that. Its inference engine powers local AI tools such as Ollama, LM Studio, and Jan. Alongside projects like MLX, it has helped make local inference a practical option for everyday use.

A recent example of what local AI can feel like:.

Sources indicate that this is where we are right now. And i’m not gonna lie it feels pretty magical 🧙‍♀️Qwen3.6 27B running inside of Pi coding agent via Llama.cpp on the MacBook ProFor non-trivial tasks on the @huggingface codebases, this feels very, very close to hitting the latest Opus in Claude… pic.twitter.com/lsIxLoUneU.

GGUF, developed by the llama.cpp team, is a widely used format for local inference. The team also shares quantized checkpoints under ggml-org on the Hub. Publishers such as Unsloth, LM Studio Community, and bartowski also provide ready-to-use GGUF checkpoints in a range of quantizations, so owners can pick the version that fits their machine. GGUF models have been downloaded millions of times.

We want to make it easier to run these models locally with transformers, too. Compatibility is only useful if the model is pleasant to run. To bring performance close to llama.cpp, we're reusing its underlying ggml kernels through the kernels library, and reducing overhead in generate. Our initial focus is local inference on Apple Silicon, starting with the Qwen3.5 architecture.

It has been revealed that GGUF packages model weights and metadata, including tokenizer information and an optional chat template, in one file. It supports different quantization levels, letting you trade some precision for a smaller memory footprint. Variants such as Q4_K_M mix tensor precisions, using mostly 4-bit weights while keeping sensitive tensors at higher precision.

Here's how quantization changes the file size of Unsloth's Qwen3.5-4B:.

Industry observers note that we suggest starting with Q4_K_M, then trying Q5_K_M or Q6_K if you have more memory available. More aggressive quantization can help larger models fit, but the quality tradeoff depends on the model and the task. Evaluate it on the work you actually want the model to do. The Hub's GGUF documentation describes the available quantization types.

To load a GGUF model, pass its Hub model_id and filename as gguf_file to from_pretrained.

Recent findings suggest that no extra configuration is needed: when the weights stay packed on Metal, transformers automatically loads the compatible ggml/Metal layer kernels and uses ggml-org/ggml-attn as the attention implementation. If that kernel cannot be fetched, the model falls back to "sdpa" with a warning, and you can always force "sdpa" by passing attn_implementation="sdpa" explicitly. See the GGUF documentation for more loading options.

Industry observers note that that is the only GGUF-specific step. Everything after it is the standard transformers API:.

Without a compatible quantization kernel, the loader falls back to dequantizing the model and uses more memory.

You can also use the same checkpoint with transformers serve, which exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:.

The model argument uses :.gguf: before the colon is the Hub repository (unsloth/Qwen3.5-4B-GGUF), and after it is the file to load (Qwen3.5-4B-Q4_K_M.gguf). This selects a specific quantization from a repository that may contain several.

In a recent development, for models whose chat template supports thinking, add --reasoning off to skip it or --reasoning on to enable it. The default, --reasoning auto, follows the chat template’s default. See the reasoning options for details.

You can connect a client such as Jan or Pi by adding a custom OpenAI-compatible provider with these settings:.

In a recent development, transformers runs the model on your Mac, while the client provides the conversation interface. The same endpoint can be used by other clients that support this API.

Our reference for local inference performance is llama.cpp. The comparison below focuses on three GGUF checkpoints: a small dense model, a larger dense model, and a mixture-of-experts model.

Industry observers note that the llama.cpp column comes from the llama-bench tool (build 5f55650a7, release b10200, Metal backend from ggml 0.18.0), run as llama-bench -m -p 0 -n 128 -r 3, which reports tg128: the token-generation rate over 128 decoded tokens, averaged across three repetitions, with prompt processing excluded. The transformers column is generate producing the same 128 tokens from a 12-token prompt, best of three warmed runs, and it includes prefill.

Measured on a MacBook Pro M2 Max, 32 GB unified memory, macOS 26.6, PyTorch 2.12.1, kernels 0.17.0, plugged in.

Transformers is close to llama.cpp across all three checkpoints. The chart uses the same measurements described above; it does not imply identical benchmark conditions, since the Transformers measurement includes prefill while llama-bench reports decode-only throughput.

In a recent development, when GGML and llama.cpp joined Hugging Face, we described their complementary roles: llama.cpp provides a foundation for local inference, while transformers provides a foundation for model definition. GGUF support brings those two closer together.

llama.cpp remains our recommended engine when your priority is efficient local inference. Its dedicated runtime, memory management, and broad hardware support are built around that goal. This integration gives developers a convenient way to work with the same GGUF checkpoints inside transformers:.

For that last case, use GgufConfig(dequantize=True):.

The bigger opportunity is bringing ggml's performance to models that llama.cpp does not support.

Recent findings suggest that transformers already provides the PyTorch implementations of these architectures. With ggml kernels and quantization schemes available in PyTorch, we can work toward accelerating their supported operations without first implementing the entire model in llama.cpp. This is especially useful for newly introduced architectures, research models, and custom variants that may never receive a dedicated llama.cpp implementation.

Industry observers note that that opportunity extends beyond the GGUF format itself. A kernel operates on tensors; it does not require the whole model to come from a GGUF file. The same building blocks can be integrated into other transformers models and loading workflows. This also opens a path to other modalities: computer vision models, audio models, and multimodal models could reuse compatible attention, normalization, and matrix multiplication kernels without first having a full implementation in llama.cpp. Each architecture still needs integration and validation; the initial GGUF examples here cover text generation.

We also wanted to show how far we can get while keeping the model and generation loop in Python. With the right kernels and an efficient generation loop, Python and PyTorch can deliver strong local inference performance. The kernels handle the heavy computation, while the generation loop keeps the GPU busy by avoiding unnecessary synchronization.

Our focus was to make eager execution fast without requiring torch.compile. For interactive use, we wanted a quick start and a steady stream of tokens, without compilation pauses or recompilation when input shapes change. The two main pieces of that work are the kernels and generate itself.

A kernel is a small program that performs an operation on the GPU. PyTorch supplies general-purpose implementations; a specialized kernel can do less work, combine several operations, or read quantized weights directly in their stored format.

The kernels library lets us distribute compatible builds of ggml's Metal kernels on the Hub and call them from transformers. That brings ggml's work into the PyTorch model without replacing the model with a separate inference runtime.

The first four packages build on ggml's kernels; the top-k kernel addresses a separate bottleneck in MoE routing. Together they reduce the GPU work needed for each generated token.

Sources indicate that to show the contribution of the layer kernels, we compare the same packed GGUF checkpoints with and without them. The quantization kernel stays enabled in both configurations: disabling it would also change how weights are represented and would measure a different tradeoff.

Sources indicate that faster kernels only help if the GPU has work to do. During generation, the CPU schedules GPU operations and controls the loop that produces the next token. Reading a result back from the GPU can force the CPU to wait until queued operations finish. Repeating even a small wait for every token can noticeably reduce throughput.

Two changes address this in generate, which results in improvements for all transformers models (not just when running GGUF files):.

These changes improve the generation loop around the model, so their usefulness extends beyond GGUF. They complement the kernel work: kernels reduce the cost of an operation, while fewer synchronization points let CPU scheduling and GPU execution overlap.

These measurements keep all layer kernels enabled; the bars isolate the changes to the generation loop.

The initial target is a single interactive conversation on Apple Silicon. There are a few boundaries to keep in mind:.

If you have a GGUF model you would like to use in transformers, open an glitch with the checkpoint and your use case. That will help us prioritize support for the models people are running locally.

We would like to thank Arthur Zucker for initiating this work and reviewing all of my PRs, and Cyril Vallez for the generate PRs. InfoQ Homepage News Qwik 2.0 RC: Replaces HTML Comment Markers for Faster Reactivity and Out-of-Order Streaming.

Nov 17, 2026 2 min read.

It has been revealed that qwik, the resumable JavaScript framework originally created at Builder.io, has released its 2.0 Release Candidate, targeting a rewrite of how the framework encodes resumable state in server-rendered HTML and introducing experimental out-of-order streaming. The RC was published on 1st October 2026 as @qwik.dev/core@2.0.0-rc.0, around two years and eight months after the initial Towards Qwik 2.0 design article.

In v1, Qwik propagated state updates by sprinkling HTML comment markers such as and throughout the rendered body to flag component boundaries and the text nodes a signal should update. That approach forced a single ordered write pass, added CPU and memory overhead, and made out-of-order streaming impossible because a slow fetch blocked everything after it. In v2 the comments are gone, with state and virtual node information instead compressed into two.

#46454. Uncensored AI models are thriving on code hosting platforms

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1426 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theregister ↗ Open Full Page

Uncensored AI models are thriving on code hosting platforms

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1426 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Uncensored large language models (ULLMs) capable of producing harmful content are readily available at popular model-hosting websites, calling into question AI industry commitments to safety.
  • Researchers affiliated with University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign in the US and Nanyang Technological University in Singapore have analysed 22,096 ULLMs collected from five major LLM hosting platforms.
  • As described in their paper, "Characterizing the Ecosystem of Open-Source Uncensored Large Language Models: Supply Chain, Governance, and Risks," authors Zilong Lin, Zichuan Li, Xiaojing Liao, and XiaoFeng Wang found that uncensored LLMs are easy to obtain from hosting platforms like US-based Hugging Face, Kaggle, and John Snow Labs, and China-based OpenCSG and ModelScope.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Uncensored large language models (ULLMs) capable of producing harmful content are readily available at popular model-hosting websites, calling into question AI industry commitments to safety.

Researchers affiliated with University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign in the US and Nanyang Technological University in Singapore have analysed 22,096 ULLMs collected from five major LLM hosting platforms.

As described in their paper, "Characterizing the Ecosystem of Open-Source Uncensored Large Language Models: Supply Chain, Governance, and Risks," authors Zilong Lin, Zichuan Li, Xiaojing Liao, and XiaoFeng Wang found that uncensored LLMs are easy to obtain from hosting platforms like US-based Hugging Face, Kaggle, and John Snow Labs, and China-based OpenCSG and ModelScope.

What's more, these unrestrained models have been deployed through applications, GitHub projects, and model routing platforms like Open Router, and users of those apps or services may not be aware of the nature of the underlying LLM.

"Uncensored LLMs generally refer to LLMs whose content filtering or refusal safeguards are absent, removed, or weakened, allowing them to respond to requests that aligned models may refuse," the paper explains.

Zilong Lin, lead author and assistant professor of computer science at the University of Missouri-Kansas City, told The Register that open source LLM hosting platforms like Hugging Face play a similar role to code hosting services like GitHub, GitLab, and Codeberg in the open source community by enabling sharing, modification, and redistribution of code artifacts.

Industry observers note that "However, unlike traditional software, whose behavior can often be examined through source code analysis, the safety alignment of LLMs is difficult to assess directly from their model files," Lin explained. "Evaluating whether an LLM has adequate safety safeguards typically requires deploying the model and testing its responses to potentially harmful prompts, which involves substantial computational and financial costs.".

Recent findings suggest that lin said this makes the identification and assessment of LLM safety particularly challenging, particularly given the large number of models available. That's why he and his colleagues chose to study the space through publicly available model metadata.

Even popular commercial LLMs that are purportedly "aligned" – to some standard not everyone accepts – may respond to prompts with content deemed harmful. The US Government Accountability Office just released a report that found Claude, Grok, ChatGPT, and Gemini can be coaxed to provide information that would help with the planning of a terror attack.

To highlight the consequences of AI advice, the GAO points to news reports indicating that generative AI helped enable the creation of an explosive device in a January 2025 attack on a Las Vegas hotel and the planning of a February 2026 mass shooting in British Columbia, Canada.

The issue with open weight LLMs is that anyone with modest technical skills (or just cluelessly assisted by a compliant LLM) can apply techniques like toxic training/fine-tuning (TTFT) or de-aligned training/fine-tuning (DTFT) to datasets that haven't been safe, in order to produce models with reduced or removed refusal behavior. Examples include toxicqa-Llama2-13B and WizardLM-7B-Uncensored. A more recent technique called refusal-direction ablation (or abliteration, e.g., Daredevil-8B-abliterated) dilutes refusal training to make the model less likely to refuse requests.

It has been revealed that uncensored (or simply less restrictive) models have legitimate uses, sometimes ironically because commercial models are insufficiently permissive and refuse legitimate security analysis. Hugging Face, for example, had to resort to using Z.ai's less rule-encumbered GLM-5.2 to analyze the hacking of its infrastructure by OpenAI's irresponsibly unsupervised AI agents.

But ULLMs can just as easily be misused to provide guidance about illegal activity, assist with malware development, or emit content that's harmful, malicious, or manipulative in some way.

"We identified more than 11,000 ULLMs appearing across multiple platforms, with Hugging Face serving as the dominant upstream source," Lin said in a blog post.

In a recent development, "This movement exposes an crucial governance gap: models can travel more easily than the information needed to assess their risks. Only about 13 percent of the ULLMs we identified carried moderation warnings, and security threat indicators were not consistently preserved across platforms.

"This creates a supply chain problem: a model can be copied across platforms while the information needed to understand its risks is lost along the way.".

In a recent development, the ULLMs were evaluated for text output and not images. The concerns raised by text-to-image LLMs, such as the ability to generate illegal images (e.g. CSAM), were beyond the scope of this particular study.

Sources indicate that "The uncensored LLMs we evaluated were generally more likely to comply with harmful requests and generate harmful content than non-uncensored models," Lin noted. "Our evaluation covered 11 categories of harmful requests, including child abuse, illegal activities, and fraud.

"However, the ability of an individual model to generate harmful content varies depending on several factors, including its training data, development methods, and the extent to which its refusal direction has been ablated.".

A small portion of these ULLMs (27 of them, which have been downloaded 136,000 times) exhibited threat indicators from security scans. Many of these, authors say, had signatures associated with malware, exhibited suspicious binary patterns, or contained unsafe deserialization mechanisms that could allow arbitrary code execution.

The number of ULLMs has been rising rapidly, according to the paper, from about 100 per month in May 2023 to more than 1,000 per month presently. And some of these models have been downloaded millions of times. The uncensored model dolphin-2.9.1-yi-1.5-34b has more than 53 million downloads, and more than 4.8 million just last month.

The authors note that many ULLMs violate the licensing terms of the models on which they've been based, not that source code licensing has had any meaningful impact on the behavior of the AI industry.

Asked whether the safety concerns arising from the availability of ULLMs might prompt a replay of the 1990s when authorities tried to limit the availability of cryptographic code, Lin said, "It is difficult to predict whether model abliteration tools will face similar legal challenges.

Sources indicate that "As shown in Section 5.1 of our paper, refusal-direction ablation (i.e., abliteration) appeared in 2024 and quickly gained popularity within the open-source LLM community. Within approximately two years, a growing ecosystem of publicly available tools had emerged to support this technique.

"In the meantime, techniques for both removing and mitigating LLM safety alignment have also become active research topics in academia, with many researchers releasing open-source tools and artifacts to support their studies.".

Recent findings suggest that dealing with the risks posed by uncensored models isn't easy because it depends on divining the intent of the user's prompt. When is a question about terrorism intended as a plan and when is it guidance for writing a thriller? When is a question about hacking intended for theft and when is it cybersecurity education?

It has been revealed that the current approach taken by commercial labs — limiting powerful models to favored paying insiders and offering hobbled models to the rest — doesn't work for those left out. Applying some similarly censorious regime to open weight models isn't likely to achieve any more success than efforts by law enforcement to make cryptography available only to "the good guys.".

Lin expects that greater transparency, auditability, and verification of models will help.

According to recent reports, "As discussed in Section 8 of our paper, our approach to identifying uncensored LLMs relies on publicly available model metadata, such as model cards, to identify models that explicitly disclose their uncensored characteristics," he said. "Our findings demonstrate the value of such transparency for identifying potentially unsafe models.

"Regulatory frameworks have also increasingly emphasized AI documentation and transparency. For example, the EU AI Act requires providers of general-purpose AI models to maintain technical documentation covering model characteristics, capabilities, limitations, and evaluation results. Similarly, the Colorado AI Act recognizes model cards and dataset cards as possible documentation supporting AI impact assessments.".

Sources indicate that hugging Face, in the process of being acquired by Nvidia, did not respond to a request for comment. Nor did Kaggle or John Snow Labs, the two other US-based companies named in the study.

According to Lin, the research findings were responsibly disclosed to Hugging Face, John Snow Labs, OpenCSG, Kaggle, ModelScope, and Open Router.

Asked whether any of the companies responded, Lin said, "We received a response from OpenCSG, which expressed appreciation for our work on identifying and measuring uncensored LLMs, stating that 'your research is meaningful and supports the development of a safe and trustworthy LLM ecosystem.'".

In a recent development, openCSG, the report notes, has committed to enhance its service based on the research findings. ®.

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This article explains how Elixir implements type inference and type narrowing using reverse arrows: a small set of composable ideas, rather than special cases hardcoded into the type checker.
  • Industry observers note that thanks to this work, the upcoming Elixir v1.21 passes all tests in the If-T: Type Narrowing Benchmark by Guo et al..
  • Industry observers note that the type system was made possible thanks to a partnership between CNRS and Remote.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This article explains how Elixir implements type inference and type narrowing using reverse arrows: a small set of composable ideas, rather than special cases hardcoded into the type checker.

Industry observers note that thanks to this work, the upcoming Elixir v1.21 passes all tests in the If-T: Type Narrowing Benchmark by Guo et al.. This means v1.21 can find even more sure bugs in existing Elixir programs and, once type signatures are introduced, narrowing will give us more precise types and fewer false positives.

Industry observers note that the type system was made possible thanks to a partnership between CNRS and Remote. The development work is currently sponsored by Fresha, Supermethod and Dashbit.

Elixir performs type inference by refining the dynamic type. This is quite different from how inference and gradual typing are implemented in most type systems, so let’s break it down.

In many gradual languages, the dynamic type, often known as any, is a “black box” and can be used in any context. For example, imagine this Elixir function, where x starts with type dynamic(), as there is no type signature:.

Sources indicate that the program above uses x both as a number (more precisely, as integer() or float() in x * 2) and as a bitstring in byte_size(x). In some gradual type systems, the type checker will accept the program above, even though it will crash at runtime, because the dynamic type can be used in any context.

However, in Elixir, the dynamic() type can be refined, and the above will report the following typing violation:.

Sources indicate that as you can see in the error message, Elixir infers that the type of x after x * 2 is a dynamic(float() or integer()). This means that x can be given to any function that accepts at least one of float() or integer(). However, because byte_size(x) expects a bitstring, we have a typing violation.

It has been revealed that this is possible because dynamic() in Elixir actually means dynamic(term()), where term() is the top type. Then, as a variable is used throughout the code, its dynamic type is refined by intersecting its type with the arguments of the functions the code invokes. In other words, we go through the following steps:.

x is given to x * 2. The left operand of * expects integer() or float(), which we then intersect with term(), and therefore x gains the type dynamic(integer() or float()).

x is given to byte_size(x), which expects a bitstring. The intersection of integer() or float() with bitstring() is empty, which will lead to a typing violation.

Now, let’s take a look at this program:.

This time, we pass x to the remainder function, rem, which expects all of its inputs to be integers. This means that, at the end of this function, Elixir will correctly infer that x can only be an integer, because x was refined from dynamic(term()) to dynamic(integer() or float()) and then only to dynamic(integer()). The inferred type for using_x_as_integer is a function, commonly written using the arrow notation: dynamic(integer()) -> :ok.

In a recent development, the best part is that all dynamic types in Elixir are refined and therefore the type system is always doing its best to find bugs, even in the presence of dynamism. And the refinement itself is often quite precise, thanks to reverse arrows, which we will explore next.

Industry observers note that an arrow is the type of a function: integer() -> boolean() is an arrow that says “given an integer, this function returns a boolean”. The type on the left of the arrow is its domain (what it accepts) and the type on the right is its codomain (what it returns). Every function has arrows, whether they come from a type signature you wrote or are inferred by Elixir from the function’s clauses.

It has been revealed that functions in Elixir can be typed with multiple arrows. As an exercise, let’s take a function that negates numbers, such as negate(1) returning -1:.

You could give it this type signature with a single arrow:.

Industry observers note that however, this type says that, if you give it an integer, it may return a float, which is never the case! This signature is too broad. Instead, we could give it this signature with two arrows:.

According to recent reports, this precisely captures that, if you give it an integer, it returns an integer. If you give it a float, it returns a float. Multiple arrows are an excellent way to type functions with multiple clauses, which are common in both Erlang and Elixir.

With this in mind, and remembering that rem only works on integers (its type is integer(), integer() -> integer()), what do you believe is the inferred type of x in the function below?

You may think x is dynamic(integer() or float()), because that’s the domain of negate. However, x will once again be inferred to be dynamic(integer()), because Elixir propagates types through the arrows in reverse: it starts from what the outermost call expects and walks inwards, from results to arguments, until it reaches the variables. Let’s break it down.

We start type checking the function and we find rem(negate(x), 2). rem has a single arrow, integer(), integer() -> integer(), so we know that negate(x) must return an integer() for this to type check.

Recent findings suggest that now we type check negate(x). negate has two arrows: integer() -> integer() and float() -> float(). Since its result must be an integer, we can discard the float() -> float() arrow, as it never returns an integer. The only remaining arrow is integer() -> integer(), so the argument of negate must be integer().

According to recent reports, now we type check x itself. x starts with the type dynamic(term()). We then intersect it with integer(), resulting in dynamic(integer()).

Recent findings suggest that in other words, inference goes in two directions. Going forward, from arguments to results, arrows tell us what each call returns. Going in reverse, from results to arguments, arrows tell us what each argument must have been for the call to produce the expected result. As we give precise type signatures to our programs using multiple arrows, the type system will use these same arrows to infer precise types. As we will learn next, Elixir uses this technique to infer types from guards and to perform type narrowing (also known as occurrence typing).

Now we have the foundation to understand how Elixir performs type inference of guards. Take this function clause:.

Both x and y start with type dynamic(term()). We also know that a guard only succeeds if it returns true and we have the following type signatures (roughly):.

Therefore, to infer the types of when is_integer(x) and is_bitstring(y), we start with true, which is the only result for which a guard succeeds, and propagate it through the arrows in reverse:.

The only arrow of and that can return true is true, true -> true, therefore we know that both operands must be true.

The only arrow of is_integer that can return true is integer() -> true, therefore we know x must be an integer.

The only arrow of is_bitstring that can return true is bitstring() -> true, therefore we know y must be a bitstring.

If multiple arrows could return true, we would then simply union their domains.

It has been revealed that it is worth emphasizing that this behaviour is not hardcoded to a handful of functions the type checker knows about. It works with any function, in any context. Let’s see more examples.

Occurrence typing refines the type of variables and expressions based on the branch taken in a conditional or pattern match, so the same variable may have different types in different branches. For example:.

According to recent reports, the mechanism we use to perform occurrence typing is quite similar to the one from the previous sections. Within the do-branch, we consider the scenarios where is_bitstring(x) will return true. Within the else-branch, we consider the ones where it returns false.

It has been revealed that and since our foundation is built on reverse arrows, the narrowing also applies to patterns and case-expressions! For example:.

Here, parse has no type signature, but Elixir infers its arrows from its clauses: integer() -> {:ok, integer()} and bitstring() -> :error. Within the first branch, we know parse(x) returned a tuple, and the only arrow that returns a tuple has integer() as its domain, so x must be an integer.

Recent findings suggest that the If-T benchmark is a collection of test scenarios designed to evaluate both the precision and soundness of type narrowing. Elixir v1.20 already handled 12 out of the 13 tests, but it could not infer the proper types for this example:.

To narrow x, we need to reverse the arrows of is_integer(x). In Elixir v1.20, we only did so for the expression given directly to if or case. Here, the expression given to if is the variable y. All v1.20 knew about y is that it was a boolean(). Inside the do-branch, y is true, but by then the connection between y and is_integer(x) had been lost at the assignment, so there were no arrows to reverse.

This would be quite harmful once we add type signatures, because it means trivial refactoring techniques, such as extracting an expression into a variable, could lead to false positives.

Elixir v1.21 solves this by keeping track of the expression each variable was assigned to. Now, when y is narrowed to true, we know y came from is_integer(x), so we continue propagating true in reverse through the arrows of is_integer, narrowing x to integer(). This works across any number of assignments:.

Our implementation also performs the narrowing lazily, by cross-referencing the variables in the if and case expressions with the variables used in each clause, trying to find any assignment they share with each other. If the clauses above do not access z, y, or x, then no narrowing is performed.

Finally, because Elixir defines reverse arrows for almost all operations, it can refine expressions which are not at the moment refined in TypeScript, such as data constructors:.

In the program above, even though foo is set as the value of a map, refining the map still refines the original variable.

Elixir’s approach to type inference and narrowing is built on a few ideas that compose well. Dynamic types are refined as variables are used, multiple arrows give precise types to functions, and propagating types through those arrows in reverse lets us infer and narrow types across conditionals, patterns, and assignments, all without hardcoding knowledge about specific functions.

It has been revealed that in Elixir v1.21, we use these techniques to find sure bugs in existing Elixir programs, without requiring any changes to your code. The same mechanisms will apply once type signatures are introduced: the more precise the signatures, the more precise the narrowing and the fewer false positives.

How UK AISI and EvalEval Are Making Benchmark Results Reproducible
