💡 Key Takeaways
  • The EvalEval Coalition is thrilled to share that the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) is using EvalEval's infrastructure to openly share evaluation results, supporting more reproducible and verifiable evaluation science.
  • Sources indicate that AISI and EvalEval have previously collaborated on research that began at a joint workshop alongside NeurIPS 2025, and feedback from the Institute has helped shape the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema.
  • As AI deployment accelerates, evaluations are becoming increasingly notable sources of evidence about model and system performance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The EvalEval Coalition is thrilled to share that the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) is using EvalEval's infrastructure to openly share evaluation results, supporting more reproducible and verifiable evaluation science.

Sources indicate that AISI and EvalEval have previously collaborated on research that began at a joint workshop alongside NeurIPS 2025, and feedback from the Institute has helped shape the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema. This next phase of the collaboration puts that shared infrastructure into practice.

As AI deployment accelerates, evaluations are becoming increasingly notable sources of evidence about model and system performance. Yet results are reported across many formats, platforms, and outlets, often without enough information to reproduce them. Running the evaluations again may itself be prohibitively expensive.

EvalEval's mission is to improve this ecosystem through a shared reporting schema, Every Eval Ever, and an open platform, Evaluation Cards, that brings evaluation results and the information needed to interpret them into a common structure.

This builds naturally on AISI's work to make evaluation more efficient through OptStop, more statistically rigorous through HiBayES, and more standardised in areas including transcript analysis and capability elicitation. Together, AISI and EvalEval are working to diagnose gaps in evaluation reporting and build shared infrastructure to close them.

Transcript-level transparency matters not only for reproducibility, but also for analysis and diagnosis. In this fresh phase of the collaboration, AISI is making publicly reported evaluation methods and findings available through Evaluation Cards where appropriate. The release includes verified results, context, and configuration information for the five benchmarks in the paper's main experiment:.

These results cover six frontier models: Claude Opus 4, Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5, GPT-5.2, and GPT-5.4. The release also includes results from two related cyber evaluations—Cyber CTFs and The Last Ones—which use a different, partially overlapping set of models. The data accompany AISI's paper, How Inference Compute Shapes Frontier LLM Evaluation, which studies how benchmark performance depends on inference-time compute and evaluation protocol.

Industry observers note that performance on Humanity's Last Exam changes with evaluation protocol and inference compute. Each curve demonstrates the cumulative share of attempted tasks solved within a given token count, using the earliest observed success per task. When models received correctness feedback from an oracle after each attempt, they continued to solve additional tasks as token use increased.

When results are openly released with setup information, researchers and practitioners can examine individual studies more closely and compare findings across the wider ecosystem. Where other reports lack these details, releases like AISI's provide verified reference points for interpreting evaluations in context—for example, by helping researchers understand how setup choices may influence reported performance. As more evaluators adopt EEE, open comparisons like these can support broader and more reliable meta-research.

AISI's Terminal-Bench 2.0 results alongside other reported evaluations for the same models, under different evaluation setups.

We are excited about this adoption and look forward to further standardising and sharing evaluations with AISI and other AI evaluation organisations.

Recent findings suggest that the EvalEval Coalition is a research community developing scientifically grounded research and robust deployment infrastructure for the evaluation ecosystem. Its goal is to improve evaluation science, address the lack of consensus around documenting evaluation applicability and utility, and broaden coverage of the impacts that matter for scientific research and policy analysis.

The coalition's flagship projects include Every Eval Ever, a shared schema and repository for evaluation results, and Evaluation Cards, which combines benchmark metadata, evaluation-run data, and model metadata into interpretable records. Together, they make it easier to understand when apparently similar scores were produced under meaningfully different conditions.

The UK AI Security Institute is a research organisation within the UK government's Department for Science, Innovation and Technology. Its mission is to equip governments with a scientific understanding of the risks posed by advanced AI. AISI conducts research and builds infrastructure to understand advanced AI capabilities and impacts, develop and test mitigations, and inform policy.

The line that matters for practitioners is quiet: apparently similar scores can be produced under meaningfully different conditions.

Once you've watched a benchmark move just by changing inference-time compute or the elicitation protocol, "Model A beat Model B on X" without a card is marketing, not comparison. Evaluation Cards that ship verified results with configuration — especially transcript-level context where it's appropriate — are how eval becomes a contract instead of a leaderboard screenshot.

One ask I'd put to teams adopting EEE: which fields get skipped first under deadline pressure (seed, tool access, attempt budget, oracle feedback), and do you treat a missing field as "do not cite the delta" rather than "assume defaults"?

Reproducible reporting won't remove disagreement. It will make the disagreement about the right variables.

Validating a High-Performance Cloud Object Store with Lightweight Formal Methods

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Abstract: We report on our experience validating S3 Express One Zone, a high-performance Amazon S3 storage class released in November 2023.
  • Abstract: We report on our experience validating S3 Express One Zone, a high-performance Amazon S3 storage class launched in November 2023.

Abstract: We report on our experience validating S3 Express One Zone, a high-performance Amazon S3 storage class released in November 2023. We focused on its distributed metadata index, which implements a hierarchical namespace using distributed transactions. We check strong consistency and durability under crashes, network delays, and timeouts. Building on our prior work on lightweight formal methods, we combined executable reference models with property-based testing and stateless model checking. Applying these techniques to a production distributed system required three new techniques: a white-box approach to checking serializability; compositional validation of the data and control planes; and long-running canaries that use reference models to check correctness across deployments. We extended Shuttle, our open-source stateless checker, to support a production async Rust runtime and failure injection, including cancelled operations and timeouts. Our main finding is that this approach is sustainable at engineering scale. After launch, the engineering team took ownership of models and test infrastructure, increasing its share of validation commits from 41% to 84% and independently extending the models for conditional writes, object append, and atomic rename, with little involvement from the formal methods team. Comments.

Sticky note on monitor provided keys to the tech giant’s kingdom

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (594 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Don't leave your credentials out in public, where any visitor can see them.
  • In a recent development, welcome, once again, to PWNED, where we talk smack about organizations that have smacked themselves down by practicing poor security hygiene.
  • In a recent development, our terrifying tale comes courtesy of Christian Espinosa, a certified penetration tester with over 30 years of experience and the CEO of Blue Goat Cyber, a security organization.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Don't leave your credentials out in public, where any visitor can see them.

In a recent development, welcome, once again, to PWNED, where we talk smack about organizations that have smacked themselves down by practicing poor security hygiene. This week's story involves everyone's favorite low-tech password manager: the sticky note.

In a recent development, our terrifying tale comes courtesy of Christian Espinosa, a certified penetration tester with over 30 years of experience and the CEO of Blue Goat Cyber, a security organization. Espinosa shared an experience where critical credentials were right out in the open for any person in the office to see.

It has been revealed that during a walkthrough of a client's office, he noticed a password written on a sticky note that was taped to an employee's monitor. While writing down your password and placing it in a physically secure paper notebook might be ok, taping it to the computer is definitely not.

According to recent reports, "Before I get my fingers on any system, I first walk the physical area that the system is located in — attackers do that when they're looking at a target too," Espinosa explained. “Physical security vulnerabilities are neglected much more often than technical security vulnerabilities and firms invest in firewalls where a sticky note is placed 3 feet from the front door.".

Espinosa took a photo of the sticky note and immediately tried logging into that employee's account. Success. Then, he tried the very same password on the VPN, which apparently had been maintained by that employee.

Once he connected to the VPN, Espinosa had full access to the company network and all of its shared drives. He opened a shared drive that this employee had access to and there was an HR folder with all kinds of personally identifiable information (PII) about employees, including home addresses, driver's licenses, and scanned W-4 forms. There were even spreadsheets that listed everyone's salaries.

According to recent reports, the accounting server was a particular treasure trove of client information. On that server, Espinosa found a folder with vendor banking information, invoices, and payment records.

According to recent reports, have a story about someone leaving a gaping hole in their network? Share it with us at pwned@sitpub.com. Anonymity is available upon request.

"At that point, a password I had read from a sticky note during a walk-through had taken me from one desk to information that could have been used for payroll fraud, identity theft, or vendor-payment fraud," Espinosa mentioned.

Industry observers note that after getting access to all this information, the pen tester presented his findings to the client. They quickly disabled the rogue account and started reviewing VPN access logs to see who else might have gotten into the network. They then searched the office to see if anyone else was exposing a password on a sticky note. Finally, they tightened permissions on the HR and accounting shares so that only people who really needed access to that data could get in.

Sources indicate that the lessons here are pretty obvious. Don't expose your passwords and, perhaps even more importantly, limit who has access to file shares that contain mission-critical data such as employee or client information.

Recent findings suggest that "The part that really got the client's attention was how easily the attack could have continued after I left the building," Espinosa posited. "Someone could have photographed that sticky note, walked out, connected to the VPN later that night, and started going through employee and financial records from somewhere else." ®.

Stricter checks for uploaded distributions on PyPI

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (782 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Pypi

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Over the past few months, PyPI has added some additional checks that can reject uploaded source distributions ("sdists") and built distributions ("bdists" or "wheels").
  • These checks are part of a larger initiative to make the Python packaging ecosystem more resistant to parser differentials, and will be followed by additional checks that aim to make PyPI's handling of distributions less permissive and more strictly conformant to their respective specifications.
  • Recent findings suggest that for downstream customers (package consumers), there are no breaking implications to these changes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Over the past few months, PyPI has added some additional checks that can reject uploaded source distributions ("sdists") and built distributions ("bdists" or "wheels").

These checks are part of a larger initiative to make the Python packaging ecosystem more resistant to parser differentials, and will be followed by additional checks that aim to make PyPI's handling of distributions less permissive and more strictly conformant to their respective specifications.

Recent findings suggest that for downstream customers (package consumers), there are no breaking implications to these changes. Package maintainers who see failures should ensure that they're using non-EOL versions of Python as well as build backends that produce distributions that properly conform to the packaging standards.

Python packaging has two primary distribution formats:.

Neither tar nor ZIP was designed for the role it serves in Python packaging1: both represent metadata that is irrelevant to Python package distribution, and are surrounded by an ecosystem of parsers that are permissive in their interpretation of inputs.

This laxity is often correct in a local user setting, where customers often want to recover key data from corrupted or otherwise slightly incorrect archives.

However, it's incorrect in a networked setting, particularly a packaging one: even small differences in parsing between separately permissive implementations can result in parser differentials that can result in identical inputs extracting differently on different platforms and with different tools.

In principle, an attacker can use differentials to violate many of the properties that Python packaging (and end users) assume, including:.

Industry observers note that violations of these properties can result in people installing distributions that look legitimate but are actually malicious, even when the distribution's own integrity (e.g. via hashing) is established.

Over the last few weeks, PyPI has begun rejecting:.

Source distributions that use "V7"-style tar archives. V7 is a legacy and mostly unspecified tar format that comes from UNIX V7 and was never produced by Python's own tarfile module.

Built distributions that include archive-level ZIP comments that could be misinterpreted as ZIP control structures.

These changes built on top of earlier work performed by Seth Larson last August aimed specifically at ZIP differential reduction.

If you're a downstream user of Python packaging: nothing! These changes will not directly affect you, and any distributions that you already depend on (through pip install or uv add) will continue to work.

Sources indicate that if you're a package maintainer: nothing, probably. The overwhelming majority of source distributions on PyPI are not affected by these changes, because they were already conforming with the pax requirement.

If you're a maintainer and you do encounter an upload rejection for archive format reasons, please consult PyPI's archives documentation. PyPI will endeavor to keep that page up-to-date as we ratchet down on malformed or non-conforming uploads.

For many maintainers, the fix will be straightforward:.

According to recent reports, make sure that your distributions (both sdists and bdists) are built with a Python build backend, and not by manually packing an archive with tar, zip, or similar. Popular build backends generally conform to both the distribution format specifications and to PyPI's additional archive restrictions.

If you're unable to migrate away from a manual packing step, make sure that you're manually conforming to the archive requirements, namely:.

In a recent development, source distributions must be POSIX pax-style tar archives. If you're using GNU tar, you'll need to pass --format=pax to override the default.

Built distributions must be valid ZIP archives.

Both formats require UTF-8 encoded filenames for their members.

This is an ongoing initiative, one that involves multiple facets of the Python ecosystem. We aim to align this work with Python itself (by reducing the number of differentials in Python's own zipfile and tarfile), as well as Python packaging's standards (by further constraining and improving the precision of the distribution specifications).

Sources indicate that going forwards, PyPI will continue to identify newly introduced restrictions that it can apply to uploaded distributions. Our goal is to identify minimally disruptive restrictions, i.e. ones that can be made without breaking (almost) any users. Archive differentials overwhelmingly take advantage of obscure or unused aspects of archive formats, so this is frequently possible.

In the near term, PyPI will be evaluating the following additional restrictions:.

Rejecting GNU-style tar archives entirely. These are already forbidden by the source distribution specification, but are currently allowed because of non-trivial use by maintainers. See #21012 for our initial plans on this.

Rejecting ZIP comments entirely. PyPI already rejects many forms of these, but allows a small subset for compatibility with ZIP encoders that put innocuous messages (like their version number) in archive comments. See #20934 for our initial plans on this.

Among so many other packaging ecosystems. ↩.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News How Shopify Orchestrates AI-Powered Mobile App Development without Overloading Developers' Machines.

Nov 17, 2026 2 min read.

To prevent AI development workflows from exhausting developer machines' resources, Shopify built Remote Dev, a remote mobile development environment that enables AI agents to independently build, test and maintain iOS and Android applications and in parallel.

Recent findings suggest that in fact, according to Shopify engineers, running agentic workflows in parallel promptly hogs all resources available on development machines. They explain that "three or four workflows were enough to max out a laptop", on top of the resources already consumed by compilers, simulators, and emulators. Moreover, "if someone accidentally closed a laptop lid, the work stopped".

According to recent reports, shopify had previously built River to address the same challenge in web and backend development, but, being River a Linux-based solution, it could not be used for building iOS apps. To overcome this limitation, Shopify built Remote Dev:.

It has been revealed that with Remote Dev, we're no longer limited by how many builds and simulators our laptops can handle. Each River session gets its own environment, so we can have one agent debugging something on Android, another working on an iOS feature, and another testing a PR, all in parallel.

Remote Dev uses a fleet of remote Macs running Shopify's development environment and iOS simulators, accessible via SSH. Android emulators run on separate Linux VMs. This architecture allows developers to build and test both iOS and Android builds through the same SSH session.

According to recent reports, agents can work on multiple tasks in parallel, each with its own environment for maximum independence. They can also be accessed through a Slack channel backed by River. Thanks to this setup, Remote Dev can.

implement changes, build the app, run tests, interact with the simulators, collect screenshots, and create a PR. If something fails, it can inspect the logs, fix the matter, and try again, all while we focus on other tasks.

Sources indicate that the platform supports automated workflows, including overnight runs that identify bugs, implement fixes, and submit PRs. Agents can also verify that a build is functional by navigating through the app, interacting with its UI, reproducing bugs, recording current behavior, implementing fixes, and running the same interaction to verify the fix.

Shopify says that, after promoting internal adoption through demonstrations and storytelling, River's share of merged PRs increased from 6% to 61%.

Recent findings suggest that commenting on Shopify's article, LinkedIn user Raiyan Jugbhery, in charge of software infrastructure and founder at SpendMe, argued that the key advantage of Remove Dev is its Xcode and iOS Simulator integration, noting that "a PR you still have to pull and verify on a Mac isn't really autonomous". However, he pointed out that the article does not explain "how they keep builds from queuing when several agents ask for a Mac at once", which he identified as a key concern.

In a recent development, junaid Raza, solutions architect at Hoboetech, raised another concern. Allowing agents to run the simulator could lead to unreliable test results, as "give [the agent] a red test and enough retries and it'll sometimes rewrite the test until it passes". To prevent this, he suggests prohibiting runner agents from modifying the tests they execute.

Shopify says it intends to expand the platform with continuous application health monitoring, automated crash detection and fixes, and PR generation for identified complications, among other capabilities.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that reinforcement Learning environments give newly introduced capabilities to agentic AI systems, and they’re a great way to measure and improve performance in your agents.
  • An environment gives an agent a task, responds to its actions with observations, and scores the outcome.
  • An RL environment on the Hub is a dataset repo that shows up in the fresh RL Environments filter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that reinforcement Learning environments give newly introduced capabilities to agentic AI systems, and they’re a great way to measure and improve performance in your agents. Therefore, Hugging Face Hub now has a special place for RL Environments.

An environment gives an agent a task, responds to its actions with observations, and scores the outcome. The resulting rewards can measure an agent's performance during evaluation or provide a learning signal during training. For an introduction to this interaction loop, see our blogpost on environments. Within the environment, the agent will perform a set of tasks that are represented as datasets. Therefore, environments can be split into broadly two parts: tasksets and runtimes. In this release, we are focusing on the tasksets.

An RL environment on the Hub is a dataset repo that shows up in the fresh RL Environments filter. The Use this dataset button gives you the command to run it in that framework. There is no new repo type, no registry, and no sign-up. There are already environments in Harbor, Verifiers, and NVIDIA NeMo Gym.

In a recent development, every RL paper or framework uses its own way to find environments. Custom hubs, runtime registries, independent task datasets, or a GitHub list of tasks with a custom loader. This means that many of the published environments are siloed: if you publish an environment for one framework, consumers of the other three can’t load it. If you want to train on an environment from another framework or a fresh paper, you’ll need to port it by hand.

In a recent development, we think this is the wrong shape. An environment is tasks, tests, containers, and a reward rule, which are data with a runtime on top. The Hub already stores data, versions it, gates it, previews it, and serves it to millions of people. It does not need a second system to hold environments. It needs a way to say "this data is an environment, and here is how you run it.".

Recent findings suggest that the frameworks keep doing what they are good at. The Hub does what it is good at, which is hosting, discovery, and versioning. Nobody has to own the catalogue. In fact, catalogues can run on other platforms too, powered by the hub.

Recent findings suggest that the dataset repository hosts your environment files. The framework runs them locally or on a supported cloud backend. Hugging Face Jobs can run cloud workloads, and Hugging Face Sandboxes, built on Jobs, provide interactive command execution. The tags describe compatibility and generate loading commands; adding a tag does not start a job or sandbox.

According to recent reports, the RL Environments filter. Go to huggingface.co/datasets?other=rl-environment. Every dataset with the rl-environment tag appears there, whatever framework it works with.

Recent findings suggest that framework tags. Four environment frameworks are registered as dataset libraries:.

Each framework tag puts the framework's icon on the dataset page and adds a generated snippet to Use this dataset.

It has been revealed that A dataset can carry more than one framework tag. That is the point. Tags describe compatibility, and compatibility is not exclusive. Each listed framework must support the files in the repository; adding a tag does not convert them.

Choose the example for your framework and run it in a separate Python environment with the prerequisites listed below.

Harbor can load task directories from a Hub repository. The oracle agent runs the task's reference solution, then the verifier scores the result. It does not call a model.

The viewer shows the task's reward, verifier output, and logs. This checks the task and its reference solution before you try a model agent.

According to recent reports, the Harbor integration of verifiers v1 can run the same task directories in different runtimes, such as Docker. It also supports different harnesses, including a minimal bash harness.

Here repo is the full Hugging Face Git URL, while dataset is the name and version in that repo's registry.json. This loader uses Harbor's registry conventions, so a bare Hub repo ID cannot replace both values.

OpenEnv's Harbor integration can run the same task directories with an agent such as OpenCode and return the verifier's reward alongside the agent's trace.

It has been revealed that the command downloads the dataset's tasks/ directories, runs one task in Docker, and writes the result. The default connection uses a temporary Gradio tunnel so the sandboxed agent can reach OpenEnv's model proxy. Read the verifier result and the number of model calls:.

According to recent reports, A reward of None means no verifier reward was produced; inspect error before interpreting the run as a model failure. This path expects Harbor task directories.

NeMo Gym supports evaluation and RL training: its environments collect trajectories and compute rewards, while a training framework updates model weights. For example, the Structured Outputs dataset pairs prompts with JSON schemas. Its verifier rewards schema adherence; it does not check whether the generated content is factually correct.

Industry observers note that the best part is that this gives one repo and one discussion tab where people report broken tasks from all major frameworks. So when an author fixes a bad test, every framework gets the fix on the next pull.

Open your dataset card and add this to the YAML header:.

That is the whole integration. Keep rl-environment, then list every framework that can load your files. If your environment works with a framework we have not registered yet, open a PR to the list of supported libraries.

The docs have the full reference.

In a recent development, we opened PRs to tag some of the environments people already train on. If you maintain one of these, merge the PR and your environment shows up in the filter.

The first version generates one default snippet per framework. Per-config snippets are next, so a repo with several task sets can show the right command for each. After that we will look at structural detection for frameworks with strict layouts. It would also be really cool build custom task UIs, we’ve been experimenting with this here:.

In a recent development, the bigger goal is for framework tagging to be automatic everywhere. OpenEnv already does it on upload. If you maintain Harbor, Verifiers, Nemo Gym, or any other environment framework, add the tags in your push path. It is a few lines, and every environment your users publish becomes visible to everyone else.

Industry observers note that if you train agents, go browse the filter. If you build environments, publish and tag them, whether they cover coding, tool use, games, robotics, or another task. Include the files, a working run command, and the rule that produces the reward so others can use them. If your framework is missing, contribute it to the list of supported libraries.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Transport for London (TfL) has copped to another cybersecurity breach, this time involving the account details of around 265,000 Oyster photocard customers.
  • Industry observers note that the capital's transport operator told The Register it first became aware something was amiss on November 16, when Oyster photocard customers started receiving emails asking them to create accounts they already had.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Around 265,000 customers potentially affected as London transport operator grapples with another security breach.

Transport for London (TfL) has copped to another cybersecurity breach, this time involving the account details of around 265,000 Oyster photocard customers.

Industry observers note that the capital's transport operator told The Register it first became aware something was amiss on November 16, when Oyster photocard customers started receiving emails asking them to create accounts they already had. The emails came from TfL's own systems, the transport body confirmed, but were generated as a result of the compromise.

Sources indicate that "We immediately took the TfL photocard website down while this was being investigated," mentioned Shashi Verma, TfL's director of technology strategy and revenue. "The protection of personal information is a priority for us, and I apologize to our customers affected by this incident.".

In a recent development, tfL reckons its speedy response spared a considerable number of customers from having their details compromised. The transport operator notes it has since contained the incident and contacted those potentially affected, though it is rather more forthcoming about what the hackers didn't get their hands on than what they did.

It has been revealed that tfL says no passwords, bank or payment card details, or customer journey information were compromised. It also believes the names and dates of birth of children with Zip Oyster cards were unaffected.

Among those whose accounts may have been compromised are holders of Zip Oyster cards – issued to children as young as five – as well as students, apprentices, care leavers, veterans, and Londoners aged 60 and over.

Despite the assurances about passwords, TfL says it will ask all photocard customers to change theirs, along with their security questions and answers. Those in the habit of recycling passwords across multiple websites are being advised to change them elsewhere, too.

Sources indicate that tfL indicates it has yet to find any evidence that the compromised data has been used and has notified the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO). The transport operator hasn't disclosed how the perpetrators got into its systems.

It has been revealed that existing photocards will still let holders through the ticket barriers, though anyone needing to renew one or check their journey history will have to contact TfL's customer services team while the website is out of action. There's no word yet on when it'll be back.

"We hope to restore the affected website services as swiftly as possible," Verma mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that tfL should be well versed in dealing with data breaches by now. In March, the transport operator told The Register it had notified more than 7 million customers following its September 2024 cyberattack. The hackers had accessed systems holding customers' names, email addresses, and home addresses, while around 5,000 customers were contacted as a priority because their bank account details may also have been compromised.

In a recent development, two teenagers were subsequently charged in connection with the attack, which authorities linked to the notorious Scattered Spider cybercrime crew. The ICO looked into that incident but opted not to take enforcement action against TfL, having deemed its response proportionate. There's nothing at present to suggest the two incidents are related.

Londoners can at least rest assured that their Oyster photocards still work. Whether the information they handed over to obtain them is in someone else's hands is another matter. ®.

Breaking: sysdeck: Raycast for Linux & BSD

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Introducing sysdeck, a command center for Linux and the BSDs that searches applications, files, the clipboard history and more from a single hotkey, and that only runs when you call it.

Sources indicate that in August I started working on a tool that I had been missing on my Linux desktop for a while, and for which I tried to build a somewhat glued-together mess of scripts that used bemenu to do what I wanted. At some point, though, I figured that I should probably try to put together an actual program, ideally using Zig and GTK.

I wanted something that, just like bemenu (or rofi, or wofi, or whatnot), is basically a single popup that I can open with a hotkey and type a few letters into, to start an application, find a file, paste something I copied an hour ago, or convert a currency without opening a browser. Now, roughly three months later, I think I got it to a point where it’s worth publishing for others to try. It’s called sysdeck, and the way I describe it is the less bloated Linux/BSD equivalent of Raycast on macOS.

In a recent development, yes, I’m aware that the title of this post is clickbait. sysdeck isn’t a port of Raycast, it doesn’t share a single line of code with it, and it doesn’t come with an extension store or a subscription initiative. However, Raycast is the name that probably most people know for this kind of tool, and considering that you’re here, reading this post, the title has obviously done its job. :-).

sysdeck is supposed to be bound to a hotkey in your window manager. When you press it, a window appears in which you start typing, and sysdeck shows the matching entries from your applications, command-line executables, files and folders, browser bookmarks, clipboard history, open Sway windows, SSH hosts, Podman containers, text snippets and emoji. Return acts on the selected entry depending on its kind, meaning it rolls out an application, opens a file or copies a clipboard entry back. Holding Alt opens a context menu with further actions. Selected images are shown along with their EXIF data, and executables show their manual page underneath the list unless the man extension is disabled in the config.

Besides searching, sysdeck calculates and converts units and currencies using the library behind whats. It also controls running media players via MPRIS, connects and disconnects NetworkManager connections, and takes screenshots of a region, a window or the whole screen. If you configure a Gemini, OpenAI or Anthropic model, or any OpenAI-compatible server, it also sends your questions to an LLM. It keeps track of what you pick and ranks its suggestions accordingly so that it can show you recommendations that matter to your personal workflow.

Oh, and its --dmenu mode can replace dmenu in scripts, just like a single line in your Sway configuration lets it replace clipboard managers like cliphist.

Recent findings suggest that what I’d like sysdeck to become is the one command center from which you start, find and control everything on a Linux or BSD desktop, instead of the collection of single-purpose tools and scripts that a typical tiling window manager setup combines for launching programs, managing the clipboard, picking emoji and taking screenshots. As mentioned before, sysdeck is written in Zig, uses GTK4 for its interface and keeps its indexes in SQLite.

Sources indicate that one part of sysdeck’s design that differs from most launchers that come with more advanced features is that sysdeck doesn’t use a background service. This is deliberate and will stay that way for the foreseeable future.

Sources indicate that raycast, for example, keeps running at all times, so that its window can appear the instant you press the hotkey. sysdeck, however, only runs when you ask for it. Every press of the hotkey starts a upcoming process that indicates the window, does what you asked it to do, and exits as soon as you pick an entry, press Escape or switch to another window. Whenever one of its indexes is older than its configured maximum age, sysdeck rebuilds it on a separate thread while the window is open, and searches the existing index in the meantime.

Similarly, even the clipboard history works without a resident process of its own, because wl-paste starts a lightweight sysdeck process (that only loads the absolute necessary bits) for every copy. That run records the entry and exits again, all within 10 to 20 milliseconds. The price for all of this is a start time of about a tenth of a second on my machine, most of which GTK spends on building and presenting the window. In my opinion this “slight delay” is a fair trade over running a background service, because RAM has become expensive and hard to get, as I’ve outlined in my posts on holding on to your hardware and on dealing with faulty RAM, and I believe that a program that is on screen for only a few seconds at a time shouldn’t occupy memory and eat up CPU cycles for the rest of the day.

sysdeck uses the whats library for conversions and can convert various units and currencies.

You can configure custom web search engines and search them directly from sysdeck, which then opens your default browser with the results.

sysdeck can be configured to index specific folders and include their contents in its search results. In disk mode it reveals only those items.

Using MPRIS, sysdeck can control media players and trigger actions such as play, pause, skip the current track or go back to the previous one, and it can also show what is presently playing from within its UI.

sysdeck builds an index of all available emoji and lets you search for individual ones using keywords that make sense, so that you find the one you’re looking for, which it then copies to your clipboard on Return.

Podman containers can be started and stopped from within sysdeck, which also shows the current status of each individual container.

In a recent development, anyway, sysdeck is open source under the SEGV License and its primary repository is on tty.fail, with a mirror on GitHub that also publishes pre-built binaries. The latest release includes builds for Linux on x86_64, aarch64, riscv64, powerpc64le and s390x, each for glibc as well as musl, a musl build for loongarch64, and x86_64 builds for FreeBSD, NetBSD and OpenBSD. The binaries use your system’s GTK4 libraries. If you’d rather build sysdeck yourself, the README lists the packages you need on each of these systems.

If a keyboard-driven command center that only runs when you need it sounds like your kind of thing, give sysdeck a try, and let me know how it works for you in the community channel.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Holo4 is our new series of agentic models.
  • Industry observers note that holo4 builds on our previous model and interacts with software through any available interface: GUIs, code, MCP and APIs.
  • It has been revealed that holo4 clicks and types on a screen, writes and runs its own code, and calls MCP or API tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Holo4 is our new series of agentic models. It comes in two sizes: 27B dense and 35B-A3B Mixture of Experts. Both are available on the H Models API. We are also releasing an updated version of Holotron 3: Holotron4 Nano.

Industry observers note that holo4 builds on our previous model and interacts with software through any available interface: GUIs, code, MCP and APIs. It scores well on academic benchmarks, but we built it for real business workflows. It was trained through supervised and reinforcement learning on a large set of environments and tasks, including those generated by our Agentic Task Factory.

It has been revealed that holo4 clicks and types on a screen, writes and runs its own code, and calls MCP or API tools. It uses whichever fits the task. Most agentic models are trained for one interface only: GUI-focused models are blind without a screen, while models that prefer tool calling are stuck in front of an application that has no API. Real work is not siloed that way, and a single business task can require combining these different approaches.

Holo4 runs on desktops, on the web, on Android, in a code sandbox and against business APIs. It is the same model in each case and it is called the same way. You do not need to select a different model for each platform.

Holo4 models improve significantly over their Qwen base. Holo4 trails only the strongest closed models on long workflows: on OSWorld 2.0, Holo4 27B scores 61.7% against 81.8% for Opus 5.5, and Holo4 35B-A3B reaches 30.9%. However, it does so with orders of magnitude fewer parameters and at a much lower cost. We open-source every trajectory behind our scores on public benchmarks: replay each step at trajectories.hcompany.ai or download them from Hugging Face.

On the hardest academic benchmarks for desktop control (OSWorld 2.0) and API use (AutomationBench), Holo4 competes with frontier models at a much lower cost per task.

Sources indicate that our internal set of agentic pipelines builds interactive environments and verifiable tasks from documentation alone, such as screenshots of real websites or open-source software. So far it has produced about 10,000 tasks across web apps, MCP servers and desktop environments, including hybrid environments that expose the same state through a GUI and MCP.

According to recent reports, alongside training, we rebuilt our harness, the loop that executes the model's actions and manages its context over hundreds of steps, using feedback from agentic performance on OSWorld 2.0. Agents tagged why each task failed and engineers reviewed their fixes. The largest changes were giving the agent a reliable memory that can keep track of hundreds of steps, and a shell on the desktop machine itself.

According to recent reports, opus 5 (70.2%) and GPT-5.6 Sol (66.2%) use max-effort partial rewards on the v2026.08.08 offline set from OpenAI's launch chart, as in the cost-performance plot. Other reference scores come from model cards and the official leaderboard. Task releases, subsets and harnesses vary.

Our post-training stack is designed to adapt to new foundation models and produce agents that generalize across interfaces and environments. As a member of the NVIDIA Nemotron Coalition, we applied our latest stack to the Nemotron 3 Nano Omni model as a follow-up to Holotron 3.

The same recipe turns Nemotron 3 Nano Omni into Holotron4 Nano, a generalist agentic model that significantly improves over the base model on GUI workflows and in environments exposing MCP, APIs or coding sandboxes.

Gains are absolute percentage-point improvements over Nemotron 3 Nano Omni.

In a recent development, these gains show that our recipe transfers well and can turn a generalist model into an agentic expert. Nothing in it is size-specific.

Both sizes are available today on the H Models API. Weights are on Hugging Face in BF16, FP8, NVFP4 and 4-bit GGUF, next to our small model, Holotron4 Nano.

We will release optimized DSpark drafter checkpoints in the coming days to further accelerate inference.

Yelp Migrates Cassandra to EKS by Moving EBS Volumes

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1007 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News Yelp Migrates Cassandra to EKS by Moving EBS Volumes.
  • Nov 18, 2026 4 min read.
  • In a recent development, yelp has moved its Cassandra fleet from legacy self-managed Kubernetes clusters to Amazon EKS by re-pointing existing EBS volumes at newly introduced pods, rather than streaming data between nodes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Yelp Migrates Cassandra to EKS by Moving EBS Volumes.

Nov 18, 2026 4 min read.

In a recent development, yelp has moved its Cassandra fleet from legacy self-managed Kubernetes clusters to Amazon EKS by re-pointing existing EBS volumes at newly introduced pods, rather than streaming data between nodes. A blog post by the site reliability team details a migration. It covered about 90 production clusters. There was zero downtime for customers and no data loss. The largest cluster, a 54-pod user-data store, took about 12 hours end to end.

Yelp had already moved its stateless workloads to EKS through its PaaSTA deployment layer, but Cassandra stayed behind. Kubernetes has no built-in way to migrate StatefulSets and their persistent volumes across clusters. The usual approach is to add nodes to the newly introduced cluster and shut down the old ones. This would temporarily double compute capacity but also lead to data transfer costs. For the largest clusters, streaming alone could have taken weeks. Yelp also considered a regional failover and rebuild, and a new Cassandra datacenter in EKS, but rated both as less transparent to customers.

Recent findings suggest that yelp's "Rolling PV Transplant" relies on the fact that an EBS volume is bound to an Availability Zone, not to a Kubernetes cluster, and that a PersistentVolume is effectively a pointer to a volume ID. The team pre-creates PVs and PVCs in EKS that reference the existing volume IDs, then creates an identical StatefulSet there, whose pods wait in ContainerCreating. The automation then deletes one pod at a time on the legacy cluster, waits for the volume to detach, and lets the EKS pod claim it. The pod rejoins the ring with the same data and token range, and the process repeats for the next pod. Cassandra's replication tolerates the few minutes each node is offline.

According to recent reports, yelp set a skipReconciliation: true flag on the custom resources in both clusters. This was done because two operators managed the same logical ring during the migration. The flag helped prevent them from conflicting over pod state. The flag was cleared on the EKS side at the end.

Across roughly 1,000 pods, about 1,000 TiB moved by pointer rather than over the wire. No node was ever decommissioned from the ring, so rollback was the same operation in reverse. Yelp used it a handful of times, for a missing subnet definition and a certificate mismatch, and restored pods within minutes. After a week of manual dev runs and a week of automation, one engineer ran the production rollout in about three weeks, migrating three to six clusters on a typical day.

The team had Claude generate the orchestration script, roughly 800 lines of bash, from its validated manual runbook, rather than asking it to design the procedure. The script needed minor adjustments after two days of testing.

Recent findings suggest that the approach relies on a previous Container Storage Interface migration by Yelp's Compute Infrastructure team. This work gave the Data Infrastructure team confidence in the volume detach and attach process. Yelp also used the technique for Kafka clusters, and says it applies to any AZ-pinned stateful workload on Kubernetes. The legacy clusters are now retired.

Industry observers note that the one failure specific to this technique was a stale VolumeAttachment object left behind by the AWS CSI controller after pod deletion. The EKS pod sat in Pending with no error, and deleting the object on the legacy cluster fixed it. Yelp advises building explicit timeouts for stalled detach and attach operations into any automation. Two other findings were unrelated to the mechanism. Backups failed with IAM AccessDenied errors for 48 hours because a upcoming -eks role was not yet being assumed by scheduled jobs, and the alert only filed a ticket instead of paging. Pausing repairs for the migration also exposed one cluster whose repairs had been silently disabled for three months, leaving accumulated data inconsistencies. Teams planning a similar move should audit repair state, backup IAM roles and alert severity before starting.

Sources indicate that yelp's approach is not the only way to move Cassandra between EKS clusters. Monday.com's engineering team describes a different one in a post on zero-downtime Cassandra migration between EKS clusters. K8ssandra-managed clusters had to move without any downtime or data loss. So, the team created a workflow to add new Cassandra data centers, safely transfer data, and remove the old ones. That is the streaming model Yelp considered and rejected. The new cluster is brought up alongside the old one and receives data over the network, and the original is retired only afterwards. The team believes success relied more on control, automation, and handling failures than on speed. They automated long tasks like rebuilds and planned the migration in stages based on operator behavior.

Sources indicate that the two migrations differ in what they trade away. Yelp's disk transplant skips data transfer and extra compute. It allows for a rollback by swapping the pointer. However, it relies on EBS volumes being linked to an Availability Zone, not a cluster. Monday.com's approach does not rely on that property, and it keeps the old environment intact until the end. The cost is a longer migration and the capacity to run both sides at once, which Yelp calculated would have taken weeks for its largest clusters.

Sources indicate that despite the different mechanics, the post-migration lessons are similar. Monday.com devotes part of its write-up to verifying that backups work after the migration, along with monitoring, dashboards and alerts. Yelp's own backups failed on an IAM role mismatch within 48 hours of its first production clusters landing in EKS. Teams planning either approach should treat those checks as part of the migration plan, not as cleanup afterwards.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness.

📅 29 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1823 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Getting the Source Right, Not Just the Fact: Source-Aware Verification for MCP Agents

📅 29 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1823 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tool-using LLM agents no longer read from a single retrieved passage.
  • According to recent reports, our latest paper, ProvenanceGuard: Source-Aware Factuality Verification for MCP-Based LLM Agents (read it on Hugging Face, or on arXiv in the meantime), targets that gap.
  • Consider a customer support agent that answers, "According to the account record, this initiative includes a 30-day refund window." The refund window may be perfectly real, but stated in a policy document, not in the account record the answer points to.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tool-using LLM agents no longer read from a single retrieved passage. Through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an agent can call a search tool, inspect a structured patient or account record, query a database, and pull metadata, then weave all of it into one answer. That m aakes the usual question of factuality more subtle than it looks. Most of the systems built to check LLM answers, from RAGAS faithfulness to fine-grained checkers like MiniCheck, AlignScore, and SummaC, ask whether a claim is supported by the available evidence once that evidence has been pooled together. In their usual form, they do not tell us which MCP tool output supports each claim, or whether that is the source the answer names.

According to recent reports, our latest paper, ProvenanceGuard: Source-Aware Factuality Verification for MCP-Based LLM Agents (read it on Hugging Face, or on arXiv in the meantime), targets that gap. The failure mode we care about is one we call cross-source conflation: a claim that is true somewhere in the evidence, but attributed to the wrong source. A source-blind verifier may pass it, because the fact does exist in the pool. A source-aware verifier should not.

Consider a customer support agent that answers, "According to the account record, this initiative includes a 30-day refund window." The refund window may be perfectly real, but stated in a policy document, not in the account record the answer points to. Pool the two together and the claim looks supported. Keep them separate and the attribution is wrong, and in a data-sensitive setting a wrong attribution can be as damaging as a wrong fact. The same pattern highlights up in a clinical agent, where a patient-specific medication detail taken from a patient-history tool becomes misleading the moment the answer presents it as a finding from the medical literature.

A claim can be supported by one MCP source while the answer attributes it to another. Source-blind scoring sees support in the pooled evidence and passes it; ProvenanceGuard separately checks whether the supporting source matches the one the answer states or implies. Source: paper Figure 1.

This is why faithfulness scores, useful as they are, are not enough for MCP agents. An answer carries provenance, sometimes explicitly ("according to the account record") and sometimes implicitly. ProvenanceGuard keeps that connection between claim and source available for inspection.

In a recent development, provenanceGuard is a post-generation verification layer that sits on top of a black-box MCP agent. It runs after an agent produces an answer, and never collapses the evidence into one anonymous context. Instead it carries the source identity all the way through the pipeline. It reads the captured MCP trace, including the tool outputs and their source IDs, without retraining the agent. Then it does five things in sequence: it breaks the answer into specific claims, finds the source most relevant to each one, checks whether that source actually supports it, compares the source with the one the answer names or implies, and finally emits both a per-claim source verdict and a global, answer-level allow or block decision.

It has been revealed that the verification flow. Source identity is preserved through decomposition, routing, support scoring, attribution checking, and repair, rather than being pooled. Blocked answers can go through RARR-style repair and be re-verified. Source: paper Figure 2.

A few of the design choices are worth calling out. For the experiments in our paper, we used local models so the captured traces could be processed in a controlled, offline setup: MiniLM helps find the relevant source, a DeBERTa NLI verifier model checks whether that source supports the claim, and a local language model helps break answers into claims. The verifier also checks literal values closely: a number, date, or identifier absent from the source cannot pass merely because the sentence sounds plausible. A calibrated decision step combines these signals. If an answer is blocked, a RARR-style repair step can try a source-grounded revision or a safe fallback, which the verifier then checks again.

Those named models are the setup we evaluated, not a requirement of ProvenanceGuard. The same claim, source, and decision steps can be adapted to hosted models where a team prefers cloud services; a fresh setup would need its own testing and calibration. Our reported results come from the local configuration. Its conservative decision policy suits data-sensitive review, where getting the source right matters more than producing the fastest possible answer.

Sources indicate that we tested ProvenanceGuard on answers from a medical agent that had used patient records, research articles, and other tools. This gave us 281 real traces to study. Medicine is a useful test because a fact from a patient's record and a fact from general research cannot be treated as the same source. The method can also be used in other fields when an agent keeps a record of its tool outputs and source IDs. For the main test, human experts checked 361 claims from 40 answers set aside from the data used to develop the system.

Industry observers note that the most direct result is this: experts said 139 claims should not pass, and ProvenanceGuard caught 138 of them. It let one through. It also held 67 claims that the experts considered supported, sending them for review or repair. This reflects the cautious setting we tested: it favors a second look at some supported claims over letting unsupported ones through. For claims with an identifiable source, it also picked the right source about 86% of the time in this test.

We ran four other support checkers on the same claims. ProvenanceGuard scored highest on the paper's measure of how well a system catches claims that should be blocked while avoiding unnecessary blocks. The other checkers in this comparison did not tell us which tool output supported each claim. ProvenanceGuard records that connection, so a reviewer can see the source checked for each claim and the decision it produced.

Recent findings suggest that binary support metrics on the same held-out claim packet. ProvenanceGuard matches or beats the source-blind baselines on blocking while also producing per-claim source verdicts. Source: paper abstract and Table III.

In a recent development, in a separate, harder test with several similar sources, ProvenanceGuard scored 0.846 F1 for deciding which claims to block, but identified the exact source correctly in 50.3% of claims. Telling similar sources apart remains an crucial area for improvement.

We also ran a controlled test focused on wrong attribution: we changed the named source in 50 cases while leaving the supporting evidence intact. ProvenanceGuard caught all 50 swaps. This shows it can detect a clear source error, while the harder test shows the challenge of choosing among many plausible sources.

Blocking is only useful if there is something to do with a blocked answer. Wired to the RARR-style repair loop, the full-trace run resolved all 173 blocked answers, though 144 of them ended in fallback text rather than a substantive rewrite, which is the system choosing to avoid an unverifiable answer rather than manufacture one. On reconstructed multi-source test traces, a fresh repair run resolved all 59 initially blocked answers with only two terminal fallbacks. As an offline gate the overhead is modest, roughly half a second per answer on the reported local configuration, with the NLI and routing calls themselves in the tens of milliseconds.

It has been revealed that as agents move from single-passage RAG to multi-tool MCP setups, the question of which source a fact actually came from stops being a footnote and becomes part of what factuality means. ProvenanceGuard makes that source connection visible claim by claim. For Multiverse Computing, that means a way to check existing agents while keeping sensitive traces in a controlled environment when needed. The medical study is one use case; the same approach can be adapted wherever an agent's trace preserves its tools and sources.

That adaptation is already visible in NVIDIA NVFlow, which merged an optional grounding-verification stage for its finance agent. It checks completed answers against the SEC excerpts the agent retrieved and saves separate decisions without changing the original rollout or training data. The NVFlow contribution uses ProvenanceGuard's source-aware verification approach; the repair loop discussed above belongs to the broader research system.

ProvenanceGuard was also presented as a poster at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 at UC Berkeley.

Industry observers note that want the full technical details, including the routing and NLI derivations, the calibration ablations, the multi-source stress slices, and the complete results tables? Read the full paper on Hugging Face, or get in touch with our team to talk about applying source-aware verification to your own agents.

The failure mode that matters for MCP agents is quieter than "hallucination": a claim that is true somewhere in the pooled tool outputs, attributed to the wrong source.

Source-blind faithfulness can still go green in that case — the fact exists in the soup. Source-aware verification is the contract upgrade: keep tool/source IDs through claim decomposition, support check, and attribution check, then allow/block with a per-claim source verdict a reviewer can actually inspect.

According to recent reports, practical ask for teams wiring MCP: when your eval notes "grounded," does it mean supported-by-any-tool-output, or supported-by-the-source-the-answer-named? Those are different release gates. In multi-tool setups the second one is the one that catches cross-source conflation before a human trusts the citation.

Industry observers note that hi, thank you for your comment. You’ve captured the problem well. For ProvenanceGuard, when a claim is “grounded” it means it is supported by the source the answer names or implies. Finding the fact somewhere else in the tool outputs isn’t enough. In the refund-window example, the policy supports the fact, but the answer credits the account record, so we flag the mismatch and show the source verdict.

I had a brief read on the paper, but I could not find any comparison with cheaper llm agent for source aware judge. Like this is my reading of the paper;.

Sources indicate that like, it seems (2 - 5) can be done via basic prompts in lifecycle, if you own the executing agent. If not, this can also be done via hooks in harness as plugin. Do you have any comparison on this. Basically, how much of random forest, and all of these eng/plumbing is buying, vs second llm call over traces+ans?

Hi, fair question. A source-aware LLM judge could do these checks, and we don’t report a direct comparison with a cheaper one in the paper.

However, part of our motivation is that introducing an LLM judge can itself give inconsistent verdicts or confuse sources (the same kinds of errors we’re trying to catch). A second LLM call can therefore introduce new errors of its own. ProvenanceGuard uses explicit source tracking and calibrated support checks to reduce reliance on another generative judgment. The comparison you suggest would indeed be a useful further study to quantify the benefit in accuracy, latency and cost.

  • A project can have a clear brief and still miss its deadline.
  • Both appear in our best AI collaboration tools guide.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that unite.AI may receive compensation when you use links to products we review. This does not influence our editorial evaluations. Read our affiliate disclosure.

A project can have a clear brief and still miss its deadline. It can also have every task assigned while nobody can find the reasoning behind it. ClickUp and Notion address both problems, but they organize the work differently. ClickUp is our stronger choice for coordinating delivery across a team. Notion is our pick when documents, shared knowledge, and flexible databases are the center of the work.

Both appear in our best AI collaboration tools guide. This comparison looks more closely at the decision between them: where your team will blueprint, discuss, document, and finish its work, and how much of that routine AI can help carry forward.

According to recent reports, clickUp makes the most sense when a team needs a dependable answer to three questions: who owns this, when is it due, and what is blocking it? Tasks sit inside a shared hierarchy, with views that let different people work from the same underlying records. A contributor can follow a task list while a project lead works through the schedule and a manager watches a dashboard.

Sources indicate that the surrounding tools matter because delivery rarely happens inside a task description alone. ClickUp Docs can hold the brief, comments can capture a decision, and Chat can keep the discussion close to the work. Its native time tracking adds another useful connection for agencies and service teams that need to understand the effort behind an assignment. That combination gives ClickUp a broader role than a simple board of cards.

Official ClickUp walkthrough of project management with ClickUp Brain.

Recent findings suggest that our recommendation is ClickUp for teams managing recurring launches, client delivery, or several interdependent projects. The tradeoff is the amount of structure available. Spaces, fields, statuses, and dashboards become helpful when the team uses them consistently; a workspace full of competing conventions creates more administration. ClickUp rewards a clear process and someone willing to keep that process coherent.

Sources indicate that notion is particularly appealing when a project begins with something people need to understand together: a research collection, a product proposal, a customer problem, or a set of operating principles. A page can contain the explanation, supporting material, and connected database views. The workspace grows around the information instead of requiring every useful detail to become a task.

That does not make Notion merely a notebook. Its project tools include tasks, subtasks, dependencies, timelines, and filtered views, while database properties give teams control over how they organize the work. A product team can connect a roadmap to specifications and meeting notes; an editorial team can keep an assignment beside its brief and reference material. The appeal is having the plan and its context together in a form that is easy to shape.

Official Notion introduction to projects and tasks.

We recommend Notion for teams whose most valuable shared asset is their knowledge. Its flexibility suits company wikis, product planning, research, and documentation-heavy collaboration. The same openness creates a responsibility: somebody needs to own the page structure, shared databases, and maintenance of important information. Notion is at its best when colleagues can find a reliable answer, rather than several attractive pages saying slightly different things.

Recent findings suggest that consider a ten-person team preparing a feature launch. It needs a brief, customer research, a landing page, an announcement email, and a clear record of approvals. Here is how we would organize the same work in each platform.

In ClickUp, we would keep the approved brief in a Doc beside the launch tasks. That is the more convenient arrangement when the team already runs delivery there and needs the document to support execution.

Recent findings suggest that our choice: ClickUp for coordinating the handoffs. Give the landing page, email, and release checklist separate tasks, owners, deadlines, and definitions of done. Link dependent work so a delayed approval has a visible consequence for delivery.

Recent findings suggest that in Notion, we would use a shared task database with an owner, status, and due date, linked back to the relevant brief. A board can support the weekly review while a timeline reveals the schedule. The advantage is that the task remains a page with room for context.

If a manager asks which launch deliverables are late or blocked, ClickUp is our stronger choice for operational oversight. If a teammate asks why the message changed or where the supporting research lives, Notion is our preferred workspace for the answer. A small team can handle both jobs in either product; the recommendation depends on which question dominates its week.

Recent findings suggest that consider a launch involving design, engineering, marketing, and customer support. The brief matters, but so do dependencies, changing deadlines, outstanding approvals, and the work each team can absorb. ClickUp gives that operating detail a more prominent place. Its Gantt views, task relationships, reporting, and time records make it the stronger choice when coordination is the difficult part.

Notion can organize a launch too. Its timelines and task databases are useful, especially when the project is closely tied to specifications and research. We would choose it for a smaller product team that spends as much time developing the proposal as tracking delivery. As the need for operational oversight grows, ClickUp becomes the more compelling primary project system.

Recent findings suggest that for onboarding guides, company policies, research libraries, and product documentation, Notion offers a particularly natural structure. Pages can become a team home, a wiki, or a database-backed collection without losing the surrounding explanation. That makes it easier to build a workspace around how people look for information.

ClickUp’s connected Docs are a credible alternative, especially when the document supports a task or project already managed there. Real-time editing, comments, and links to work reduce the distance between discussion and action. Our preference is Notion for a knowledge-centered workspace, and ClickUp Docs when delivery is already the organizing principle.

ClickUp Brain² draws on tasks, documents, and conversations to answer questions and help produce work. Its AI tools can create and edit tasks and Docs. Its strongest practical case is proximity to execution: the assistant can work with the same project context the team uses to coordinate delivery. Agents extend that approach into recurring work. For managers who want help gathering updates and moving a shared process forward, ClickUp is our preferred fit.

Notion AI works across pages and databases, with an agent that creates and edits pages and databases, Custom Agents, meeting notes, and search across supported connected sources. We favor it for turning shared knowledge into useful output: developing a brief, finding an earlier decision, organizing research, or preparing an update from workspace material. Its enterprise search is currently labeled beta.

Sources indicate that neither assistant can make an abandoned workspace reliable by itself. The meaningful advantage comes from putting AI beside the information people actually maintain. Choose ClickUp when that information is primarily an active delivery system; choose Notion when it is a living collection of documents and databases.

Sources indicate that for ClickUp, a useful request is: “Extract the launch actions from these notes. Keep the stated owner and deadline; flag missing information instead of inventing it.” Brain can turn selected Doc text into proposed action items, and the team can create tasks from its response. That is a concrete handoff from discussion to execution.

Recent findings suggest that for Notion, we would start with the brief and connected research: “Draft a launch summary using these pages, link the supporting decisions, and organize the agreed actions in our task database.” Notion Agent can create and edit pages and databases within the user’s access. We prefer this approach when the shared knowledge is the assistant’s most useful context.

It has been revealed that the practical limit is the action each assistant can actually take. Notion Agent cannot create fresh database automations or change page-sharing permissions. Ask it to organize the work; use the workspace’s dedicated controls to set the recurring rule or grant access. For either product, review the generated assignments before treating a suggestion as someone’s commitment.

ClickUp’s automations fit work that moves through task stages. They can connect changes in a project with the next action, while integrations carry selected events into other tools. Its automation allowances are workspace-based: Core includes 1,000 actions a month and Business includes 10,000. Automations pause for the month when the allowance is exceeded.

Notion’s database automations act on changes to records, such as assigning an owner when a status changes or sending a notification. Most custom database automations require a paid initiative. An important limitation is that one database automation cannot trigger another, so a long chain of dependent rules needs a different design.

We prefer ClickUp for repeatable delivery processes and Notion for workflows built around a shared information collection. Both offer agents as well, but an agent doing open-ended work and a fixed rule changing a field serve different purposes.

Paid prices above are monthly equivalents with annual billing. ClickUp’s pricing page displays discounted Core and Business rates of $9 and $17 alongside regular rates of $12 and $25. Those displayed discounts should not be treated as a guaranteed renewal price. Notion lists Plus at $10 and Business at $20 per member per month with annual billing.

For this comparison’s AI workflows, the Business plans are the more useful starting point. ClickUp Business includes Brain², standard model use, and a pooled premium credit allowance. ClickUp lists 1,500 premium credits per user each month, pooled across the workspace. Notion Business generally gives each member 1,500 Standard credits and 500 Select credits monthly; its documentation notes that allowances can vary by purchase arrangement. Notion’s included credits are individual rather than pooled, and additional workspace-funded usage uses Notion credits. The vendors count usage differently, so 1,500 credits does not represent the same amount of work in both products. Notion’s credit guide explains that unused included credits do not roll over and that usage can pause when an allowance runs out.

It has been revealed that clickUp is our value pick when the subscription is replacing a project tracker, time tracker, and scattered delivery reporting. Notion earns its price when it becomes the team’s main knowledge workspace. The cheaper seat is less important than which tool removes a meaningful part of the team’s existing workload.

Sources indicate that for ongoing Business-level AI, ten paid ClickUp Business seats at the advertised $17 annual-billing rate total $2,040 a year. Ten Notion Business seats at $20 total $2,400 a year. These are annual commitments expressed as monthly seat prices, before tax and optional usage charges.

ClickUp’s displayed regular $25 rate would make the same ten-seat subscription $3,000 a year, so its offer should not be treated as a guaranteed renewal rate. The base subscription also does not promise unlimited use of every AI feature. Budget separately for additional usage or optional agents where they are needed.

Sources indicate that both products connect AI to workplace content, so the way information is shared matters. ClickUp offers document permissions and higher-tier administrative controls. Notion AI respects the user’s existing access, and Notion Business adds private teamspaces and granular database permissions. Enterprise governance is a separate buying decision in either product, rather than a feature every paid seat automatically includes.

ClickUp is our default recommendation for teams whose main challenge is delivering work together. It puts assignments, deadlines, supporting documents, communication, and reporting in a structure that can support a shared operating rhythm. Agencies, project leads, and teams coordinating several functions have the clearest reason to choose it.

Industry observers note that we recommend Notion when the team’s main challenge is preserving and using its knowledge. Its pages and databases are a stronger foundation for research, documentation, product thinking, and flexible planning. Choose it when understanding the work is the center of collaboration, and ClickUp when coordinating its delivery is the harder job.
