📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Minister calls notification delay 'not acceptable' after October attack on Irish banking player Wellington IT came to light in November.

An attack on software provider Wellington IT exposed saved payee details held by around 40 Irish credit unions, prompting a minister to criticize the tech giant's delay in notifying them.

Robert Troy, Ireland's minister of state with responsibility for credit unions, remarked the breach happened in October but many affected institutions only learned of it in recent days.

Troy told Irish broadcaster RTÉ that the breach occurred "sometime in October," and Wellington IT's delay in providing details to its credit union customers was "not acceptable.".

News of the challenges affecting Irish credit unions broke on Tuesday, although the government mentioned at the time it was only investigating a "possible cybersecurity incident" in the first instance, and did not name Wellington IT until Wednesday.

Affected credit unions mentioned attackers exploited a vulnerability in their provider's online banking platform between October 2 and 4. The flaw was closed on October 6.

Troy remarked the affected credit unions were only informed for the first time in recent days.

According to recent reports, the exposed records concern payees saved in members' online banking accounts. Those records can also be linked to the members who created them.

The information exposed varies between institutions and individual records, but disclosures list the following data types:.

Names on payee bank accounts and saved nicknames.

Business Identifier Codes (BICs).

International Bank Account Numbers (IBANs).

Internal reference numbers that do not identify customers.

According to recent reports, credit unions including St. Canice's said online banking passwords, PINs, and login credentials were unaffected, and that the exposed payee details did not provide access to members' accounts or funds.

St. Canice's warned members not to transfer money in response to anyone claiming it needed to be moved to safety because of the breach.

The CEO of Belfast-based Wellington IT, Colin Mitchell, mentioned in a statement that the firm notified the affected organizations "as soon as we confirmed the potential risk to customer data.".

He mentioned Wellington IT has engaged outside cybersecurity experts to help investigate the breach, and reported the matter to the relevant authorities.

Mitchell added: "We are directly supporting our customers in their assessment of the potential impact on affected individuals and to help them meet any applicable regulatory obligations.

"We recognize the importance of this matter to our customers and their members and are treating it with the utmost seriousness. We remain focused on completing a thorough investigation and communicating directly with our customers as the investigation progresses.".

Owned by Canadian firm Vencora, Wellington IT has offices in Belfast and Dublin, and provides credit unions with software, mobile apps, private cloud infrastructure, and fully managed services.

Around 40 credit unions in Ireland were affected, roughly a quarter of the national total, Troy noted.

Credit unions operate similarly to traditional banks, offering savings accounts and loans, but are owned by their members and are not-for-profit organizations.

Troy told RTÉ that cybersecurity is a constant challenge for financial institutions, as technology and threats evolve over time.

"What's most crucial is that financial institutions take all the right measures to mitigate against these threats and that is what is happening," he noted.

Separately, the UK's Financial Conduct Authority, Prudential Regulation Authority, and Bank of England opened a joint consultation on cyber resilience guidance on Thursday.

The FCA mentioned October brought its second-highest monthly tally of reported cyber incidents in five years, and the highest in 18 months. The proposed guidance clarifies how firms should meet existing requirements rather than introducing new rules. ®.

Latest Update: Open TTS Leaderboard: Scalable Evaluation for Multilingual Text-to-Speech and Voice Cloning

📅 30 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1393 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the pace of open-source text-to-speech (TTS) model releases has been incredible.
  • Evaluation, however, hasn't kept pace: it remains fragmented and unstandardized.
  • Industry observers note that these arenas compare models by presenting people with TTS outputs from two models, and asking them to choose one over the other.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the pace of open-source text-to-speech (TTS) model releases has been incredible. On the Hugging Face Hub (as of Sep 30, 2026) there are more than 8K TTS models available 🚀.

Evaluation, however, hasn't kept pace: it remains fragmented and unstandardized. The gold standard is human preference scores such as MOS or MUSHRA (more on metrics). To this end, several arena-based leaderboards have established themselves as useful reference points for the community:.

Industry observers note that these arenas compare models by presenting people with TTS outputs from two models, and asking them to choose one over the other. After collecting a sufficient number of votes, an Elo score is computed to rank models, typically with the Bradley–Terry model (see Voice Arena methodology).

While human preference is the ultimate decider, arenas cannot scale to keep up with the pace of TTS releases. This may partly explain why open-source models are underrepresented on arena-style leaderboards: as of Sep 30, 2026, only 16 of the 92 models on Artificial Analysis are open-weights, with a similar skew on Voice Arena. This likely reflects practical factors: adding an API model requires little more than an API key, whereas an open model must be hosted and served by the arena operator, and commercial providers have more reason to seek placement than open-source authors. Another limitation with arena-style evaluation is voter consistency: no arena can ensure that the same voters with the same criteria of “better” can consistently evaluate models over time. Even the preferences of a single person change over time (“A man cannot step into the same river twice” as famously said by Heraclitus).

To this end, we've built the Open TTS Leaderboard, which uses objective metrics to evaluate models on complementary aspects of performance:.

By relying on objective metrics evaluating a model drops from a couple weeks (for collecting votes) to a couple hours ⚡.

Importantly, the Open TTS Leaderboard does not replace human preference ranking. ASR-based WER provides a proxy for intelligibility, while speaker similarity estimates voice identity preservation. Neither directly measures naturalness, expressiveness, or listener preference. Nevertheless, they can even inform voting-based leaderboards which models to include in their evaluations.

It has been revealed that our intention with this leaderboard is for it to be shaped by the community; we want to hear your feedback so the evaluations stay relevant and insightful. The next few sections give an overview of main features of the Open TTS Leaderboard.

From the default view of the leaderboard, models are ranked by macro-average WER on the English splits of Seed TTS Eval (paper) and CV3 Eval (zero shot) (paper).

hexgrad/Kokoro-82M, Supertone/supertonic-3, and fishaudio/s2-pro lead the pack on English WER when averaged on these two splits, while the Pareto plots visualize which models strike a good balance between WER, batched inference (RTFx), and size.

In a recent development, english performance doesn't necessarily translate to other languages. Multiple languages can be toggled to rank models on multilingual performance. Seed TTS Eval only has audio for English and Chinese, so the other languages are simply the score on CV3 Eval (zero shot). Note that Chinese, Japanese, and Korean are character-based languages and so character error rate (CER) is reported, and the “Average WER” across languages is a macro-average across languages.

k2-fsa/OmniVoice, fishaudio/s2-pro, and FunAudioLLM/Fun-CosyVoice3-0.5B-2512 are strong multilingual models.

By toggling “Voice cloning”, the models that support this functionality (on the selected languages) can be compared.

Moreover, a SIM column for speaker similarity now appears in the table, as well as two more Pareto plots for visualizing the tradeoff between SIM, batched inference, and size.

The average WER of some models, such as bosonai/higgs-tts-3-4b and openbmb/VoxCPM2, improve under voice cloning, namely when a reference audio is provided.

Numbers only tell part of the story, and as mentioned earlier human preference is the ultimate decider. From the “Listen” tab, you can compare the generated outputs that are behind the metrics, to find which model(s) you prefer!

Pick the language/dataset you're interested in, whether you want to compare voice cloning, and optionally pick the models or listen to outputs from a random selection.

The “Listen” tab fills an important gap in existing TTS leaderboards: a space to explore model outputs of various models.

You can even give feedback on the generated outputs. As we collect more votes from the community, we may include this data on the leaderboard. So vote! But please login with your HF account to help us weed out spam/bots.

Recent findings suggest that the “Streaming” tab compares the streaming capabilities. Models are ranked by TTFA (time-to-first-audio), which quantifies how long a user waits after probing a model in order to obtain audio that can be played. This is important for voice agents and other interactive apps.

Recent findings suggest that for streaming models (✅ under “Streaming API”) it's the time until the first audio chunk arrives. For non-streaming models, it's the time until the whole utterance is generated, because playback can't start any earlier. Every model runs one audio at a time (batch size 1), on the same 50 English prompts from CV3-Eval, on the same hardware and in its default voice. We drop the first 3 runs as warm-up and report the median TTFA across the rest.

Sources indicate that the default view compares performance on an H200 GPU. Results are also available for CPU for a small (but growing) set of models!

kyutai/pocket-tts is a great model for streaming on both GPU and CPU!

Recent findings suggest that the goal of the Open TTS Leaderboard is not only to keep up with the incredible pace of TTS model releases, but to be shaped by the community; we want to hear your feedback so the evaluations stay relevant and insightful. Let us know which datasets, models, and metrics you want to see!

Sources indicate that we will soon open-source the evaluation scripts, much like the Open ASR Leaderboard repo, so that you can directly provide your feedback and suggestions via GitHub Concerns and PRs! Let's shape TTS evaluations together 🤗.

Glad this board splits multilingual TTS quality from voice-cloning identity instead of one aggregate green.

The check I'd keep reading: whether the ranking still holds when you hold language/domain fixed versus when cloning is the axis. Otherwise teams optimize the easier subscale and still call the result "SOTA TTS.".

Sources indicate that english performance doesn't necessarily translate to other languages. Multiple languages can be toggled to rank models on multilingual performance. Seed TTS Eval only has movie box audio for English and Chinese, so the other languages are simply the score on CV3 Eval (zero shot). Note that Chinese, Japanese, and Korean are character-based languages and so character error rate (CER) is reported, and the “Average WER” across languages is a macro-average across languages.

In a recent development, open TTS Leaderboard is an open evaluation platform designed to make multilingual text-to-speech and voice-cloning models easier to compare at scale. Traditional TTS arenas usually let people listen to outputs from two models and choose the one they prefer. Those votes can then be used to calculate an Elo-style score, often through approaches such as the Bradley–Terry model, giving users a simple way to understand how different systems perform based on human preference.

Human feedback remains an crucial part of evaluating speech quality, but relying only on arena-style voting can be difficult as new TTS models are released at a rapid pace. Open-source models can also face practical barriers because they generally need to be hosted and served by the evaluation platform, while API-based commercial models can be added more easily. This can result in open-weight systems being less visible on public leaderboards. Another challenge is consistency: people's preferences and listening criteria can change over time, meaning that votes collected months apart may not always represent exactly the same standards.

Open TTS Leaderboard aims to address these challenges by providing a scalable and transparent space for evaluating multilingual TTS and voice-cloning systems. The goal is to make comparisons easier to reproduce, expand coverage of open models, and provide useful evaluation signals alongside human preference. By bringing together scalable testing and community feedback, the project can help researchers, developers, and users better understand how speech models perform across different languages, voices, and use cases.

Sources indicate that gitHub repo with the eval scripts is public! https://github.com/huggingface/open-tts-leaderboard.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Nov 18, 2026 4 min read.
  • Recent findings suggest that AWS has published a technical walkthrough of tunnel endpoints, a VPC endpoint type launched in September that lets an application in one VPC reach every address in a CIDR range shared from another account, instead of one resource at a time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News AWS PrivateLink Tunnel Endpoints Open a Whole CIDR Range to Another Account.

Nov 18, 2026 4 min read.

Recent findings suggest that AWS has published a technical walkthrough of tunnel endpoints, a VPC endpoint type launched in September that lets an application in one VPC reach every address in a CIDR range shared from another account, instead of one resource at a time. The provider shares a CIDR-type resource configuration through AWS Resource Access Manager and the consumer creates a tunnel endpoint against it. From then on, anything inside the range is reachable, including resources that did not exist when the share was made.

Bruce Pinsky and Ashish Kumar of AWS frame it as a vendor-access problem, for "a vendor or service provider whose software must reach applications and resources in a customer's network." Until now, that meant a separate PrivateLink resource configuration per database or host, which breaks down when the resources are ephemeral, or the customer does not want to enumerate them. With a CIDR configuration, the customer defines a perimeter in address ranges, and "resources located outside the perimeter can't be reached by the vendor." Two further properties come with the design: the consumer and provider VPCs can use overlapping CIDR blocks, and connections "can start only from the consumer VPC, not from the provider network.".

(Source: AWS Networking & Content Delivery blog).

Sources indicate that on the r/aws thread about the September launch, the first question was what this does that VPC peering does not, from a self-described veteran of AWS's advanced networking components. The answers that followed are the use cases: a peering connection exposes the whole VPC in both directions, while a tunnel endpoint shares a subset of the address space in one direction only; one commenter at a bank wrote that "peering with unregulated partners is a massive no-no, the auditors will rip you to shreds for it." Another pointed to clusters that do client-side load balancing, such as self-managed Kafka or Aerospike, which until now needed port-based routing on a Network Load Balancer and a separate port-mapping horizon for connections arriving over an interface endpoint. The same thread drew the line against VPC Lattice itself: Lattice services work at layer 7, tunnel endpoints at layer 4 without a resource configuration per target.

Sources indicate that the unusual part is on the consumer side: the application's traffic has to arrive at the tunnel endpoint wrapped in GENEVE, the encapsulation protocol defined in RFC 8926, over UDP port 6081 and in the same Availability Zone. The endpoint strips the header, checks that the inner destination falls inside the shared range, rewrites the source to a resource gateway address, and forwards a plain packet into the provider VPC. Linux can do the wrapping in the kernel. The walkthrough creates an ip link add ... type geneve id 0 device inside its own network namespace with a default route through it, which sends the provider's ranges into the tunnel and leaves the instance's other traffic alone. On the far side, the resources see the resource gateway as the client, so the post advises security groups that reference the gateway's security group or subnet rather than a single address.

It has been revealed that the documentation lists the constraints. Inner traffic must be TCP, with UDP permitted only for DNS, so ICMP and ping do not work, and IP fragments are dropped. Private DNS names are not supported on tunnel endpoints. The endpoint's subnets must sit in Availability Zones that overlap with the resource gateway's, or the association demonstrates as inaccessible. A resource gateway's DNS setting cannot be changed after creation. And the access logs identify the consumer's endpoint but carry no field for the inner source address, so a provider can attribute traffic to a vendor and not to a workload behind that vendor's endpoint. The post also warns that sharing 0.0.0.0/0 grants access to everything the provider VPC can route to, including networks behind VPC peering, Direct Connect or a Site-to-Site VPN, and recommends sharing the narrowest ranges that work.

Both points have been tested in practice. Ryo Suzuki of the Japanese consultancy Classmethod connected two VPCs that both use 10.0.0.0/16 and got HTTP through, but only by running a GENEVE relay as root on the client, by routing a /32 per destination host, or by putting an HAProxy or NAT instance in front, each of which adds a hop or a single point of failure; his conclusion was that "route management according to the number of destinations is required." In a second experiment, he shared 0.0.0.0/0 from a VPC with a NAT gateway and reached the internet from a VPC with no gateway at all, which confirmed AWS's warning from the other side; he judged it workable as a temporary path and "difficult to use in a permanent production setup.".

Pricing is an hourly charge per tunnel endpoint plus a per-GB charge for data processed, under PrivateLink pricing, with the provider side billed per GB through the resource gateway under VPC Lattice pricing, and the feature is available in 28 regions. Terraform support followed from the community: a contributor request opened two days after launch was implemented by another contributor and shipped in version 6.71.0 of the AWS provider, as a Tunnel endpoint type on aws_vpc_endpoint and a cidr_resource block on the Lattice resource configuration.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apps retire in June 2027, with no automatic task migration and no Planner replacement for personal accounts.

Microsoft has slipped some bad news into this week's Ignite AI puffery: the To Do apps are retiring on June 30, 2027, ending a journey that began with its acquisition of Wunderlist more than a decade ago.

Sources indicate that the confirmation came in an announcement about unified tasks and plans for Copilot and Microsoft 365. Until now, there was To Do or Planner (in basic or premium guise). The idea is "a single system for tracking your work as an individual, as a team, and as an organization." To Do contributes features to that future, but its apps don't get to join it.

It has been revealed that the problem is that Planner doesn't do everything To Do does. Microsoft would like customers to migrate to Planner but, by the firm's own admission, there are plenty of gaps. No native Windows or Mac desktop apps are planned to replace To Do; file attachments aren't supported on tasks in the Planner private blueprint, and there's no equivalent to To Do list groups in Planner. "Equivalent To Do printing and email-list capabilities are not presently planned for the replacement experience," and so on.

Sources indicate that existing To Do tasks and lists won't migrate to Planner either. They'll remain accessible through Planner until June 30, 2027, but that access ends with the apps. Microsoft says the date does not itself trigger deletion of the underlying data.

Very much a case of "don't let the door hit you on the way out.".

Sources indicate that unifying tasks and aims is a good idea – the current situation does create confusion, as Microsoft acknowledged. However, taking an axe to To Do, which was developed to be a successor to Wunderlist (acquired in 2015 for a figure between $100 million and $200 million, an early action under Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella), seems extreme.

Microsoft calls the replacement "a unified platform for people and agents across Microsoft 365" and stated: "This unified platform makes accessing Planner through Copilot, Cowork and Autopilot easier.".

Some users responding to the announcement were unimpressed, with one declaring "What a mess," and another asking if To Do might be spun off into an open source project: "Not everything needs to be put into an AI/Copilot agent.".

According to recent reports, indeed, it doesn't. But a useful service that doesn't ram Copilot and AI integration down customers' throats at every opportunity? That would never do.

Sources indicate that the message for To Do users appears to be: Get with the Strategy(ner) or just get out. ®.

#46428. Tech Report: Design for Understandability

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 28m • 📚 Deep Dive (5638 w)

Tech Report: Design for Understandability

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 28 min read (5638 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jschuster

⏱️ ~28 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that this is a talk I gave at Google’s internal Code Health Summit in November of 2025.
  • Industry observers note that in a world where LLMs generate much of our code, understanding that code is more important than ever.
  • It has been revealed that there’s a better way to go about this.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that this is a talk I gave at Google’s internal Code Health Summit in November of 2025. I’m sharing it here in the hopes that it sparks further learning and discussion.

Industry observers note that in a world where LLMs generate much of our code, understanding that code is more important than ever. But with a system as large and complex as Google’s codebase, SWEs can easily fall into a pattern of learned helplessness where the best you can do is tweak the code and pray that it passes the tests. Without understanding, LLMs are little more than complexity-generating machines running at top speed.

It has been revealed that there’s a better way to go about this. Just as our industry has learned to design software for testability, we can also design it for understandability. We can use ideas like design by contract, class invariants, modularity, and more to create systems that we can understand one piece at a time, rather than piling more onto the big ball of mud and hoping it doesn’t all collapse.

According to recent reports, is it easy? No. But is it worthwhile? Absolutely. These ideas aren’t new, but they’re not nearly as widely taught or well understood as they deserve to be, and mastering them leads to a world where we can have more confidence in our code and increase velocity at the same time.

Industry observers note that hi everyone, thanks for having me! Let’s get started.

I’d like to start this talk with a question: If LLMs can code, then what is left for human SWEs?

Industry observers note that the tech industry is quickly looking to large language models to write all of our code. But you might say: isn’t writing code our job as software engineers? Where does this leave the responsibility of SWEs? What is the essential human element that SWEs add on top of LLMs?

In a recent development, every one of you is going to have a different answer to this question, and that’s fine. But here’s my take.

Recent findings suggest that that necessary human element is judgment. Judgment of whether the code is maintainable. Judgment of whether it is healthy.

It has been revealed that LLMs can follow patterns and generate code that looks like what it was trained on. Sometimes they can produce useful tips and critiques for a piece of code. But that critical piece of judgment, of deciding whether some code is suitable for the task it was designed for, is still up to you, the human.

Industry observers note that because here’s the thing: LLMs today are still a sloppy intern. Sometimes the code they produce is good, but sometimes it’s completely off-track and needs correcting. You wouldn’t incorporate a sloppy intern’s code into your system without a close review first, so you shouldn’t do so for an LLM’s code either.

YOU are responsible for the quality of your code, regardless of whether you had an LLM generate it for you or wrote it the old-fashioned way with fingers on a keyboard.

According to recent reports, so where does that leave us? If LLMs are going to write a lot of the code for us, then we’re looking at a future where we humans are going to spend less time writing code, and more time reading code and understanding it, in order to make sure it passes our quality bar.

This means it’s more crucial than ever to get better at understanding code, and to speed up that reading and understanding process.

Now: if you want to get better at something, it’s helpful to set an aspirational goal for yourself. Something that’s above your current skill level, and drives you to get better and better every day.

Here’s the goal I propose: we should be able to predict the behavior of every line of code, without running a single test.

Let me say that again: We should be able to predict the behavior of every line of code, without running a single test.

Now, I know you may be thinking: “Understand every line of code? Without testing? Are you serious?! There’s way too much complexity and legacy code for me to ever be able to do that!”.

Recent findings suggest that you might think so. And if we take our hands off the wheel and relinquish all control, you might be right. But I’m here to tell you there’s a better way.

We can design our code to be understandable.

In a recent development, consider that a decade or two ago, we used to think that writing multiple tests for every public method in an API would have been infeasible. It wasn’t because we didn’t want to, or that we weren’t trying. It was because we hadn’t designed our code to make testing possible at that level. But gradually, across the software industry, we changed our practices to design for testability. Today, designing our code for testability is so ingrained into our culture that doing anything else is practically unthinkable. We can do the same for understandability, so that our code enables us to understand it better.

Industry observers note that our own Code Health guide makes a strong case for understandability. It claims “For code to be sustainable, it must be understood. Change cannot be made unless a developer knows what the system currently provides, and what needs to change to adapt to new circumstances. As a result, key components of code health include good documentation, easy to understand error messages, and clear, simple code”.

Industry observers note that not only is designing for understandability crucial, but it’s a learnable skill. It’s not some magical ability that you either have or you don’t. There are specific, concrete actions you can take to improve the understandability of your code.

I’m going to introduce you to a few of those today. Think of it as a “starter kit” for designing for understandability. We’ll also talk more about a general theme that runs through all of these practices, so that at a certain point you can find even more ways to design your code for understandability.

The ideas I’m going to show you today are not newly introduced. But they’re not taught as well as they should be, when they’re taught at all, and most of us have only a rough understanding of how to apply them. My goal today is to sharpen that understanding just a little bit, and make it just a little more practical, so we can kickstart a process of making our code more understandable over time.

So let’s get started on each of these Design for Understandability practices.

The first one is Design by Contract.

To motivate the idea, let’s ask the question: when calling a method, what behavior should you rely on?

Let’s say we have this binary search method, but its documentation is not terribly helpful (you’ve probably seen something like this before).

Binary search is reasonably well understood, but as a caller of the method, we have some questions we want to ask about this specific implementation. Such as:.

According to recent reports, the documentation doesn’t answer these questions. So what can we do?

First, we could guess. But we’ll probably be wrong.

It has been revealed that second, we could read the code. But that might take a long time, especially if the particular behavior we care about is buried several levels deep.

Third, we could test the code on some examples and see what happens. But just because it works a certain way on some examples doesn’t necessarily mean it works that way for all such inputs. Furthermore, even if it works that way now, there’s no guarantee that it will continue to work that way in the future.

Recent findings suggest that the point is that without a clear statement of what this code is intended to do, there’s no distinction between implementation and intent. The SWE who wants to use this code has to guess at which behavior the method commits to, versus which behavior is an implementation detail that might change over time.

This is where contracts come in.

There are many ways to define a contract, but for the sake of this talk I’m going to define it as a formal-ish description of the observable behavior that each participant in an interaction commits to.

In the real world, a basic contract is something like “If I cook dinner, then you will wash the dishes”.

In programming, an example might be: “If the caller provides a non-negative integer n, then the square-root function returns the square root of n”.

Let’s see how contracts can help us with our binary-search example.

It has been revealed that here’s a possible contract for this function. It says, “If the list is sorted, binarySearch returns the index of the first occurrence of t in the list, or -1 if not found. Behavior is undefined for unsorted lists.”.

We can see that this contract answers the questions we asked about it:.

In a recent development, the power of a contract is that it defines a clear boundary between the author’s intent and the implementation. The caller doesn’t have to guess at the behavior anymore: they can just read the contract, and if a specific detail of the behavior isn’t there, they will know that it’s unspecified.

According to recent reports, in reality, this isn’t always perfect. Whether intentionally or accidentally, we still tend to end up with code that relies on implementation details rather than specified behavior. But contracts at least give us a way to minimize this behavior.

Now that we understand what a contract looks like, let’s talk about how contracts can help us reason about and understand our code better.

Sources indicate that suppose you just wrote a method. I’m going to draw that method as a little circle here.

You want to know if it’s correct.

I’m going to use a purple circle to stand for methods we’ve read the code for.

Now, our method doesn’t live in isolation: it calls some other code.

In a recent development, so, you think “Okay, well, I need to understand what those do. I’m going to read the code for those methods.”.

Well, those methods call other methods, and we start thinking about this, and figure out how we’re going to reason about those. And at this point you can maybe see where I’m going.

Oh no. Now we have lots and lots of code we have to read across our entire code base.

Recent findings suggest that why do we need all this reasoning just to reason about one single method? That’s all we’re trying to do! How did we get so out of control?

So, let’s back up and try again, using Design by Contract this time.

Recent findings suggest that you still have to read your own code. We can’t get around this part; that’s the change we just made.

It has been revealed that and we haven’t changed the code. It still calls those other methods.

But now, the trick is that we can read just the contract on those called methods, not the code.

Sources indicate that and that’s it! We can stop here. We don’t need to worry about all of that other code. The contracts tell us all we need to know about calling these other two methods.

The rest of that code still exists, but we don’t have to think about it. The contract abstracts away all that other behavior that doesn’t matter to us as the caller of these two methods.

So that is the power that contracts give to us to reason about our code.

Finally, I’ll wrap up this section with a few tips for writing contracts:.

It has been revealed that first, document the behavior that you’re willing to commit to. This is usually the same as what you want your callers to rely on. For example, you probably want to document the return value of your method. But the exact human-readable text in your error messages? Not so much.

In a recent development, second, describe your error handling in your contracts. A contract does not and should not be just about the happy path. If your method might go wrong in some way, tell the caller under what conditions it might go wrong, and how you’re going to signal that to the caller, whether it be through a special return value, or an exception, or something else.

Sources indicate that finally, keep in mind that the more callers your method has, the harder it is to change the contract. If it’s a private method used only by your team? Sure, that’s probably an easy case to change both the contract and change the callers to match. If it’s a public method on a popular framework used by hundreds of other projects? Then renegotiating the contract is a much more expensive effort, so you should evaluate the costs and benefits carefully before deciding to do that.

So that was the first element in our Design for Understandability starter kit.

The next one is data invariants.

Let me explain this idea with a little story.

It has been revealed that early in the COVID-19 pandemic, when my wife and I started working from home, we missed having free soda at work. So we got in the habit of keeping cans of Diet Coke in the fridge.

But there was a problem: we were great at taking cans out of the fridge, but not so great about putting newly introduced ones back in. So if you’re working hard and looking forward to taking a break with a nice cold beverage, it was a substantial disappointment to open a Coke-less fridge and resort to drinking room-temperature soda from the pantry instead.

Recent findings suggest that the problem was that we hadn’t set any rules on how we retrieve Diet Coke and how we replenish the fridge. Without any rules governing access to the fridge, we eventually got into an unwanted state: in this case, an empty fridge.

It has been revealed that this happens in code, too. For example, let’s say you have this proto to represent a customer’s order [Note: “proto” is Google jargon for a Protocol Buffers message, similar to a JSON object]. If you receive this proto, how much do you trust that the total actually indicates the total amount on the items?

Industry observers note that probably not much, right? This proto could have come from any part of your code, so it’s easy to imagine that someone forgot to set that field appropriately.

According to recent reports, protos give you completely uncontrolled access to the underlying representation of your data. Protos are great for transferring data back and forth across the network, but they’re poorly suited to situations where you want to rule out certain states.

It has been revealed that to solve these kinds of problems, we can use data invariants. A data invariant is a statement about a piece of data that is always true.

According to recent reports, data invariants are a principled way to enforce these kinds of valid states in your data. If you use them well, you can avoid a lot of bugs in your code.

Let’s see how we can use invariants to solve the Diet Coke problem, and similar problems you might come across in your own code.

First, identify the invariant you want to maintain.

Ask yourself: What’s the property you want to rely on for this piece of data? Where are the places in the code where you explicitly validate and return an error if invalid? Alternatively, where do you make the assumption that it’s invalid, but you’re not actually sure?

In this case, the invariant we want is “the fridge always contains a Diet Coke”.

Second, you need to document the invariant.

It’s key to note this is a separate step. It’s one thing to have an invariant in your own head. It’s another thing to write it down so that you communicate it to everyone else who might touch this code. Not to mention that if you come back to this code months or years later, you yourself might have forgotten which exact invariant you meant to maintain.

Write it down where people will see it: probably close to the relevant data members, or maybe in a class-level comment at the top.

Sources indicate that third, establish the invariant at creation time. Usually this will be done in a constructor or factory method. In this case, we’re constructing the fridge with a few drinks already added.

Fourth, every time you change your the data, make sure you maintain the invariant.

This is the part my wife and I didn’t do for our fridge. What we should have done is established a rule where if you take a Diet Coke, you put another one back in the fridge to make sure there’s another for the next person.

You can maintain the invariant many ways – that part is up to you. The notable thing is that you always maintain it. Without that, you have to think to yourself “Wait, are there going to be Diet Cokes in the fridge? Did I already take them out earlier? Let me go back and check all my callers to see if they did that already”. With an invariant, though, you just know: If I have a Fridge object, then it definitely has Diet Cokes, regardless of the sequence of operations that led to this point.

According to recent reports, finally, one last step, and this might be the hardest one: you need to maintain the invariant as the code evolves. It’s relatively easy to maintain the invariant for a single version of code. But over the weeks, months, and years, complexity will creep in, fresh requirements will force you to change the code, and you might accidentally break the invariant or forget you even had one.

Establish the culture on your team that maintaining invariants is just a thing you do. If you have a mental checklist of things you look for in code review, make sure that maintaining the invariants is on that checklist.

So how do data invariants help us design for understandability? Let’s first consider what we have to do when we don’t have an invariant.

Recent findings suggest that recall this representation of all the methods in your codebase, calling each other in various ways. Suppose you have a proto-based version of the fridge, and you want to know if it has any Diet Cokes in it. Because it’s a proto, you don’t have a way of knowing what state it’s in.

So, you need to check all the callers of the current method.

And you do the check, crawling across the codebase, and you find that there’s one particular case where you didn’t enforce it.

Of course you can fix these concerns one at a time as they crop up, but all that searching sounds like a lot of work, right? What do you think are the chances you’re always going to find that one particular buggy spot? What are the chances that upcoming methods added to this web of code are going to maintain that condition?

In contrast, let’s try the version with our Fridge class and its invariant.

In this case, the class has an invariant: the Fridge always has at least one Diet Coke, no matter what operations have been done previously or where we came from. By maintaining that invariant, we’ve removed the need to check what every single caller does.

This is what data invariants do for you: they let you focus on the state you’re in now, and not how you got there.

That wraps up the section on data invariants.

The final practice I want to discuss today is isolating side effects and dependencies on global state.

To motivate this idea with an example. Let’s say there’s a supermarket point-of-sales system with this method to compute sales tax. Now ask yourself: what are the inputs and outputs for this method?

It has been revealed that seems pretty obvious, right? It takes in a customer’s grocery order and returns the sales tax as an integer.

It has been revealed that but that’s not the whole story. If you dig into the implementation of this method, you’ll find that it reads in a set of sales tax rates from a separate file. That’s effectively a new input channel! The code depends on that data to compute the tax just as much as it depends on the content of the grocery order itself.

Sources indicate that and if you look further, you’ll find that the method also records the computed tax in the store’s account database for bookkeeping purposes. That’s a new output, but it’s nowhere to be found in the type signature!

So functions have two kinds of input and output: the ones that are visible in the type signature, like the order and the computed sales tax, and the ones that are hidden, like the tax rates file and the entry in the accounting database.

Industry observers note that the hidden outputs are more commonly known as side effects. Side effects generally come in two flavors: mutation, so modifying something like a global variable or one of your input arguments, and outputs outside of your process. That would be things like database writes, remote procedure calls, printing to the console, etc.

It has been revealed that I don’t know a common term for the hidden inputs, but I would call these dependencies on global state. Again, there are two flavors: dependency on the state of some global variable, or a dependency on the state of the system your program is running in. That’s things like permissions to access the database, the existence of a given file on the file system, and even the ability to read the system clock.

So why are these hidden inputs and outputs a problem? They make code hard to test, hard to reuse, and hard to reason about.

In a recent development, hard to test because you have to make sure you have all the necessary dependencies are set up before you can even run the method in your test. And then once you do run the method, side effects often force the test to rely more on interaction verification than state verification, which can be brittle.

It has been revealed that hard to reuse because the code now makes assumptions about what kinds of resources you have available to you. If you need to reuse some method in another part of the codebase, but the input data needs to come from a different source, or you need to store the results in a different place, those side effects and global states are going to create a tight coupling between your computation code and the specific sources and destinations for that computation, which will make your life harder.

Hard to reason about because, by definition, these inputs and outputs are hidden! If you don’t even know that your method is making these kinds of assumptions on the system that it’s running in, then you’re going to make some faulty conclusions about how your code will behave.

Now I’m not saying all side effects or global state are bad. And I’m not saying we should all immediately switch to a pure functional programming language like Haskell.

Industry observers note that effects have to happen somewhere. Without side effects, computation is just the process of making a metal box hot for a little while(and even that heat is a side effect! although not usually one we care about).

But by default, we tend to sprinkle them everywhere throughout the code. Need some input? Just read the file at whatever point you happen to be at in the code. Need to store your result? Go ahead and do it 4 layers deep into your business logic.

Without a principled approach to side effects and global state, we’re constantly running into the kinds of problems we just described.

According to recent reports, there’s a better way, which is to isolate the side effects and the dependencies on global state. Much of our code is just logic on top of the data (once we get it) and creating fresh data based on that. Divide your code into the computational parts on one hand, and the parts that deal with side effects and global state on the other.

There are a few common patterns for this.

According to recent reports, one of them is Command/Query Separation. It’s a pattern where each method is either a command, which performs some side effect, or a query, which is a pure function that returns its output as the return value. But you maintain a strict separation so that no function does both of those things.

In a recent development, another pattern is called “Functional Core, Imperative Shell”. This is a pattern at the architectural level. You focus the inner modules of your system on the business logic and computation, not performing side effects – this is the “functional core”. The outer modules coordinate the effects of your system with that computation, so that the complexity of the side effects is isolated to just that outer layer, and the majority of your system is simpler due to the functional purity.

As with the other two practices, side effects and global state have a big impact on how we think about code.

For example, you might be working on a method and need to delete a file. Your assumption is that it should be okay, you think no one is using it.

It has been revealed that but then it turns out, some other part of the codebase was relying on it, and you just broke them. The code was so far away and unrelated that you didn’t even think to check there.

On the other hand, if you isolate your side effects and global state such that they only happen in a known region of the code, then you can have confidence that you really aren’t going to break anyone else.

So, those are the three starter practices for Design for Understandability: Design by Contract, Data Invariants, and Isolating Side Effects and Dependencies on Global State.

Now, I’ve presented these as independent practices, but in fact they’re not so distinct. There’s a unifying theme to them. That theme is local reasoning.

What do I mean by local reasoning?

Local reasoning means you can come to conclusions about some chunk of code by looking only at that chunk of code, plus just a small amount of the neighboring code, like the specifications or contracts of the components that you directly interact with.

This is as opposed to global reasoning. That’s the kind of reasoning where to answer even a simple question, you have to read a large chunk of the codebase, because the answer could be in any method, at any level of the call stack.

The benefit of local reasoning is that it puts a hard boundary on how far you have to look in order to figure something out about your system: there’s always a limit to how far you have to search.

Sources indicate that so let’s talk about how each of the practices we talked about enables local reasoning. You may have noticed we covered this already, but let’s review.

Design by Contract defines the expected behavior for a caller and a called method. That means that to understand what behavior a caller can rely on, or what behavior a called method is obligated to implement, the only place we need to look is the defined interface for that called method. Without that, we would revert to global reasoning to find all the parts of the code that might depend on some aspect of this method’s behavior.

Data invariants often go hand in hand with contracts, but they usually say something about an entire object rather than a single method on that object.

If you have a piece of data and you want to know something about its validity, like “does this fridge have any diet cokes?”, an invariant is what lets you immediately conclude yes, without looking at the callers that produced that data.

Sources indicate that finally, by isolating side effects and global state, you minimize the number of places in your code where a change in one part of the code can cause a problem in a completely unrelated part. So it lets you say things like “this is the only part of the code that’s allowed to touch this file, so I know for sure that it’s safe to delete”.

Another way of looking at local reasoning is to say that it minimizes the amount of context we need in order to reason about the system.

Sources indicate that with global reasoning, you might need to know about any arbitrary part of your codebase, because the part that breaks your assumptions could be anywhere. You need to have the whole system loaded into your head in order to understand it.

Local reasoning keeps the amount of stuff you need loaded into your head to a reasonable size.

And guess what else benefits from small contexts: LLMs!

Industry observers note that A key portion of making an LLM useful for your work is giving an LLM the right context to give good suggestions. But contexts costs tokens, and your tokens are limited. So LLMs give us another great motivation to use local reasoning and minimize our context.

According to recent reports, in other words, if you want your LLMs to be useful to you, then design your systems for understandability. Keep the necessary context small to make it easier for both you and your LLM to work with your code.

Sources indicate that at the beginning of this talk, I compared “Design for Understandability” to “Design for Testability”. I’d like to revisit that for a moment.

Before designing for testability was the norm, the default testing approach was application-level testing. Our code wasn’t set up for practices like dependency injection, so there was no way to run your code without setting up a huge set of dependencies as well. It wasn’t until we started designing and building our systems with testability in mind that we were able to make unit testing practical.

Sources indicate that that’s how it is with understandability and local reasoning, as well. If you don’t design for it ahead of time, it’s somewhere between hard and impossible to use local reasoning. But if you design for it along the way, you can make it work.

According to recent reports, if you’ve never heard of unit testing, then application-level testing seems obvious, and straightforward. But it’s not sufficient for modern software engineering. The same is true for global reasoning. I say it’s time we made designing for understandability a required part of our work, just like we did for testability.

So you may be thinking: that all sounds good, and these practices sound good on paper, but is designing for understandability feasible in practice? You’re probably not working in a brand-new greenfield project. You’re probably working on old code, with lots of old warts and complexity, and the situation may seem hopeless. Can you really do this?

I’m here to say yes, this is feasible, if you take it one small step at a time. I’ll share some tips for getting started.

First off, take little bits at a time. Don’t try to boil the ocean. Don’t say “We’re going to take two weeks off from our normal work, make all of our code perfectly understandable, and then we’re done!”. That’s not going to work; you’re going to have a bad time.

Industry observers note that instead, try applying some of these practices to just newly introduced methods that you write. You might have some old code out there that’s hard to change. So be it. Start with just the new methods and build some momentum.

Sources indicate that teach your teammates, as well. Maybe share this talk, or find other ways to help your teammates design for understandability.

According to recent reports, and finally, you might consider group programming sessions where you all get together and discuss: what does designing for understandability mean in your context? The Monarch team at Google did this with their Design by Contract practice and it worked well for them.

Here are some further resources to learn more about Design for Understandability. I’m not going to go into them in detail, but please feel free to go revisit the slides after the talk and check these out.

[Public links reproduced here for the blog post:].

Recent findings suggest that in conclusion: design your code for understandability. Whenever you’re working on some code and realize that you’re falling back to global reasoning, pause for a moment. Ask yourself: can I do this with local reasoning instead? Would a contract or an invariant help here? Or what if I moved the side effects and global state somewhere else? Or, maybe you’ll think of some other practice that fits here – you probably know a lot of local-reasoning practices, even if you didn’t have the terminology to call it that until today.

Recent findings suggest that it’s time to make design for understandability just as much a part of software engineering as designing for testability is today. Understandability is not just helpful – it’s crucial, especially with Google-size systems. And not just that, but making your code understandable is doable if you design for it along the way.

Trust me: you’ll be glad you did.

AutoSynthData: Generating Training Data for Enterprise Agents

📅 02 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2034 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that enterprises need agents that work well in their own environments.
  • The difficulty is turning those weaknesses into training data.
  • At ServiceNow CoreAI, we built AutoSynthData to turn those capability gaps into training data.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that enterprises need agents that work well in their own environments. The work they ask these agents to do is shaped by the systems they use, the rules they follow, and the state of their data. A model may be broadly capable and still struggle with a particular environment: a workflow it handles poorly, a combination of tools it misuses, or a constraint it fails to respect. Those are the weaknesses an enterprise needs to improve.

The difficulty is turning those weaknesses into training data. An individual failure tells us something, but training a model requires many upcoming tasks that exercise the same capability in different situations. Those tasks must also be possible to complete in the environment, resemble work someone would actually request, and have a reliable way to check whether the agent succeeded.

At ServiceNow CoreAI, we built AutoSynthData to turn those capability gaps into training data. It uses a target model’s failures and a stronger teacher’s successes to decide what the model should learn next, then generates and validates latest tasks that exercise those capabilities. As the model improves, the curriculum shifts toward what it still finds difficult. We illustrate the pipeline with EnterpriseOps Gym (Malay et al., 2026), using the released dataset. We begin by describing the environment an agent operates in and what makes a task useful for training.

An agentic environment defines the world in which an agent operates: the state it can observe and modify, the tools and APIs it can invoke, and the state transitions produced by its actions.

In a recent development, A task is instantiated within this environment. We use the following abstraction:.

The system specification defines the constraints under which the agent operates, including system instructions, environment policies, and, when applicable, task-specific initialization such as a seeded database state or a set of knowledge articles.

In a recent development, the specification must be compatible with the environment’s tools, state, and supported actions. Its instructions should be clear and avoid arbitrary constraints introduced solely to manufacture difficulty.

The user prompt specifies what the user wants the agent to accomplish, together with any user-level constraints. A generated task should satisfy three properties.

Feasibility. There should exist at least one trajectory in the current environment that satisfies the user prompt while respecting the system specification. This rules out tasks that depend on unavailable tools, inaccessible knowledge, impossible state transitions, or actions prohibited by policy.

Sources indicate that realism. The user prompt should resemble something a user would plausibly ask in the target environment. The space of executable behaviors is usually much larger than the space of realistic workflows.

Industry observers note that difficulty. For training, the task should expose a weakness of the current agent. Tasks that are already solved reliably provide little fresh training signal. The useful region is therefore tasks that are feasible and realistic, but not yet consistently solved.

The verifier determines whether the resulting trajectory successfully completes the task. It should satisfy three properties.

It has been revealed that consistency. It should agree with the user prompt, the system specification, and the task-specific environment state.

Industry observers note that soundness. It should reject trajectories that fail to satisfy the task or violate relevant constraints.

Completeness. It should accept valid solutions rather than encode one particular reference trajectory.

These properties matter directly during training. A lax verifier can reward incorrect behavior, while an overly restrictive verifier can penalize valid solutions.

Industry observers note that given an environment and a target model, AutoSynthData generates training tasks consisting of a system specification, user prompt, and verifier. The generated tasks are grounded in the environment and selected to provide useful training signal for the current model.

AutoSynthData first evaluates the target model in the environment using diagnostic tasks and identifies patterns in the tasks it struggles to complete. A stronger teacher helps characterize which of those tasks are solvable and what successful behavior looks like. AutoSynthData turns the resulting capability gaps into new executable tasks, checks each task in the environment, and uses accepted samples for post-training. Evaluating the updated model reveals which gaps remain and can guide the next round of generation.

AutoSynthData uses evaluation runs in the target environment to identify what the model needs to learn next. In our EnterpriseOps Gym experiment, we run both the target model and a stronger teacher on the evaluation tasks. We examine those runs to identify:.

We distill these findings into sanitized capability specification cards. The evaluation tasks guide what the model should learn, but the generator does not receive their original prompts, entities, trajectories, or verifier details. It receives the cards and uses them to create fresh tasks with different prompts, states, and solution paths.

Recent findings suggest that identifying a capability gap tells us what to teach, but training requires many varied tasks that exercise it. AutoSynthData uses the specification card to generate those tasks.

Suppose the target model struggles with tasks that require the following workflow:.

Recent findings suggest that the generator creates new tasks that exercise this workflow, varying the entities, initial environment state, workflow composition, tool combinations, wording, and difficulty. The stronger teacher then demonstrates a successful trajectory for each task. For supervised fine-tuning (SFT), these demonstrations teach the target model how to apply the capability in new situations.

AutoSynthData builds the dataset in two phases: first generating and validating core samples, then expanding them into novel variants.

Recent findings suggest that the target phase creates the core set of training samples from the capability specifications. Workers generate independent tasks in parallel, picking up a new target when they finish. Each candidate goes through validation, execution, solver evaluation, and repair before acceptance. The result is a batch of vetted examples built around what the target model needs to learn.

Sources indicate that the multiply phase expands the dataset by creating novel variants of accepted target samples. Each variant has its own user request, environment state, entity configuration, reference trajectory, and verifier, and must pass the same validation and execution checks. A multiplied sample cannot seed another multiplied sample. This anchors expansion to the vetted target set and limits drift across generations.

Industry observers note that to support both phases, AutoSynthData separates generation control from environment-specific execution. A shared controller coordinates generation, quality control, coverage, and dataset construction, while an adapter handles environment execution, task and state management, reference replay, deterministic verification, solver execution, and task profiling.

Industry observers note that together, parallel target generation and multiplication provide a path to training-scale datasets. Their usefulness depends on the checks applied to every candidate: the task must be executable, the solution must work, and the verifier must distinguish success from failure.

Generating a plausible request is not enough to produce useful training data. A task may be impossible in the target environment, its reference solution may fail when executed, or its verifier may reward the wrong final state. AutoSynthData checks these properties before accepting a task for training.

AutoSynthData reviews quality at two levels: individual candidates must pass verification, and batches must provide useful coverage and diversity.

According to recent reports, each candidate must clear a quality-control loop before entering the training dataset. We begin with solver evaluation to measure difficulty. In the configuration used here, we favor tasks the target model solves on no more than one of three trials and the stronger solver solves on at least two of three trials. Candidates also undergo positive and negative verification and a bounded repair process.

The positive gate asks: Does the intended solution solve the generated task?

The pipeline executes the reference trajectory in the target environment and checks the resulting state against the candidate’s verifier. This reveals mismatches among the prompt, initial state, solution, and success criteria.

The negative gate asks: Do relevant incorrect outcomes fail?

Industry observers note that for example, it can mutate parts of the expected outcome and confirm that those states no longer pass verification. This catches weak verifiers that award success without requiring the intended behavior.

Failed candidates go to a critic before being discarded. The critic examines the sample and its failure, looking for inconsistent state, impossible workflows, incorrect task construction, bad reference trajectories, weak verifier logic, or a mismatch with the intended capability. The critic’s findings guide repairs, with a fixed limit on retries:.

Industry observers note that A repaired task must pass the relevant checks again. The diagnosis guides repairs to the existing candidate rather than requiring generation to start over.

Industry observers note that passing these checks makes a sample eligible for training, but individually valid samples can still form a repetitive or unbalanced dataset. AutoSynthData therefore also reviews generation at the batch level.

A batch may overrepresent a few easy task families, miss a capability, or reflect too much generation effort spent on a low-yield pattern.

A meta-review examines accepted samples, rejected samples, and generation behavior across each batch. It asks:.

It has been revealed that the controller tracks coverage in the accepted dataset, reduces generation in overrepresented regions, and directs more work toward gaps. When a region repeatedly produces poor candidates, critiques and meta-review guide changes to the generation strategy. These adjustments balance useful learning signal, task quality, coverage, diversity, and low redundancy within the available generation budget and dataset size requirements.

Together, these feedback loops improve both individual tasks and the dataset they form: sample-level checks guide candidate repair, while batch-level review guides future generation.

Recent findings suggest that the useful training distribution changes as the model improves. AutoSynthData treats synthetic data generation as a search for tasks near the target model's capability boundary: difficult enough to expose weaknesses, but solvable enough for the teacher to provide reliable demonstrations.

According to recent reports, after post-training, we evaluate the updated model in the same environment. Tasks it now solves reliably are less useful for the next training round; persistent failures point to capabilities that still need attention. Those results can guide the next generation round.

Recent findings suggest that our experiments focus on SFT, but the same mechanism could support reinforcement learning (RL): generate tasks that challenge the current policy and provide reliable learning signal, train, then move the generation target with the updated policy. We proposal to test this moving, difficulty-calibrated frontier beyond SFT.

It has been revealed that we use EnterpriseOps Gym to test whether this approach improves a model on tasks in a stateful enterprise environment. We generate training tasks in the Gym’s Hybrid and ITSM environments, fine-tune the target model on accepted samples, and evaluate the resulting checkpoints.

We tested the pipeline on the Hybrid domain of EnterpriseOps Gym using Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it as the target model and Qwen3.8-27B as the teacher.

AutoSynthData generated 2,000 synthetic training samples in about 18 hours. We fine-tuned Gemma on this dataset and evaluated the resulting checkpoints on the benchmark. The best checkpoint was epoch 5.

The synthetic SFT checkpoint improves mean Pass@1 by 7.2 percentage points, a 35% relative improvement, and raises verifier success from 63.01% to 68.55%. It closes 59% of the original Pass@1 gap between Gemma and the reference model.

The training tasks were newly generated from capability specifications; the generator did not receive the original evaluation tasks. The result demonstrates improvement in EnterpriseOps Gym Hybrid, the environment used for this experiment.

We also applied AutoSynthData to the ITSM domain of EnterpriseOps Gym, using Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it as the target model and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash as the teacher. AutoSynthData generated 1,994 synthetic training samples in 66 hours. Generation took longer than in the subsequent Hybrid run described above, primarily because the ITSM run used a larger teacher model and preceded pipeline optimizations that improved throughput.

On ITSM, synthetic SFT raises mean Pass@1 from 18.77% to 27.18%, showing that the approach also improves performance in a second domain.

Sources indicate that the tasks most useful for training depend on both the environment and the model working in it. AutoSynthData uses the model’s failures to choose what to generate, validates latest tasks against the environment, and makes those tasks available for post-training. Our EnterpriseOps Gym results show the value of that approach in a controlled setting. As the model changes, the same process can focus on the gaps that remain.

Perplexity Brings Voice-Controlled AI Teammates to Mobile

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A user can tap a call button to start an assignment, then call back to discuss revised priorities.
  • Sources indicate that perplexity remarked nearly a third of the most demanding work on Computer already starts on an iPhone.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A user can tap a call button to start an assignment, then call back to discuss revised priorities. The teammate plans the work, checks its findings and returns results for review. It can also work inside connected apps and send a notification when it needs a decision. The user can answer aloud or open the thread to inspect completed and upcoming work.

Sources indicate that perplexity remarked nearly a third of the most demanding work on Computer already starts on an iPhone. That usage figure positions the phone as an existing entry point for complex assignments; voice mode now covers both starting those assignments and steering them after the initial request.

Perplexity’s role examples emphasize assignments with monitoring and follow-up built in. A research analyst can examine market changes, identify new developments and patch a blueprint daily. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Carrier signal still reaches Earth, but science and engineering data have gone AWOL.
  • Voyager 1 marked its milestone of one light-day from Earth in time-honored fashion: by giving controllers the silent treatment.
  • It has been revealed that on November 14, the mission team noticed that the veteran spacecraft had stopped returning science and engineering data.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Carrier signal still reaches Earth, but science and engineering data have gone AWOL.

Voyager 1 marked its milestone of one light-day from Earth in time-honored fashion: by giving controllers the silent treatment.

It has been revealed that on November 14, the mission team noticed that the veteran spacecraft had stopped returning science and engineering data. A Deep Space Network antenna in Canberra, Australia, picked up its carrier signal, but no data.

The carrier signal indicates that Voyager 1 can still keep its antenna pointed at Earth and operate its transmitting equipment. However, something could be amiss with the system responsible for collecting and collating data from the spacecraft.

Something similar happened in 2023. After a few months of troubleshooting, engineers managed to coax a response from the probe, and by June 2024, NASA was delighted to announce that the spacecraft was back in action.

The problem was traced to a faulty computer chip, and engineers devised a software update to work around the defective hardware. That experience will stand the team in good stead this time around.

It has been revealed that there was also a brief interruption in communications with Voyager 1 in October, which could have been caused by the spacecraft dropping into safe mode after a thruster failover occurred. Engineers are investigating whether the two incidents are connected.

In a recent development, the Voyagers have an impressive amount of fault protection built in, which has contributed to their extraordinary longevity. It will be half a century in 2027 since the spacecraft were released, so glitches are understandable and likely.

Sources indicate that NASA expects to confirm on November 19 that Voyager 1 was still operating when it reached one light-day from Earth on November 18, using its carrier signal and trajectory calculations. The day's delay neatly illustrates a major headache for engineers: communication latency.

It now takes more than 24 hours for commands to reach the spacecraft, and the same amount of time for a response to be received. Diagnosing the fault could therefore take weeks or longer. ®.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, vercel has released UI SDK, an open-source TypeScript library that treats keyboard navigation, focus, selection, popups, and drag and drop as reusable behaviors rather than details buried inside finished components.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Vercel Releases UI SDK for Agents to Compose UI from Reusable Behaviors.

Nov 18, 2026 2 min read.

According to recent reports, vercel has released UI SDK, an open-source TypeScript library that treats keyboard navigation, focus, selection, popups, and drag and drop as reusable behaviors rather than details buried inside finished components. Vercel UI SDK is published on GitHub as vercel-labs/ui and is right now in beta.

The behaviors live in @ui-sdk/core. Vercel says it built more than 50 of them, including createPopup, createSelection, createTypeahead, createRovingFocus, createReorder, createResize, createViewport, createListbox, createChange, createFocusRecovery, and createVirtualizer. A developer, or more often an agent, combines those helpers inside definePrimitive, which declares a component's state, API, and slots once. Framework adapters then render the same primitive through createParts in React, Vue, Svelte, Solid, or as Web Components. The parts are unstyled and expose attributes and CSS variables. The same behaviors also back a starter library of more than 50 unstyled components, from Color Picker, Token Input, and Command to Calendar, Tree, and OTP Input, with the same part names in all five adapters.

Recent findings suggest that UI SDK is meant to be used by agents, not only written by them. The ui-sdk skill, installed with npx skills add vercel-labs/ui --skill ui-sdk, points an agent at the Markdown docs shipped in the installed packages. At runtime, createAgent, imported from the matching framework package such as @ui-sdk/react/agent, exposes snapshot, act, and query so an agent can read component state and call actions through the component API, without screenshots. Apps can approve or refuse those steps, and change callbacks receive a source of "agent" and may cancel a change. registerTools can expose the same methods to a browser's built-in agent through WebMCP, when the browser provides document.modelContext.

Developers already have several headless libraries at this layer, including Radix UI, Base UI, React Aria, Ark UI and its Zag.js state machines, and Headless UI. shadcn/ui sits one level above those primitives as a copy-into-your-repo component kit. UI SDK aims lower, at composable behaviors shared across frameworks, and adds a first-class agent bridge. The changelog thanks the teams behind Radix, Base UI, React Aria, shadcn/ui, Nuxt UI, and Geist. Vercel has not said whether shadcn/ui will be rebuilt on UI SDK.

Rahim, a product engineer at Mux who built Vidstack, wrote after reading the source:.

Sources indicate that this is so genuinely cool. I love how it's been packaged up. So elegant @shadcn and @shuding! I'll be studying this for a while. 1. createAgent is an "agent bridge" which gives a snapshot, act, and query tool. It allows agents to interact with the actual UI components directly 2. Change callbacks know when the agent made the change (details.source === "agent"), and the app can refuse it with cancel (I love this).

A developer identified as Stefan looked at the repository and asked how the idea compares with existing headless libraries:.

I tried looking at the repo a bit but I’m not sure I quite understand the value prop of this versus something like Base UI. Is the thought process that we should be thinking about UIs/components as combinations of behaviours?

In a recent development, UI SDK is in beta as 0.1.0-beta.1, licensed under the Apache License 2.0, and subject to Vercel's public beta terms; the APIs, documentation, and behavior may change before general availability. Install @ui-sdk/core plus the adapter for your framework, for example npm install @ui-sdk/react @ui-sdk/core, which requires React 19 or later. The Vue, Svelte, and Solid adapters document peer ranges of Vue 3.5, Svelte 5.33, and Solid 2 from 2.0.0-rc.14. Setup details are in the documentation.

Recent findings suggest that zellij is a relatively new entrant in the terminal-multiplexer category. Like GNU Screen and tmux it gives owners the ability to manage a workspace inside a terminal with split panes, provides session management, and so forth; but Zellij also includes a web server for browser access to a terminal session, is extensible via a plugin API, and is likely more beginner-friendly than its predecessors. Its most recent release, version 0.46, adds a standalone terminal emulator, a built-in inbox for notifications, and a settings screen so users can configure the application without fussing with configuration files. While the low version number might suggest that it is not yet ready for serious use, it seems stable and full-featured enough to meet the needs of many users.
