The Agent Mentioned It Was Done. The Database Disagreed.

📅 03 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2633 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Microsoft ThinkingBox grades AI agents on the records they leave behind, not the sentences they generate, and then asks whether they can do it twenty times in a row.
  • Figure 1: ThinkingBox runs an agent against isolated MCP tool sessions, then grades the terminal backend state and side effects it leaves behind.
  • Recent findings suggest that A customer writes in.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Microsoft ThinkingBox grades AI agents on the records they leave behind, not the sentences they generate, and then asks whether they can do it twenty times in a row. It is now available through Hugging Face.

Figure 1: ThinkingBox runs an agent against isolated MCP tool sessions, then grades the terminal backend state and side effects it leaves behind. From our ThinkingBox paper.

Recent findings suggest that A customer writes in. Her $745 kitchen appliance has been stuck in a courier "exception" at a Nashville distribution center, fifteen days past its estimated delivery date.

Recent findings suggest that the AI agent does careful work. Nine tool calls: it pulls the order, checks tracking, looks up her customer profile, searches the refund policy twice, confirms no ticket exists, opens one, documents the timeline, and reads the policy correctly; her account segment genuinely does not qualify for late-delivery compensation.

Sources indicate that then it closes the ticket as resolved and replies “ Since your query is resolved, is there anything I may assist you with? ”.

Two things are wrong. The carrier exception is still open, so the required end state was on hold, pending resolution. And the customer never got a real answer to what she actually asked.

Recent findings suggest that an AI grader checking tool calls would see nine well-formed ones. The grader checking whether the agent wrote to the database would see that too. The database is what disagrees.

Sources indicate that that gap is what ThinkingBox measures. Across 507 stateful business workflows, each run 20 times against various LLM models, it grades agents on terminal backend state and side effects. This post covers what we found, what consistency costs, and how to run the benchmark yourself through OpenEnv.

According to recent reports, you can run this one yourself: the example above is adapted from a benchmark task sandbox_external_retail_group1.py:test_case_ST003_006, and the executable check that fails is a single field: the ticket's status is solved where the required end state is hold. The full trace is in Appendix D.4, Case 3 of our paper.

It has been revealed that want to try it before reading the results? Skip to section Run it yourself.

Sources indicate that final responses and valid tool calls are only proxies. An agent can sound correct while leaving the wrong value, changing the wrong record, or creating an extra side effect. Only the records it leaves behind settle the question.

Sources indicate that the gap is substantial. In a common-set ablation covering 121,680 valid trials across 12 LLM models, 79,853 attempts failed the executable checks. Of those failures, 67.24% still terminated cleanly, invoked a state-changing tool, and reported no final tool error. Executable checks nevertheless found wrong field values in 77.61% of them, unintended extra effects in 43.30%, and missing required effects in 25.36%. Those state-check findings overlap.

A trajectory is a claim. Database state is the evidence. Repetition is the trust test.

An agent that processes a refund correctly once and mishandles it the next four times is not a working refund agent. So every task runs 20 independent times, each from an identical clean backend, and we report three different things:.

Table 1: The three numbers we report, and the question each one answers.

Recent findings suggest that we use observed 20/20 in this blog post as the literal count of how many of the 507 tasks passed 20 out of 20. No estimator, no smoothing.

Recent findings suggest that starting with the familiar view. The table below reports pass@1, the single-attempt score estimate, broken out by domain. This is the number most leaderboards publish, and on its own it reads like an ordinary capability ranking.

Recent findings suggest that table 2: ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain. Each model is evaluated on every task for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the group leader; underline marks the runner-up. The standard errors for the single attempt score estimates are provided in Table 4 in our ThinkingBox paper.

Claude Opus 5.5 leads overall at 67.16%, two-thirds of a point above Claude Opus 5. Kimi-K3 is the strongest open-weights model, within a point of GPT-6-Astra. Domain matters just as much: Claude Opus 4.6 scores 68.62% on retail but 8.30% on auto insurance.

Sources indicate that one good run tells you a model can do the work. It does not tell you whether it will do it again. So run every task 20 times and ask how much of that score survives.

Figure 2: How much of each model's single-attempt score survives 20 repeats.

In a recent development, only three hold on to most of their pass@1 scores: GPT-6 Astra retains 78% of its single-attempt rate, and Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Opus 5 each retain 71%. At the other end, GLM-5.1, Kimi-K2.6 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro each keep about 8%.

The gap between what a model can do once and what it does every time is the whole story.

Industry observers note that figure 3: Breadth and consistency pull apart. Twelve of the eighteen models are shown; six below 33% pass@1 are omitted for legibility.

Kimi-K3 has the broadest coverage of any model we tested. It solves 93.89% of the benchmark at least once: 476 of 507 tasks. Only 31 tasks defeat it entirely, the lowest count in the field. On retail workflows it leads outright at 82.24% pass@1, ahead of every proprietary model.

In a recent development, kimi-K3 is also among the least consistent. Just 68 of 507 tasks, 13.41%, succeed in all 20 attempts.

According to recent reports, claude Opus 5 inverts this. It solves fewer tasks at least once (79.09%; 106 defeat it entirely) but completes 47.53% of the benchmark on every single attempt.

It has been revealed that A newer model does not fix this. Claude Opus 5.5 scores higher than Claude Opus 5 on every-attempt average, 67.16% against 66.50%, and solves more tasks at least once. It passes exactly the same number of tasks on all 20 attempts: 241. Half a point of headline accuracy bought no additional dependability at all.

If you are choosing a model for work that touches real records, pass@20 is the wrong column to look at.

According to recent reports, capability comparisons usually stop at the score. For anyone deploying, the relevant question is what a successful unit of work costs. We measure that as cost per successful task attempt. We say task attempt because every benchmark task is run repeatedly and cost is incurred per attempt, so pass@1 is the matching quality denominator.

Industry observers note that we took each model's recorded token usage from its full 507 × 20 campaign and priced it at undiscounted list rates available on OpenRouter+, reversing promotional discounts and excluding endpoints that declare quantization. Input, output and cache rates all come from one provider endpoint per model.

Then we divided one run's cost by the number of attempts that succeeded:.

Cost per successful task attempt = estimated cost for 507 attempts, one per task ÷ (507 × pass@1).

This is a comparative efficiency index, not an invoice, and not the price of serving one production request. It also prices single successes, not consistency. We price consistency next.

Example: GPT-5.4 costs $43.49 for 507 attempts (one attempt per task) and has 65.36% pass@1, so $43.49 ÷ (507 × 0.6536) = $0.131 per successful task attempt.

In a recent development, A model is on the frontier if no other model is both no more expensive and at least as accurate. Three models qualify; every other model is dominated on at least one axis.

Recent findings suggest that figure 4: Cost per successful task attempt against pass@1. Ringed dots are pareto cost frontier models.

Sources indicate that the frontier has three steps. GPT-5.6 Sol has the lowest cost per success at $0.127; GPT-5.4 raises pass@1 by 3.45 percentage points for $0.004 more per success; Claude Opus 5.5 adds another 1.80 points at $0.276 per success. Each of the three remains on the cost frontier line because no cheaper model matches its pass@1.

Claude Opus 5 is the clearest case: at $0.475 per successful attempt and 66.50% pass@1, it is both more expensive and less accurate than Claude Opus 5.5 at $0.276 and 67.16%.

In a recent development, cost per success rewards a model that is cheap and often right. It does not reward a model that is right every time. So we also compute cost per dependable task: the cost of the full 20-run campaign divided by the number of tasks the model passed on all 20 attempts.

Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of 20 runs of 507 attempts ÷ tasks passing 20/20.

Example: GPT-6-Astra costs 20 × $86.03 = $1,720.60 for the campaign and passes 231 tasks on every attempt, so $1,720.60 ÷ 231 = $7.45 per dependable task.

Table 3: The nine lowest costs per dependable task among models with at least one observed 20/20 task, sorted low to high. Estimated $, not actual cloud bills.

Industry observers note that now rank by consistency. GPT-5.4 is the cheapest at $6.80, though only 128 tasks meet the bar. GPT-6 Astra reaches 231 at $7.45, and Claude Opus 5.5 the joint-highest 241 at $7.80.

None of the three dominates the others: each additional dependable task costs more. Claude Opus 5 also passes 241, but at $13.30, so Opus 5.5 dominates it outright. GPT-5.6 Sol, the cheapest per single success at $0.127, costs $9.76 per dependable task. The cheapest way to get a right answer is not the cheapest way to get a dependable one.

Industry observers note that we assign each failed trace one deterministic diagnostic signature, and the headline is actionable: roughly four in five failures are tool handling, not reasoning. Across an ablation study in Table 5 of our paper:.

These are unweighted averages of per-model shares and observable labels, not unique causal explanations.

Sources indicate that the practical pattern is simple: agents usually get far enough to attempt the workflow, then fail to recover from tool errors, failed preconditions, or empty lookups. That is a retry and error-recovery problem before it is a model problem.

Difficulty also changes by domain: across the models listed in Table 2 above, retail averages 59.52% pass@1 while auto insurance averages 33.83%.

According to recent reports, what to do about it. Treat the 20/20 rate as a design input, not a verdict. The same signal the benchmark grades on is available in production: check the terminal state before you commit, not the model's summary of it.

Classify tool and system errors so retries target the recoverable ones. Cut the tool surface to what the workflow needs. And require human approval on the changes you cannot cheaply reverse. We have not measured the lift from any of these on this benchmark, which is exactly the kind of thing the environment now makes testable.

Recent findings suggest that thinkingBox is the agent sandbox, while ThinkingBox-Bench is a dataset benchmark to evaluate agents. The diagram at the top of this post highlights the loop; here is what each part does.

Figure 5: The sandbox loop from panel A in Figure 1 above: isolated tool session, terminal database state, side effects, executable judges.

According to recent reports, each task defines a starting backend state, a user goal, the available MCP tools, the domain policy, and executable checks over the terminal state. A simulated user holds private context (a booking reference, a preference, or a date of birth) and releases it only when asked.

Every attempt gets an isolated MCP session with freshly initialized state. Two attempts of the same task never share a database row or cached tool state, which is what makes 20-trial comparison meaningful.

At the end, a side-effect extractor derives what actually changed, and deterministic judges compare it against the required end state, accepting any trajectory that produces the right outcome while rejecting wrong, missing or extra effects. For requirements with no clean database value ("did the agent disclose this is not guaranteed?"), a narrow binary rubric question handles the semantics. 477 of the 507 tasks are graded on state alone; 30 add response rubrics.

The trust boundary: the model sees tasks, dialogue and tool schemas. Golden state, assertions, grading internals and credentials stay on the evaluator side.

According to recent reports, thinkingBox is now on Hugging Face, both the harness and the dataset. ThinkingBox-Bench now sits behind the OpenEnv interface, and each finished episode returns a binary pass/fail reward. The released adapter is designed for evaluation; separate, non-benchmark scenarios can use the same interface in training workflows.

Tested on Linux and WSL, with Python 3.11+, uv and Docker. You also need a thinkingbox-data checkout at the pinned release and model endpoints for the agent, simulated user and judge. One endpoint can serve all three roles, which is the simplest way to start. The OpenEnv image starts only the OpenEnv API; everything else you run yourself.

In a second terminal, start Typesense 30.1 and wait for its health check:.

In a third terminal, start the Session Proxy and MCP servers.

Back in the first terminal, start the OpenEnv server against a ThinkingBox YAML config naming your three models (config guide):.

Gate on readiness before running anything. It returns 503 until its observable data, configuration and Session Proxy checks pass. It cannot observe Typesense or live-probe every model endpoint, so confirm those separately:.

Now score a real episode. example_usage.py only resets and lists tools; for agent actions, effects and assertions use the packaged evaluator:.

It has been revealed that the OpenEnv adapter writes operational failures to an errors sidecar so they can be rerun rather than silently mixed with model outcomes. A canonical result must resolve or explicitly account for those attempts; we counted system errors as unsuccessful trials.

Runs are gated on a pinned framework commit, a pinned data release and a bundle hash, so a canonical result is verifiable rather than asserted.

The useful part of this work is not our pass@1 leaderboard. It is the environment.

If you are evaluating an agent that touches real records:.

In a recent development, disclaimer: every task in the public benchmark is a synthetic reconstruction. The workflows and policies are modeled on real AI agentic enterprise patterns; the customers are not real.

It has been revealed that thinkingBox and ThinkingBox-Bench is built by the Microsoft Copilot Studio team in partnership with Toloka with collaborators from the University of Pittsburgh, Northwestern University, Columbia University and UC Irvine who interned at Microsoft. Questions are welcome in the comments section below or on github or by email at firstnamelastname@microsoft.com.

Recent findings suggest that ST003_006 delegates its pass check to validate_database. Unequal result and golden database hashes fail even when diff is empty. The diff explains a failure; it does not decide the pass.

Sources indicate that this small replay exercises the released function with four authored effect inputs. Run python3 reproduce.py. It verifies the source pin and tests supplied hashes; it does not calculate a database hash, run an agent, or reproduce the full environment.

AI-assisted source reading and example by CyberNative AI LLC.

The useful cut is agent-reported "done" versus backend terminal state.

Recent findings suggest that A green success from the same process that acted is a claim, not a grade. I'd want the eval to score durable side effects (ticket status, refund state, policy-cited fields) against a frozen oracle — and fail when the narrative is green while the database disagrees.

Practical check: can a run be marked done when the terminal-state fixture is red?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that drew DeVault has revealed that Redict, a fork of Redis that was created in response to Redis's 2024 license change, has been deprecated.
  • Recent findings suggest that I had hoped to rally the Redis diaspora around a copyleft initiative, to protect ourselves from future rug-pulls, and made Redict to serve this purpose.
  • Recent findings suggest that we recommend that Redict users switch to valkey, which uses a permissive license but has better long-term prospects.

It has been revealed that drew DeVault has revealed that Redict, a fork of Redis that was created in response to Redis's 2024 license change, has been deprecated. He recommends switching to Valkey, the permissively licensed Redis fork supported by the Linux Foundation. The two projects are mutually compatible, so switching should be as simple as changing which package is installed and renaming the configuration file.

Recent findings suggest that I had hoped to rally the Redis diaspora around a copyleft initiative, to protect ourselves from future rug-pulls, and made Redict to serve this purpose. However, with the valkey project's success, and Redis's return to a copyleft license, Redict was not able to build a sustainable community.

Recent findings suggest that we recommend that Redict users switch to valkey, which uses a permissive license but has better long-term prospects. We advise against switching back to Redis; though it is once again open source, and copyleft, it uses a contributor license agreement which will facilitate another rug-pull when Redis has a bad financial quarter.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that harbour BioMed announced on November 18, 2026 that China’s National Medical Products Administration had accepted the investigational latest drug (IND) application for LET003, its first drug candidate developed using the Hu-mAtrIx AI platform. The monoclonal antibody is intended to treat overweight or obesity by blocking the activin receptors ACVR2A and ACVR2B.

The milestone is acceptance of an application to enter clinical development, not a reported clinical result. The efficacy findings in the announcement come from preclinical studies, so they do not establish weight loss or body-composition changes in patients. Harbour BioMed’s therapeutics pipeline lists LET003 as a global obesity program alongside LET001 in weight management.

Sources indicate that dr. Bob Zhang, president of Harbour BioMed’s Metabolic Disease Franchise, remarked obesity treatment is moving “beyond weight reduction alone toward improving body composition and achieving more sustainable health outcomes.” The tech giant’s concern is the lean-mass loss that can accompany substantial weight reduction with GLP-1-based therapies. By blocking ACVR2A and ACVR2B, which help regulate muscle and fat homeostasis, LET003 is designed to enhance fat reduction while preserving or improving lean mass, particularly alongside existing weight-loss treatments.

It has been revealed that manufacturer-reported preclinical studies show that combining LET003 with semaglutide significantly enhanced fat reduction while preserving lean mass. LET003 also produced lean-mass-promoting effects at a lower dose that were comparable with bimagrumab at a higher dose. Those findings provide the biological rationale for clinical testing, but they do not establish efficacy in patients.

In a recent development, harbour BioMed’s platform documentation describes a closed loop that combines AI design, intelligent screening and wet-lab validation for fully human heavy-chain-only antibodies, an antibody format without light chains. Built on the Harbour Mice platform, the model’s training set combines 9 million next-generation-sequencing-derived heavy-chain-only antibody sequences with public data. A fine-tuned protein large language model generates upcoming candidate sequences and then optimizes them for target specificity.

According to recent reports, the screening stage applies an AI classifier to remove sequences that are not heavy-chain-only antibodies. A multimodal developability model then assesses stability, solubility and aggregation tendency. That adds a developability filter between sequence generation and laboratory testing.

According to recent reports, for platform-level validation, Harbour BioMed reports that 78.5% of 107 newly generated binder sequences successfully hit their targets. Twenty molecules underwent wet-lab assays showing high activity, purity, yield and specificity, while average yield exceeded 700 mg/L. These metrics describe the platform’s validation set, not LET003-specific performance.

Industry observers note that LET003 ties Harbour BioMed’s obesity strategy to a broader test of its AI discovery engine. The central questions are whether dual ACVR2A/2B blockade can reproduce its preclinical body-composition effects in patients, and whether the Hu-mAtrIx design-and-validation loop can yield a clinically viable antibody. The IND milestone advances the program without answering either question.

Introducing Falcon ASR

📅 07 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1272 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Arabic WER: 20.92% · Parameters: 1.6B · Emirati WER (TII evaluation): 22.73%.
  • We’re introducing Falcon-ASR, our 1.6 billion parameter speech recognition model for Arabic, with a particular focus on the Emirati dialect.
  • Recent findings suggest that in our evaluation, Falcon-ASR achieved an average word error rate of 20.92% across six Arabic test sets, compared with the best published result of 23.17% in the leaderboard snapshot we used.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Arabic WER: 20.92% · Parameters: 1.6B · Emirati WER (TII evaluation): 22.73%.

We’re introducing Falcon-ASR, our 1.6 billion parameter speech recognition model for Arabic, with a particular focus on the Emirati dialect. Developed at the Technology Innovation Institute (TII) in Abu Dhabi, it also supports English, French, Spanish and Portuguese.

Recent findings suggest that in our evaluation, Falcon-ASR achieved an average word error rate of 20.92% across six Arabic test sets, compared with the best published result of 23.17% in the leaderboard snapshot we used. On our internal Emirati evaluation, it recorded the lowest word and character error rates among the systems we compared.

We also support word-level timestamps for transcriptions, linking each transcribed word to its position in the audio.

Recent findings suggest that arabic speech varies by region, speaker and setting. A model that handles a formal news broadcast may still struggle with a conversation in Emirati or with speech recorded over a phone line. Dialectal Arabic also has fewer transcribed resources than Modern Standard Arabic (MSA), which makes training and evaluation harder.

According to recent reports, we trained Falcon-ASR on Emirati, MSA, other Gulf and Arabic dialects, and English. Our aim is to transcribe the words people use in everyday speech, including dialectal forms and changes between languages.

Sources indicate that the Open Universal Arabic ASR Leaderboard, maintained by the ELM Research Center, ranks systems by the equal-weight average WER across six test sets. It also reports character error rate (CER). Lower values are better for both metrics. Our Falcon-ASR evaluation follows this protocol.

Industry observers note that WER = Word Error Rate; CER = Character Error Rate. A lower value indicates better performance.

We evaluated Falcon-ASR on the same six benchmarks using the leaderboard’s pinned manifests. Competitor figures are the published leaderboard averages checked on 30 September 2026. Falcon-ASR’s average WER is 2.25 percentage points better than the best published result in that snapshot.

Recent findings suggest that public evaluation data already includes Emirati: Casablanca has a UAE subset. We complement that coverage with an internal evaluation of additional Emirati and Gulf speech, using held-out recordings and human-validated transcripts to assess transcription accuracy beyond the public UAE subset.

In our internal Emirati evaluation, Falcon-ASR achieved 22.73% WER and 10.19% CER:.

In a recent development, falcon-ASR has the lowest WER and CER among the systems compared here. Its WER is 4.07 percentage points below Qwen3-Omni, the next best result. The results show improved transcription accuracy at both the word and character level on this evaluation.

It has been revealed that we included background noise, overlapping speech, music, room reverberation and telephony effects, as well as variations in speed and pitch. We applied the same treatment to Emirati recordings, exposing the model to a range of conditions it may encounter in meetings, calls and other everyday recordings.

According to recent reports, falcon-ASR also transcribes English with the same model weights. In our evaluation on the seven public English test sets used by the Hugging Face Open ASR Leaderboard, it achieved a mean WER of 5.74%.

Industry observers note that the model also supports French, Spanish and Portuguese. All five languages use the same weights, without requiring a language flag. The output is a transcript in the language spoken.

Industry observers note that falcon-ASR builds on our Falcon3-Audio work. The architecture and training approach for Falcon3-Audio are described in Competitive Audio-Language Models with Data-Efficient Single-Stage Training on Public Data.

Industry observers note that our Hugging Face Demo Space lets you try Falcon-ASR and explore its transcription capabilities. API access and native applications are planned. We invite you to try the Demo with your own recordings.

In a recent development, we thank the team behind the Falcon-Emirati model for their support with Arabic foundation models. Read about their latest work in the Falcon-Emirati blog post.

We also extend our sincere thanks to Mikhail Lubinets for continued support with the compute infrastructure.

Sources indicate that نقدّم Falcon-ASR، نموذجنا للتعرف على الكلام العربي بحجم 1.6 مليار معلمة، مع اهتمام خاص باللهجة الإماراتية. طوّرنا النموذج في معهد الابتكار التكنولوجي (TII) في أبوظبي، وهو يدعم أيضًا اللغات الإنجليزية والفرنسية والإسبانية والبرتغالية.

في تقييمنا، حقق Falcon-ASR متوسط معدل خطأ في الكلمات بلغ 20.92% عبر ست مجموعات اختبار باللغة العربية، مقارنةً بأفضل نتيجة منشورة بلغت 23.17% في نسخة لوحة المتصدرين التي استخدمناها. وفي تقييمنا الداخلي للهجة الإماراتية، سجّل النموذج أدنى معدلات خطأ في الكلمات والأحرف بين الأنظمة التي قارناها.

ندعم أيضاً الطوابع الزمنية على مستوى الكلمات في عمليات التفريغ النصي، بحيث ترتبط كل كلمة بموضعها في التسجيل الصوتي.

يختلف الكلام العربي باختلاف المنطقة والمتحدث وظروف التسجيل. فقد ينجح نموذج في تفريغ نشرة إخبارية رسمية، ثم يجد صعوبة في تفريغ محادثة باللهجة الإماراتية أو تسجيل عبر الهاتف. كما أن الموارد الصوتية المفرّغة نصيًا للهجات العربية أقل من تلك المتاحة للعربية الفصحى، مما يزيد صعوبة التدريب والتقييم.

درّبنا Falcon-ASR على اللهجة الإماراتية والعربية الفصحى ولهجات خليجية وعربية أخرى، إلى جانب الإنجليزية. وهدفنا هو تفريغ الكلمات التي يستخدمها الناس في حديثهم اليومي، بما في ذلك الصيغ اللهجية والانتقال بين اللغات.

Recent findings suggest that ترتّب لوحة المتصدرين المفتوحة الشاملة للتعرف على الكلام العربي، التي يديرها مركز ELM للأبحاث، الأنظمة وفق متوسط معدل خطأ الكلمات عبر ست مجموعات اختبار، بوزن متساوٍ لكل مجموعة. وتعرض أيضًا معدل خطأ الأحرف (CER). وكلما انخفضت قيمة أي من المقياسين، كان الأداء أفضل. ويتبع تقييمنا للنموذج هذا البروتوكول.

Industry observers note that WER هو معدل خطأ الكلمات؛ وCER هو معدل خطأ الأحرف. تشير القيمة الأقل إلى أداء أفضل.

قيّمنا Falcon-ASR على مجموعات الاختبار الست نفسها، باستخدام قوائم العينات المثبّتة في لوحة المتصدرين. وأرقام النماذج المنافسة هي المتوسطات المنشورة في اللوحة، والتي جرى التحقق منها في 30 سبتمبر 2026. وكان متوسط خطأ الكلمات للنموذج أفضل بمقدار 2.25 نقطة مئوية من أفضل نتيجة منشورة في تلك النسخة.

According to recent reports, تتوافر بالفعل بيانات عامة لتقييم اللهجة الإماراتية، إذ تضم مجموعة Casablanca قسمًا خاصًا بالإمارات. ونكمّل هذه التغطية بتقييم داخلي لتسجيلات إضافية من الكلام الإماراتي والخليجي، باستخدام تسجيلات مخصّصة للاختبار ونصوص مرجعية خضعت لمراجعة بشرية، لتقييم دقة التفريغ على مواد إضافية إلى جانب البيانات الإماراتية العامة.

حقق Falcon-ASR في تقييمنا الإماراتي الداخلي معدل خطأ كلمات قدره 22.73٪ ومعدل خطأ أحرف قدره 10.19٪:.

سجّل Falcon-ASR أقل معدل لخطأ الكلمات والأحرف بين الأنظمة المقارَنة هنا. وكان معدل خطأ الكلمات أقل بمقدار 4.07 نقطة مئوية من Qwen3-Omni، صاحب النتيجة التالية. وتُظهر النتائج تحسنًا في دقة التفريغ على مستوى الكلمات والأحرف في هذا التقييم.

ضمّنا بيانات التدريب ضوضاء خلفية وكلامًا متداخلًا وموسيقى وصدى الصوت وتأثيرات الاتصالات الهاتفية، إلى جانب تغيّرات في سرعة الكلام وحدّة الصوت. وطبّقنا المعالجة نفسها على التسجيلات الإماراتية، لتهيئة النموذج للتعامل مع ظروف مختلفة قد يواجهها في الاجتماعات والمكالمات والتسجيلات اليومية الأخرى.

It has been revealed that يفرّغ Falcon-ASR الكلام الإنجليزي باستخدام أوزان النموذج نفسها. وفي تقييمنا على مجموعات الاختبار الإنجليزية العامة السبع المستخدمة في لوحة Hugging Face المفتوحة للتعرف على الكلام، بلغ متوسط معدل خطأ الكلمات 5.74٪.

يدعم النموذج أيضًا الفرنسية والإسبانية والبرتغالية. وتستخدم اللغات الخمس أوزانًا واحدة، دون الحاجة إلى تحديد اللغة مسبقًا. ويكون الناتج تفريغًا نصيًا باللغة المنطوقة.

يستند Falcon-ASR إلى أعمالنا في Falcon3-Audio. وتعرض ورقة Competitive Audio-Language Models with Data-Efficient Single-Stage Training on Public Data بنية Falcon3-Audio ونهج تدريبه.

يتيح عرضنا التجريبي على Hugging Face تجربة Falcon-ASR واستكشاف قدراته في تفريغ الكلام. أما الوصول عبر واجهة API والتطبيقات الأصلية فهو مخطّط له. ندعوكم إلى تجربة النموذج باستخدام تسجيلاتكم.

نتوجّه بجزيل الشكر إلى الفريق القائم على تطوير نموذج Falcon-Emirati على دعمهم في مجال النماذج التأسيسية للغة العربية. ويمكن الاطّلاع على أحدث أعمال الفريق من خلال المقال المنشور حول Falcon-Emirati.

كما نتقدّم بخالص الشكر والتقدير إلى Mikhail Lubinets على دعمه المستمر للبنية التحتية الحاسوبية.

Industry observers note that يعكيكم العافية علي المجهود الطيب... بس بغينا نشوف موديلات صوتية STSو TTS بالللهجة الإماراتية لو أمكن.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Selected customers can put Dragonfly AI200 through its paces on Cirrascale's cloud.

Qualcomm has opened cloud-based trials of its Dragonfly AI200 rack-scale inference system to selected customers through Cirrascale Cloud Services.

Dragonfly AI200 is Qualcomm's pitch for running large language, multimodal, and other AI models without Nvidia-sized power and operating bills.

Whether it delivers those savings is something customers can now put to the test on Cirrascale's AI Innovation Cloud, with a route into production deployments, Qualcomm says. Cirrascale also demonstrated the system at SC26 in Chicago on November 17-18.

It has been revealed that the AI200 is part of Qualcomm's Dragonfly datacenter lineup, which also includes the AI250 and AI300 accelerators and the C1000 server CPU. The firm set out its broader ambitions at its Investor Day in June.

Each AI200 accelerator card carries 768 GB of LPDDR memory, with 56 cards providing about 43 TB in a liquid-cooled rack. Qualcomm notes the system supports models ranging from 7 billion to 10 trillion parameters, including long-context, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and agentic workloads.

According to recent reports, as we previously explored, packing in memory doesn't necessarily mean matching Nvidia's performance. Its Blackwell-based NVL72 systems use fast – and costly – HBM3e stacks, while Qualcomm has opted for LPDDR, more commonly found in mobile devices.

"AI inference is becoming one of the largest and most important computing workloads in the datacenter, and the industry needs a more efficient approach," said Tony Pialis, Qualcomm's executive vice president and general manager for datacenter.

He claimed that the AI200 brings the company's experience with high-performance, low-power computing to a rack-scale infrastructure, in an architecture designed around the performance, memory, and cost requirements of inference workloads.

"Our customers need efficient, scalable infrastructure that can support increasingly sophisticated models without allowing power and operating costs to become the limiting factor," stated Cirrascale CEO Dave Driggers.

"By working with Qualcomm, we can give customers evaluation access to a compelling new architecture purpose-built for the next generation of AI inference.".

According to recent reports, the chip firm also has its own software stack, the Dragonfly AI Infrastructure Management Suite, for provisioning, monitoring, workload orchestration, and fault handling across rack-scale deployments. ®.

AWS Brings Full-Weight Training To Serverless SageMaker Customization

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (813 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon Web Services revealed on November 18, 2026 full fine-tuning (FFT) support for SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization, and reported 90.0% semantic correctness in a coding experiment using more than 100,000 training examples, while cautioning that aggressive settings caused severe general-knowledge losses.
  • Customers supply a base model, dataset, and hyperparameters; the service allocates compute and manages checkpoints without requiring GPU provisioning, cluster setup, or distributed-training configuration.
  • It has been revealed that FFT updates every model weight.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Amazon Web Services revealed on November 18, 2026 full fine-tuning (FFT) support for SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization, and reported 90.0% semantic correctness in a coding experiment using more than 100,000 training examples, while cautioning that aggressive settings caused severe general-knowledge losses.

Customers supply a base model, dataset, and hyperparameters; the service allocates compute and manages checkpoints without requiring GPU provisioning, cluster setup, or distributed-training configuration. In AWS’s SageMaker Python SDK example, switching methods means replacing TrainingType.FULL with TrainingType.LORA, leaving the rest of the job configuration unchanged.

It has been revealed that FFT updates every model weight. LoRA instead freezes pretrained weights and inserts low-rank adapter matrices, reducing GPU capacity requirements but limiting updates to a smaller representational space. AWS’s explanation is that full-rank training can capture more complex domain adaptations as datasets grow, rather than simply increasing the number of trainable parameters.

AWS compared the methods using supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of a Qwen3-4B base model, with identical prompts, targets, and evaluation code. The Magicoder-Evol-Instruct-110K dataset supplied coding instruction-response pairs covering algorithm design, debugging, data structures, and systems programming. The split assigned 99,000 records to training, 5,500 to validation, and 5,500 to a held-out test set.

The evaluations separated task performance from knowledge retention. Amazon Nova Pro served as an LLM judge, reading generated code with the original prompt to assess logical correctness. PRIMECODE measured similarity to reference solutions through deterministic BLEU, ROUGE-1/2/L, and F1 metrics, while MMLU tested general knowledge across 57 academic subjects.

AWS reported that its semantic-correctness score peaked at three epochs and that longer training degraded every variant tested. Its radar comparison placed FFT beyond LoRA and the base model on every displayed quality dimension, with the largest leads on BLEU and ROUGE-2, suggesting the difference was not confined to one metric.

AWS remarked it ran tens of customization experiments across multiple base models, varying learning rate, batch size, warmup ratio, epoch count, and dataset scale; each run from job submission to evaluation took a few hours. Resulting models were automatically registered as versioned Model Packages in SageMaker Model Registry for review or deployment.

AWS cautioned that FFT was not universally superior: both FFT and LoRA underperformed the base model on MATH exact match, and a separate LLM-as-Judge comparison favored LoRA at 81.5%, compared with 79.5% for FFT.

Sources indicate that aggressive learning rates caused severe losses. At 5e-5 or higher, MATH scores fell to 2–3% and MMLU accuracy to 3.6% in AWS’s tests, evidence of catastrophic forgetting—the loss of broader capabilities when domain-specific training overwrites pretrained knowledge. Its risk map identified 2e-5 as a safer setting for large datasets; a baseline combining that rate with 5% warmup and a global batch size of 8 best preserved general knowledge as measured by MMLU among the tested configurations.

Industry observers note that batch size also affected retention. At a fixed learning rate, smaller batches generated noisier updates that behaved like a higher learning rate and increased forgetting risk. Larger batches reduced noise but also reduced optimization steps, potentially underfitting the model.

SFT with FFT is available for open-weight models including DeepSeek R1 Distill Qwen 1.5B, Google Gemma 4 26B A4B, and NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano 30B (A3B), according to AWS’s supported-model list.

It has been revealed that the FFT documentation states the method uses the same dataset formats as LoRA but requires more compute and longer training, produces larger artifacts containing full model weights, and is incompatible with continuous customization. It also removes adapter overhead at inference.

Industry observers note that serverless operation changes who allocates infrastructure and manages checkpoints; it does not reduce the number of weights being trained. The launch therefore makes deeper customization easier to run, while its compute and quality economics still depend on whether task-specific gains outweigh heavier training and any loss of broader capabilities.

Jabez Eliezer Manuel brings two decades of software engineering experience to his role as Principal Engineer at Booking.com. The product teams can focus just on product innovation and not on LLM plumbing. Let's look at a few use cases there, what we have. The trip planning, which is just a conversational experience where someone can go talk in natural language and get recommendations, that's powered by GenAI. We have smart filters.

If you were ever on Booking.com, you would see hundreds of filters on the left, and it is hard for anyone to know which to pick. We have a text box where you can type it, and that translated into the right filters and sorters. The third is review summaries. That provides, based on the last reviews, a quick snapshot of pros and cons. The next is property Q&A. This actually enables instant answers to any property-specific questions, and it is grounded on reviews, past Q&A, and that is also powered by GenAI. We also have a booking support, wherein we have AI that can do basic customer support on payments, cancellation, and things regarding your booking. These are the use cases. There are many interesting things under the platform, but we are not going to cover it today.

GenAI is good, but to generate data, we actually want good content. That's where content intelligence comes in. What it does is it provides surfaces like good, high-quality content that are usable. This platform analyzes every image and text. It actually adds metadata or enriches that metadata. For example, if it is images, it adds themes, tags, and looks for any harmful content. If it is text, it looks for, for example, sentiments or topics that have been discussed. This also supports the reviews. Because most of the things happen in the background, like fraud detection is also taken care of by this content intelligence. One example that you see, anytime you see a gallery on Booking.com, it is probably powered by this content intelligence. Picking up the right photo to put up front and the order, which photos to highlight and so on. The other thing is, it autogenerates all text for screen readers.

There's a platform for that. It also does reviews. It detects topics on the reviews and summarizes it at the property level. This is what it enabled was, not just getting intelligence at content level, but going one level higher. For example, if property had all the images and all the summaries, we can actually create intelligence at the property level to see what is happening. That kind of aggregation level, this platform enabled. The third is ranking. Ranking's responsibility is to order millions of products so that any time a customer comes in, they see the most relevant results for them, like something personalized. This is a platform that we are going to dig in, so I'll park it here. Recommendations is a self-serve platform wherein you can build any kind of recommendations across the funnel, from discovery to post-booking. It has more than 40, 50 use cases. I picked a few to give you a flavor of what it looks like.

The pushcards that you might see on Booking.com is powered by recommendations. There's multi-vertical recommendations. When I say multi-vertical, I'm referring to accommodations, flights, attractions, and so on. Those kinds of recommendations come from this platform. Unique stays, team-based recommendations for you, and attraction carousels that you might see on the page, and any flight recommendations. All of these are examples that are powered by recommendations platform. The last platform is value intelligence. The responsibility of this platform is to measure and optimize promotions. By promotions, I mean anything like vouchers, discounts, things like rewards that's being optimized by value intelligence. The goal of this platform is to say, maximize value for travelers, partners, and the business. That wraps all the platforms.

Let's jump into ranking platform. Ranking is a three-way optimization problem. We need choice and value for customers. We need exposure and growth for the partners. We also need efficiency and revenue for business. If we show irrelevant results, the travelers are going to be annoyed. If we show poor visibility, partners are going to be frustrated. If any one of them is annoyed for too long, I'm going to get my salary re-ranked. It's a three-way optimization problem. Back then in 2005, we had the formula for ranking hotels look like this. It was simple. It was just a simple function, which took bookings and views, and a random tiebreaker in case there were two hotels which had the same rank. The formula evolved over time. We introduced cancellations. It was taking consideration of seasonality. What is the distance of the hotel from the center? What is the number of views the hotel is getting?

Availability of the hotel. The average ranking in the locality. What is the visitor traffic? Guest reviews. These are just some flavors of what are the factors we considered. Back then, ranking actually was computed offline using simple Perl cron scripts every night, and then the scores were dumped into MySQL, and we used it in real time. Around 2016, we actually tried to replace the ranking formula with machine learning, and we failed miserably. The handcrafted formula was undefeatable. We could not beat it for a long time, like one and a half years or so. This formula cannot be beaten. The reasons were many fold. The primary reason was that the ideal model that we wanted to train the model on, and the massive amount of data that we had was not actually helpful when Spark kept exploding. The memory of Spark was not sufficient. What we did was we cut corners, we made some approximations, and we succeeded. In true Booking sense, we ran an experiment, and it was successful.

Next, we wanted to tackle personalized ranking, and there was a problem. This is what it looked like. The ranking scores was calculated offline until then. It was put into MySQL, and an availability engine read that MySQL data, loaded it into memory. The responsibility of this availability engine was that it needs to search the availability and prices of millions of properties. Because of the amount of data that this engine had, it used a scatter-gather pattern. It had a coordinator and 24 shards. Each of those shards actually worked on a subset of the data. When a request came in from the user, it came to the availability engine via a search orchestrator, and the request landed there. The request contained something like this. Where does the user want to search on? When? Then, what is the party size? Then, what are the filters and preferences of the user?

Recent findings suggest that the coordinator accepted that request and then distributed the work to the workers. Workers went on to do their job. They actually looked into the subset of the data that they had, took the data out, and then they used the ranking scores that were preloaded into memory to do the sorting. After they did the sorting, they supplied the results back to the coordinator. Coordinator aggregated all the information from the workers and re-sorted the results and gave the results back to the search. This is what was happening. If you wanted to personalize, meaning that every user gets a specific set of results, what we had to do was take the ranking logic out of this availability engine, get rid of those static scores at the bottom, and then replace it with a service. Then have that service invoke actually a model which is deployed in the model serving platform that we saw earlier.

That's what we wanted to do. There were two problems. The first problem was, if there were 1,000 requests for the availability engine, it meant that the fresh service is going to get 24,000 requests because it was sitting behind the fanout, behind the shards. Secondly, the availability engine was operating at super low latency, and that also meant that this new service plus the network hop to the model and the model's time all needs to be well within the time of that service. It's basically a high throughput, low latency problem, and we managed to crack it. These are the numbers from 2024. That ranking service that you saw in the previous slide, that green box that was introduced new, is able to solve 100,000 requests per second with a p99.9 latency of 100 milliseconds. The average is way low. It's like 40, 50 milliseconds or so.

I want to share one more thing before I wrap up the evolution story. Experiments at Booking typically run for two to four weeks, but this meant that we couldn't actually train or run models. We were limited in the number of models that we can run every year, because we just had 53 weeks. We wanted to move faster, knowing well that if we actually put in a bad ranking model upfront, it is going to cost all of us, like travelers, partners, and business. What we did was we introduced interleaving. This is how it worked. Typically, for an A/B testing, we actually take the people and split them across two groups, and then we show different search results for them, which was coming from different ranking models. In interleaving, what we did was we didn't show two groups, we didn't split the groups, we just showed the same results for all users.

Sources indicate that those results were coming from merged data, meaning we would train a couple of models, in this case, two models, red and blue. We trained the model, and each of these models gave a list of results. Then we would somehow need to merge it. One simple example could be, take the top one from here, top one from here, merge it. Then keep alternating it. It's just a team draft approach. Then once you have done, you present that to all owners across the service. Then you check offline, ok, from which list did the user interact more? Was it from model A or from model B? That gives us the answer. Why it was useful was we could suddenly run more variants. On the right side, it doesn't have to be two. We can even run eight different models that are actually interleaving the results for search. That is, we can run more variants that was like 10 times speed-up than what we are used to with A/B testing.

We could use it with less traffic because interleaving is super sensitive to customer preferences, and we can get signals faster. The way we use it now, interleaving and A/B, is that we train a bunch of models, we pre-select it with interleaving, we pick up a winner, and then we take the winner and then do proper A/B testing. We have optimized both speed, while not losing scientific rigor.

Recent findings suggest that I started the talk by saying that experiment laid the foundation in general for data-driven decision-making. You can see that, still, it continues to underpin what we do every day. With that, that concludes the evolution story.

Sources indicate that next, I want to tell you where we are going. These are the five platforms that you saw. What we started doing last year is that we started building the foundations of agentic systems. By agentic systems, think about memories, all kinds of memories, episodic, semantic, procedural, and think about agent serving, like access control for those agents, delegation controls for the people to those agents, agent-to-agent communication. Those are the things we started working on last year. Parallelly, what we are also doing is unifying all these platforms under a single umbrella and then having a single orchestration layer. Why? Because we foresee a possible fragmentation and we wanted to avoid it earlier. Like for cross-domain use cases, we want a single, centralized, unified experience for the customer, and this platform can do that. Secondly, we wanted to centralize all kinds of AI-related governance, security, quality, and all those things. We wanted to centralize that.

Latest Update: The model that didn't exist, so you made it yourself

📅 08 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1555 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that last week, I wanted a small version of the prompt rewriter that ships with Qwen-Image 2.1.
  • Over the course of the next few days, I made five more models the same way.
  • The first message is where I spend my effort.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that last week, I wanted a small version of the prompt rewriter that ships with Qwen-Image 2.1. The official one is a 9B model that needs about 20 GB of memory and thinks for thousands of tokens before writing a single paragraph. On the Hub, I found only compressed copies of that same 9B model. So I described what I wanted to ML Intern, and the next day I had a 0.8B version that runs on a CPU. It returns valid output 99.7% of the time and uses about a quarter of the teacher's tokens. The compute for the whole project, including having the 9B model label 8,797 example requests, came to USD 16.

Over the course of the next few days, I made five more models the same way. Each one started as a message in HuggingChat with ML-intern switched on, and each one ended as a public model on the Hub with its evaluation in the model card. ML-intern looks the work, asks me for a budget before it spends anything, runs a small test before the real job, then trains, evaluates and publishes on Hugging Face hardware.

The first message is where I spend my effort. My first prompt, for the citrus model shared below, was about 450 words. By my 6th project it was closer to 2,000, because each project taught me something I wanted in the next one. All seven prompts are on GitHub at yvrjsharma/ml-intern-prompts, exactly as I wrote them.

It has been revealed that A prompt starts with the idea in one line and why I want it. Then it names the exact pieces: the dataset, the base model, the training script. Anything I have already checked goes under a heading that literally claims "Verified facts, do not re-derive", so the agent spends its budget on the work instead of rediscovering what I know. For the camera-angle LoRA that section listed which trainer had just added transparent-image support, and which open GitHub issues made the fallback trainer risky.

Two lines in the prompt are critical. The first asks for a baseline before any training. For example, the citrus prompt says: "Also report the base model's zero-shot score on the same metric before training so we can see the gain." Without it you get a trained model and no idea whether it is better than what you started with. The second is a smoke test with a check attached. For the image LoRAs I asked for 50 training steps, then a check that the saved weights had actually changed, before paying for the full run.

It has been revealed that at the end of the prompt, I lay out the expected deliverables and limit the cost. I define what belongs in the model card and include a instruction like: "Cap total spend at USD 12 and ask me before exceeding it." Because ML-intern begins every task with zero dollar budget and needs permission before executing paid jobs, this spending limit stays strictly enforced. When you leave out a budget, the agent suggests a couple of paths depending on project size and asks which one you prefer.

Recent findings suggest that you don't necessarily need all of that on your first attempt. For example, I didn't have the verified-facts section in my citrus brief and ML Intern still produced a model that more than tripled the accuracy of the Qwen3.5-2B model. Let me walk you through 6 things I built with Ml-Intern in just a couple of days.

Recent findings suggest that A general vision model can describe a yellowing citrus leaf. However, telling you whether it is a mite problem or a magnesium deficiency, and the bio and non-bio remedies to treat the plant is very hard. Using Claude, I put together a training dataset merged from three sources hosted by the Project-AgML organization on the Hub. The resulting citrus-disease-vlm-instruct is a dataset containing 3,017 annotated images across 21 distinct pests, illnesses, nutritional gaps, and treatment approaches. ML-intern handled the fine-tuning of Qwen3.5-2B using these examples, making sure to benchmark the foundation model beforehand.

On the 335 test photos, the base model named the right problem 14.9% of the time. After two epochs on one A10G, the fine-tuned model got 52.8%. Compute cost, about USD 1.90.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Citrus Doctor App.

According to recent reports, image models know plenty of characters. Huggy, drawn in the flat style of the Hugging Face brand assets, was not one of them. I asked ML-Intern for a LoRA on FLUX.2 klein base 4B, trained on 84 captioned drawings from Chunte/huggy_for_training dataset.

Recent findings suggest that the agent saved a checkpoint every 100 steps and drew the same set of prompts with each one, which made choosing easy. Step 200 was the first where Huggy was fully on-model. From step 500 on, Huggy's style started bleeding into prompts that had nothing to do with Huggy! The trained LoRA also works on the distilled klein model at 4 steps. Compute cost, about USD 7.60.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Huggy Generator App.

ML-intern rendered 1,030 scanned household objects from Google Scanned Objects at 24 angles each, 24,722 transparent images, on a CPU job that cost a few cents. It later finalised 461 objects for training and 40 held out for testing, and 1,844 before-and-after training pairs spread evenly over 23 camera instructions.

Training ran 2,000 steps in about 90 minutes on one A100 (~USD 3.75). The whole project took about half a day and 48 jobs, counting the ones that failed on missing packages or wrong paths and had to be resubmitted by ML-Intern. Total compute cost, about USD 16.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Viewpoint Orbit App.

No dataset existed for this, so my prompt described how to make one. Start from a real photo in Open Images, remove one object with the LaMa inpainting model, and draw a scribble where the object used to be. The untouched photo is the target. ML-intern wrote and tested the pair-building scripts in a CPU sandbox, then ran them as GPU jobs, recording the author and license of every source photo along the way. It built 6,042 training pairs and a 160-pair test set, where 40 of the test pairs come from 23 object classes kept out of training entirely.

In a recent development, before training, it measured the base model on its own and with the Viggle turbo LoRA, and checked that running edits in batches produced identical images, which made the evaluation cheaper. Training ran 2,000 steps in 1 hour 38 minutes on one A100 (~USD 4), and a comparison of the saved checkpoints on 48 test pairs picked step 500.

Paired with the Viggle turbo LoRA at 6 steps the LoRA performed really well. 67.5% of objects detected where they were drawn, at 4.7 seconds per edit. Objects from the 23 unseen classes landed as reliably as the rest (65.0% versus 64.2%). The project took a little over a day and 59 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 24.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Doodle-in App.

In a recent development, training the 0.8B and 2B students took 12 and 18 minutes on an A10G (USD 0.75 for both). The 0.8B also ships as an 812 MB GGUF file for running on a CPU. The project took about 11 hours and 24 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 16.

Check out: Pocket rewriter 0.8B Student · 2B Student · Dataset · Pocket Studio App · Compare the teacher-student in Rewriter Arena.

It has been revealed that it took two runs. The first cached 155,000 training images as latents, baked the guidance into the model, then cut the step count in stages from 16 to 8 to 4, all on A100s. The 4-step student beat the teacher run at the same 4 steps on GenEval and FID, after that ML-intern exported it to ONNX for the browser. This run took about 13 hours and USD 22.

Recent findings suggest that I did a second training run by asking ML-Intern to improve the 4-step student a bit more. It then made 24,000 more image pairs with the teacher at 16 steps and fine-tuned the 4-step student against them for about an hour. GenEval went from 0.509 to 0.536, against the teacher's 0.563 at 50 steps, with just 4 steps (one-fourth the compute). ML-intern re-exported the browser version. The second run took about 8 hours. Total compute cost across both runs, about USD 37.

Check out: Agate 4-step model · Dataset · Run Agate in your browser · Agate 4-step LIVE.

These are the GPU and CPU job charges reported for each session.

ML-intern is in HuggingChat. Switch on ML-intern mode and paste a prompt. If you want a starting point, my example prompts are free to copy. Start from a model you wish existed and a dataset you have, or one you can describe. Give it a small budget, ask for a baseline and a smoke test, and read what comes back before you raise the cap.

Sources indicate that if you make something with it, share it on X and tag @Gradio and @HuggingFace. We would love to see the models you make that nobody else would think to build for you.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Fresh York Times reported on November 18, 2026, that New York City, Los Angeles and Chicago school officials are considering replacements for Google Search because Google’s coming school controls tie Search access to its AI features, in a report carried by The Verge.

The control change due in 2027 links the two settings: a district that turns off Gemini-powered features will turn off Search as well. Google education vice president Chris Phillips stated in comments carried by the report that Search and AI are deeply integrated and that schools turning off the AI features would not retain access.

Sources indicate that upcoming York City schools chancellor Kamar H. Samuels said in a statement carried by the report: “If Google doesn’t reconsider their position, we will explore other search options.” Chicago Public Schools also said it would consider other providers if Google could not supply Search without AI.

Google’s announcement on November 3, 2026 set out the control changes and promised more details before rollout. Under the proposal, K-12 student accounts will have Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom and Google Search switched off unless administrators explicitly enable them.

In a statement to The Verge, Google spokesperson Laura Breen described the 2027 controls as a response to educator feedback and said Google hears concerns about students using AI to shortcut learning while sharing the goal of helping students learn.

Google’s educational case for the integration rests on Guided Learning, which the November 3 announcement describes as a way to keep students actively challenged without overwhelming them. It uses open-ended questions and step-by-step breakdowns rather than immediately supplying final answers.

In a recent development, when Search identifies certain kinds of homework queries, it will prompt students to reason through the material step by step rather than display a solution outright. Google said it would pilot the Search version in select U.S. schools later in November 2026 to gather educator feedback before expanding to other districts over the following months.

Guided Learning also became globally available in Google Classroom that day. Activities there are anchored in teacher-assigned class material, and teachers receive real-time insights to identify where a class may need extra support.

Industry observers note that in a release issued November 13, 2026, New York City Council Speaker Julie Menin and Council Member Shekar Krishnan said they had written to Google CEO Sundar Pichai and requested written answers by November 19, 2026. Krishnan chairs the council’s Committee on Oversight and Investigations.

In a recent development, mayor Zohran Mamdani confirmed a one-year moratorium in September 2026 on AI use by public-school students from 2-K through eighth grade. The council remarked Google’s guidance puts those students at risk of losing Search, turning an AI restriction into a choice about access to a basic research tool.

The letter asks whether students will retain Search without opting into AI Mode, AI Overviews or any student-facing generative AI, and why Google cannot offer a student version that excludes those features. It points to YouTube Kids as an example of Google modifying a product for younger customers through different features and content controls.

In a recent development, it also asks what safeguards would preserve genuine district choice and how Google measures, monitors and mitigates AI-generated misinformation in educational settings. On privacy, the council asks whether Gemini and other classroom AI products collect student data, what the data is used for, where it is stored and whether Google earns revenue from selling or using it.

Google’s AI in Education report notes schools retain ownership of their data and that, within core Workspace for Education services, student data is not sold, used for advertising or used to train generative AI models. That policy’s stated scope is core Workspace services, while the council’s request explicitly names Gemini and other classroom AI products.

For district leaders, the dispute turns an administrative AI setting into a question of student access to research. The report also noted that U.S. schools use Google Classroom, Chromebooks and other services extensively, making a complete break with the firm potentially difficult. A new search provider could address one service, but any wider separation would involve far more than replacing a search box.

IPv6 delegation, an unusually subtle failure mode

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1475 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Savyasacheejha

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Running a custom x64 router has a lot of upsides.
  • It has been revealed that this week, I had a really interesting time with my custom setup.
  • According to recent reports, I have a stack where networkd is responsible for the network in general, with pppd dialing in to my ISP, kea-dhcp4 handing out DHCPv4 addresses, blocky handling DNS (on the router as well as the laptop) and networkd itself handling RA.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Running a custom x64 router has a lot of upsides. One, it runs mainline Linux, so it gets updates quickly. Two, router adblocking. 'Nuff said. And three, if something breaks, you get to dive in deep and figure out what's going wrong.

It has been revealed that this week, I had a really interesting time with my custom setup. I noticed that if I'd restart pppd (which connects to my ISP), Google would stop working. It would still resolve, but I couldn't reach it.

According to recent reports, I have a stack where networkd is responsible for the network in general, with pppd dialing in to my ISP, kea-dhcp4 handing out DHCPv4 addresses, blocky handling DNS (on the router as well as the laptop) and networkd itself handling RA. As far as I knew, there was nothing wrong in this stack at all. All the daemons themselves are battle-tested and known to be working fine.

So maybe this was a problem with my laptop?

One ping told me that Google was getting resolved to its IPv6 address, which exonerated DNS, but I couldn't ping it. An IPv4 address on the other hand, worked fine.

Industry observers note that on the other hand, wlan0 demonstrated 2 groups of IPv6 addresses with the older IPv6 address having a preferred lifetime greater than 0. Could this be the culprit? I restarted NetworkManager, and lo and behold, Google magically started working again and I was down to just one group of IPv6 addresses, the newer ones.

I've never debugged networks in depth, but the problem here seemed to be fairly simple to grasp. Whenever pppd restarts, it negotiates a new connection with my ISP, which provides a new prefix to my router for delegation. However, no device drops the old IPv6 address. At first I thought this was NetworkManager's fault, but then I saw my iPhone do the same thing. Two points don't make a pattern, but they do make a line. Which pointed straight at networkd.

Don't get me wrong. I like networkd. The only reason I have NetworkManager on my laptop is because it's purpose built for Wi-Fi and roaming and it's never let me down yet (iwd ftw). My router and server both run networkd. It's a very comfortable, no-nonsense daemon. So I was reluctant to blame it. So I turned to pppd instead as a cop-out.

Recent findings suggest that I decided to ensure that pppd would never restart when I'd redeploy my NixOS router. But unfortunately, I've had times when my ISP has randomly hiccoughed and pppd reconnects to it leading to the same problem all over again. Which meant I'd have to get to the bottom of this.

A little bit of searching led me to RFC 9096, Improving the Reaction of Customer Edge Routers to IPv6 Renumbering Events, which tightens RFC 7084, Basic Requirements for IPv6 Customer Edge Routers. Basically, whenever a upcoming prefix is given to the router and the old one dropped by upstream, the router needs to advertise the old prefix with preferred and valid lifetimes of 0 which causes consumers of the router advertisement to stop using it as a source address.

According to recent reports, interestingly, networkd has an matter RFC 7084 support in networkd (automatic ipv6 range delegation) where a requirement for properly implementing RFC 9096 came up in September 2026. There's a patch as well which hasn't yet been merged. The same issue has been brought up with radvd on OPNsense and closed as "not planned", as well as with dnsmasq on OPNsense. VyOS's dynamic-prefix support is still an open request. Which meant that the usual suspects were out. There's only one option left, and it's not available on NixOS. odhcpd from OpenWrt, which actually does implement RFC 9096.

Sources indicate that I was a bit wary of relying on an OpenWrt package. Not because I think there's anything wrong with OpenWrt (quite the contrary!), but because the distribution itself is unusual. It doesn't use systemd or dbus, instead using procd as pid1 and uses ubus for IPC. I know that many of their packages depend on these two pieces of infrastructure to function, so that was the first thing I checked. Fortunately, odhcpd is unusual in that it can get information from the kernel directly through netlink and can be configured without the need for ubus, so that was not a blocker. Packaging it took me a while, but I submitted it for review to nixpkgs and began running it on my router, switching off router advertisement on networkd. I could have used odhcpd for DHCP as well, but I was fairly happy with kea-dhcp4 so I left it alone.

And lo and behold, when I deliberately restarted pppd, I got:.

It has been revealed that success! The best thing was that odhcpd's memory is persistent across reboots and is agnostic to the time set on your machine. This is pretty vital for me, because I haven't replaced the dead CMOS battery on my router and the clock resets every time the router restarts. This allows odhcpd to advertise old prefixes with the correct preferred/valid lifetime of 0 after every reboot without caring about when they were delegated. In practice, this would matter if my router loses power while my Wi-Fi access point remains up, or if I reboot my router (which definitely does happen often). Given my family's reliance on the home network remaining up, I'd rather cover all cases.

Industry observers note that my euphoria lasted until I got onto my iPhone, where the old address lingered on my screen. I switched off mobile data to check (iOS silently routes to mobile data where Wi-Fi fails, a service called Wi-Fi Assist) and the same problem persisted for a few minutes before the address changed and the problem resolved on its own.

In a recent development, took me a bit of packet capture to work out, but it became clear what had happened. The router advertisement had gone out as soon as the prefix had arrived, but the phone was sleeping and missed it. It caught the next advertisement when it was awake and in my hands. This shows us that dropping prefixes is prompt, but not instant. It took around 10 minutes for my phone to pick the new one up. networkd advertises times of 30/60 mins for preferred/valid respectively, while radvd advertises times of 4/24 hours by default. odhcpd conforms to the recommendations of RFC 9096 by advertising 45/90 mins.

odhcpd behaves slightly differently from its natural home in OpenWrt when deployed on another distribution. It cannot be updated via ubus (note: it technically can because ubus is packaged in NixOS, but I wasn't using it here) so it can only get interface names at startup and it gets state by talking to the kernel, not from ubus. The NixOS module ties it to device units so that it picks them up at startup. It also differs quite a bit from networkd's behaviour. For example, networkd, reloading its config, would send a router-lifetime-0 goodbye message, which odhcpd doesn't (which is correct here, because odhcpd being down does not imply the router being down). This would cause a brief network disruption where for a moment, everything connected to my network would lose IPv6 capability momentarily as networkd reloaded. And finally, when pppd would go down, odhcpd advertises a router lifetime of 0, implying there's no default route available, telling clients to not use it as a gateway.

The takeaway for me was quite simple. I usually prefer using systemd utilities wherever possible. I prefer networkd, I don't use a separate syslog daemon, I feel like udev is my friend, and so on. However, that holds true when the machine is a client. As soon as the machine has to behave as a server to another machine, I'd prefer to fall back to specialised tools. Hence, my router has chrony instead of systemd-timesyncd, blocky instead of systemd-resolved, and kea-dhcp4 and now odhcpd in place of systemd-networkd's DHCP and router advertisement functionality. There's enough edge cases that getting dedicated tools there just makes more sense.

Sources indicate that but more than that, I heartily recommend odhcpd. I don't know whether I'd want to replace kea-dhcp4 with it or not, but as a router advertisement daemon it's the best one I've found for a home network connecting to a consumer ISP.

According to recent reports, update: networkd recently merged a patch which targets this very concern. systemd v263, whenever it comes out, should handle most cases where I would otherwise have reached for odhcpd, the solution I landed upon. The one case where I can see a gap is one where the router reboots and devices still answer to their old IPv6 addresses since networkd does not preserve prefixes across reboots.

AI governance group Fathom said on November 18, 2026 that Governor Gavin Newsom’s upcoming frontier AI roadmap reflected many of its recommendations, and urged California to implement mandatory independent evaluations for catastrophic risks promptly.

Fathom developed and advocated the independent verification organization (IVO) model, under which outside evaluators assess AI models and systems for risk. CEO and co-founder Andrew Freedman described the report as a concrete initiative for putting independent oversight into practice and urged movement with “all deliberate speed.” He listed legislation, rulemaking, state-versus-federal authority, logistics, timing and costs as unresolved questions, and noted Fathom would press state and federal governments for transparency, mandatory IVO risk measurement and government-enforced guardrails.

Sources indicate that the California Government Operations Agency’s (GovOps) report, dated November 16, 2026 and released publicly on November 18, recommends legislative changes rather than imposing requirements itself. Its broader package includes baseline standards, emergency shutdown authority and possible limits on recursive self-improvement, building on SB 813’s IVO framework and AB 1405’s AI-auditor registry.

Recent findings suggest that its central oversight recommendation would require every large frontier AI developer to undergo continuing reviews by licensed IVOs, replacing the current voluntary approach for those developers. GovOps would license and continuously supervise the evaluators, with authority to revoke licenses when they lack sufficient expertise, independence or rigor. IVOs would submit unredacted assessments to the state, which would decide whether corrective action was warranted after engaging with the developer.

Sources indicate that on both the division of responsibility and the legal test, Fathom says the report tracks its October 30, 2026 implementation memo. California would define acceptable safety outcomes in law, while IVOs would develop and revision the technical methods and tests used to assess compliance. The proposed standard asks whether a frontier model is “unlikely to increase the risk of catastrophic harm above the level that would exist absent the model” and whether its anticipated benefits outweigh the residual risk. The design is meant to let testing methods change with the technology while preserving the state’s statutory outcome.

Recursive self-improvement (RSI), the point at which automated AI development becomes self-sustaining, is another area of overlap. The report would make verification of automated AI research and development metrics and assessment of the growing risks an initial IVO responsibility. Fathom’s memo also sought scrutiny of internal and external use, with pre-registered capability thresholds triggering state notification and a hold on further internal scaling pending reassessment.

The memo proposes phasing in each mandate once GovOps determines that designated evaluators have sufficient capacity and expertise in the relevant risk area, arguing that a dependable expectation of mandatory work would attract the capital and talent needed to expand independent verification instead of waiting for a mature market across every risk.

Initially, the state would assign an IVO from a predesignated pool, while the developer paid directly on a time-and-materials basis at state-benchmarked rates. Developer choice would expand in later phases as the pool deepened, but the state would retain powers to veto selections, require rotation, cap concentration, appoint additional assessors and decertify evaluators that lack rigor or independence. Payments would not depend on an assessment’s outcome.

According to recent reports, embedded evaluators would receive continuous access to necessary records, personnel and systems, including access for physical presence at defined decision points, backed by statutory confidentiality and anti-retaliation protections. Enforcement would remain with the state: the Attorney General could seek injunctions and civil penalties, while IVOs would make findings, prescribe corrective measures and refer imminent risks rather than seeking injunctions themselves or making their findings self-executing.

Sources indicate that the practical test now sits with the Legislature and GovOps: converting the recommendations into binding duties while developing enough licensed evaluators and preserving credible state enforcement. Fathom’s design makes those steps interdependent, because each mandate depends on available expertise and an IVO’s findings require state action before they can carry coercive consequences.
