That range makes the network and operating model vital: the infrastructure has to coordinate many accelerators for both training runs and production inference.

Nscale says it is the first in the industry to deploy Dell’s fully integrated, liquid-cooled L11 networking rack. RoCE, short for RDMA over Converged Ethernet, supplies high-throughput, low-latency communication for distributed AI traffic. Nscale’s Ethernet fabric incorporates high-performance switching, congestion management, telemetry, and automation on a standards-based foundation. The design is intended to keep GPUs working on parallel jobs rather than waiting on memory, networking, or operational bottlenecks.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, nginx is one of the most widely deployed web servers in the world.
  • It has been revealed that xint also found a separate vulnerability in the Linux kernel which can be chained with any of the nginx vulnerabilities to gain root privileges on the host.
  • If you run nginx, upgrade to 1.31.9 as soon as the fixed release becomes available.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, nginx is one of the most widely deployed web servers in the world. Finding an unauthenticated remote code execution bug in it has long been a holy grail for security researchers. The Xint research team recently found five. Each one leads to remote code execution on its own, but they affect different configurations.

It has been revealed that xint also found a separate vulnerability in the Linux kernel which can be chained with any of the nginx vulnerabilities to gain root privileges on the host. Together, we call these six vulnerabilities nginx2root.

If you run nginx, upgrade to 1.31.9 as soon as the fixed release becomes available. This article explains the root cause of each nginx2root vulnerability and summarizes our exploitability assessments. For exposure checks, see Section 2 and for patching and temporary mitigations, see Section 3.

The most impactful of the five findings, CVE-2026-123007, allows an unauthenticated attacker to execute commands on an affected nginx server with HTTP/2 enabled. The commands run with the privileges of the nginx worker process that handles the request.

We chained this vulnerability with a separate flaw in the Linux kernel's SCTP subsystem to gain root privileges on the host. In our tests, the chain also escaped a Docker container running nginx and obtained root on the underlying host.

In the video below, we use CVE-2026-123007 to execute commands as the nginx worker inside a container, then use the kernel vulnerability to escalate to root on the host.

Recent findings suggest that we ran this demo on AWS, attacking the server over its public IP address. Demos for AWS, GCP, Azure, and bare-metal servers are available at nginx2root.com.

Each one of the five nginx vulnerabilities are independent attack paths and do not need to be chained together. They differ in what configuration is affected.

First affected release for this path.

resolver, a request-derived proxy_pass destination, and mirror with mirror_request_body off.

HTTP/3 with requests forwarded to an upstream (backend) server.

Industry observers note that for CVE-2026-123634, the table reveals the setup we tested, which uses the mirror directive. Other nginx features that create subrequests, such as SSI, may reach the same bug, so turning off mirror alone does not make a server safe.

CVE-2026-123007 has been present since nginx introduced HTTP/2 in 2015, more than a decade ago. Every official release from 1.9.5 through 1.31.8 contains the vulnerable code, including the master branch on Nov 10, 2026. Even servers running recent releases therefore need the same checks for patch status and HTTP/2 exposure as older installations.

Patch to 1.31.9 when it is available. Until then, disabling HTTP/2 on affected listening ports blocks CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633. It does not block the other three nginx vulnerabilities. Check your configuration against the table above and apply the matching mitigations in Section 3.3.

It has been revealed that while preparing for ZeroDay Cloud 2026, a Xint researcher found CVE-2026-123007. A few days later, a fully automated Xint scan found the other four without human guidance.

An unauthenticated remote attacker can execute arbitrary commands with nginx worker privileges.

Affected versions (CVE-2026-123007).

All official releases from nginx 1.9.5 through 1.31.8. The vulnerable code was also present in master as of November 10, 2026.

Sources indicate that section 2 focuses on CVE-2026-123007, the vulnerability that affects the most servers. It only requires HTTP/2 to be enabled. For the other four nginx vulnerabilities, first check the configuration table in Section 1.

CVE-2026-123007 affects every official nginx release from 1.9.5 through 1.31.8. As of November 10, 2026, the vulnerable code was also still present in the development branch (master).

The version number alone may not show whether a server is patched.

Industry observers note that three of the most common versions are the default package versions shipped by major Linux distributions. Ubuntu 24.04 comes with 1.24.0, Ubuntu 22.04 provides 1.18.0, and Debian 12 provides 1.22.1. These distributions may backport security fixes to the existing version instead of replacing it with a upcoming nginx release.

It has been revealed that A backport can fix a vulnerability without changing the version reported by nginx -v. Only the distribution's full package version changes. For example, Ubuntu 22.04 originally shipped 1.18.0-6ubuntu14. By October 26, 2026, security updates had brought the package to 1.18.0-6ubuntu14.22, while the nginx version remained 1.18.0.

To determine whether a specific fix is included, compare the full installed package version with the distribution's security advisory.

As of November 10, 2026, Shodan returned 56.7 million hosts for product:nginx. Of these, 11.94 million (21.1%) reported an identifiable version. Among hosts with an identified version, 98.9% fell within the version range affected by CVE-2026-123007: 1.9.5 through 1.31.8.

Industry observers note that these numbers are based on reported version strings and don’t confirm that a server is vulnerable. Exploiting CVE-2026-123007 also requires HTTP/2 to be enabled, and a reported version may already include a backported fix.

A server is affected by CVE-2026-123007 if it runs an unpatched version, includes the HTTP/2 module, and has HTTP/2 enabled. The first three checks below test each of these conditions. The fourth tests whether HTTP/2 is reachable over the Internet. The table at the end of this section shows how to read the combined results.

First, print the nginx version.

The command prints a version string such as nginx version: nginx/1.31.8.

1.31.9 or later: Likely patched, but confirm that the build includes the changes referenced in github.com/nginx/nginx/releases#release-release-1.31.9.

In a recent development, distribution or appliance-specific version: Do not rely on the version string alone. Confirm whether the fix was backported.

Check whether the binary was built with the HTTP/2 module.

HTTP2_MODULE=present: The binary contains the HTTP/2 code, which is vulnerable if not patched. Continue with the next check.

HTTP2_MODULE=absent: The binary does not contain the HTTP/2 code and is not affected by this vulnerability.

According to recent reports, output, such as listen 443 ssl http2; or http2 on;, means HTTP/2 is enabled. No output means it is not. Note that nginx -T reads the configuration on disk. If you changed it without reloading nginx, the running configuration may differ.

If you see ALPN protocol: h2, the server accepts HTTP/2 from the Internet, while No ALPN negotiated means it doesn’t. Anything else means the connection failed, so check that the server is reachable and try again.

If a CDN or reverse proxy sits in front of nginx, the test only reaches the proxy, so also run it directly against the nginx server.

Sources indicate that upgrade nginx to 1.31.9 when the fixed release is available, and confirm that the installed build includes fixes for all five vulnerabilities. If you cannot patch immediately, apply the mitigations for your configuration in Section 3.3. Note that disabling HTTP/2 addresses only two of the five nginx vulnerabilities.

After installing the update, restart nginx or complete a supported live binary upgrade. A configuration reload alone does not replace the running executable.

An attack using CVE-2026-123007 may leave little evidence in nginx access logs. The WINDOW_UPDATE and RST_STREAM control frames used to trigger the vulnerability are not logged as requests, and TLS encrypts them in transit. The subsections below cover four other places to look: connection statistics (3.2.1), requests per connection (3.2.2), programs started by workers (3.2.3), and worker crashes (3.2.4). Section 3.2.5 explains how to weigh them together.

On the target server, inspect TCP statistics for port 443.

These patterns match the attack we tested. It sends a large number of WINDOW_UPDATE frames over one long-lived connection, so bytes_received keeps climbing while nginx sends little back. It also opens many short TLS connections from the same IP. If you see both for several minutes and there is no legitimate explanation, such as a large upload, block the source and investigate.

It has been revealed that the default access log does not show which connection each request belongs to. The log format below adds the connection ID (conn), the number of requests on that connection, and the size of each request. Add it to the nginx http block. No debug build is needed.

Take a suspicious IP from Section 3.2.1 and add up the request_length of its log entries, per conn. Compare that total with the bytes_received that ss highlights for the same IP. If bytes_received keeps growing quickly while the logged request lengths stay small, the client is sending a lot of data that never shows up as requests. That fits a flood of HTTP/2 control frames, as in the attack. Long request_time values in the same period are another sign.

Our exploit uses execve() to start a shell or another program. A normal nginx worker has no reason to run external programs, so any program it starts warrants immediate investigation. First, identify the worker account's UID.

On systems that use the Linux audit subsystem auditd, replace NGINX_UID with the numeric UID from the previous output and add the following rule.

According to recent reports, the rule records executions only after it is installed. An empty result cannot rule out an earlier compromise. It also matches other processes using the same UID, so check the process and parent process IDs to establish whether an event came from nginx.

Industry observers note that look for /bin/sh, /bin/bash, or any other program started by an nginx worker. If other applications run under the same account, check each event’s parent process against your service configuration to tell which ones came from nginx.

A failed exploit attempt can crash an nginx worker, so look for abnormal exits and core dumps with the commands below.

A worker can crash for reasons unrelated to an attack. Correlate these records with the other signals before drawing a conclusion.

It has been revealed that A program started by an nginx worker (Section 3.2.3) is the clearest sign of a successful attack. Investigate it immediately. The signs below are weaker, and each one can have a normal cause on its own. If several show up together and you cannot explain them, block the source and investigate:.

Sustained high inbound traffic (Section 3.2.1).

Many connections from the same source (Section 3.2.1).

Before a patch is available, disabling the affected features can block the known attack paths. These measures are temporary. Install the fixed release when it becomes available.

Recent findings suggest that both vulnerabilities arise while nginx handles HTTP/2 connections. Disable HTTP/2 on affected ports until the patch is installed. Clients that support HTTP/1.1 can continue using the service, but services that require HTTP/2, such as native gRPC, will be affected.

It has been revealed that for nginx 1.25.1 and later, set http2 off; in each affected server block and remove any legacy http2 parameter from its listen directives. Check all server blocks sharing the listening address and port.

For nginx 1.9.5 through 1.25.0, remove http2 from listen 443 ssl http2;.

The last command prints nothing once HTTP/2 is disabled. It also prints nothing if the connection fails, so make sure the site still loads normally over HTTPS.

This mitigation is for servers that choose their upstream (backend) per request and also use mirror. This happens when proxy_pass contains a variable, such as proxy_pass http://$host;, and nginx uses its resolver to look up that name with DNS while handling the request.

According to recent reports, the bug is triggered while the main request and its mirror wait for the same DNS answer. Until the patch is installed, point proxy_pass at a fixed upstream group instead. This removes the DNS lookup during the request and blocks the path we tested.

Setting mirror_request_body on also stopped our exploit, but it does not fix the resolver bug. Do not rely on this setting alone.

According to recent reports, in every affected server block, remove the listen directives that contain quic, set http3 off, and replace any Alt-Svc header advertising HTTP/3 with Alt-Svc 'clear'. The regular TLS listener on TCP stays, so the result should look like this:.

This mitigation only applies if you use nginx as a mail proxy in front of IMAP, POP3, or SMTP servers. You are affected if the mail block uses proxy on together with auth_http. With auth_http, nginx asks an HTTP service whether each login is valid. The bug is triggered during login, and the attacker does not need valid credentials. Until the patch is installed, keep untrusted clients away from the mail proxy.

If the proxy does not need external access, bind every IMAP, POP3, and SMTP listener to a loopback address. Only programs on the same machine can then connect. Remote clients, such as users' mail apps, will no longer be able to reach the proxy. For example:.

Industry observers note that A reload applies the upcoming configuration only to new connections. Connections that were already open, such as HTTP/2 or mail sessions, stay with the old workers and keep using the old configuration. In ps these workers show up as nginx: worker process is shutting down.

In a recent development, if such workers are still running after the reload, restart nginx through your service manager (for example, systemctl restart nginx). A restart forcibly disconnects every client and cuts off downloads, uploads, and mail sessions in progress, so expect a short service interruption.

In a recent development, finding five remote code execution bugs at once is unusual for nginx. In more than twenty years of security research, nginx has had very few unauthenticated RCEs. One example is CVE-2013-2028, a stack buffer overflow triggered by a crafted HTTP request.

Recent findings suggest that we aren’t the only ones finding more nginx bugs this year. In 2025, the nginx security advisory list recorded two latest vulnerabilities. By November 17 this year, it had recorded 26, not counting nginx2root, and several were memory corruption bugs such as buffer overflows and use-after-frees. AI-assisted research is finding bugs faster than ever, even in code as heavily studied as nginx. With nginx2root, Xint adds five more at once.

According to recent reports, the timeline below covers discovery, disclosure, and the scheduled patch release. All dates are provided in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC+0).

Xint research team discovered the vulnerabilities.

nginx team requested patch validation.

This section examines the five nginx vulnerabilities. CVE-2026-123007 begins with an error in window arithmetic that leads to an out-of-bounds write. The other four are use-after-free vulnerabilities. For each, we explain the relevant nginx features and behavior, trace the code behind the bug, and summarize how it leads to remote code execution. We explain how to achieve address disclosure and controlled memory corruption, but we intentionally omit the final steps needed to reproduce the full exploits.

CVE-2026-123007 is an integer overflow vulnerability in HTTP/2 flow control. A send window exceeds its permitted maximum, eventually producing an invalid memory-copy length which leads to out-of-bounds reads and writes on the heap.

HTTP/2 handles multiple requests and responses over a single connection. Each request and response pair uses a stream. Streams created by the client receive distinct identifiers called Stream IDs, such as 1, 3, and 5. Within each stream, HEADERS frames carry the headers and DATA frames carry the body.

HTTP/2 uses flow control to keep the server from sending more data than the client is ready to receive. The server tracks this with send windows, one per stream plus one for the whole connection, which we call the h2c window. Each window holds the amount of DATA the server may still send. The server can only send DATA on a stream if both that stream's window and the h2c window have enough credit left. When the client is ready for more, it sends a WINDOW_UPDATE frame, and the server increases the matching window by that amount.

In a recent development, the Stream ID in WINDOW_UPDATE determines which window is increased. Stream ID 0 updates the h2c window, while a nonzero Stream ID updates only that stream's window.

nginx uses a default window of 65,535 (0xffff) and a maximum of 0x7fffffff ((1U << 31) - 1).

According to recent reports, nginx holds outgoing frames in an in-memory output queue before sending them through the socket. When it queues response DATA, ngx_http_v2_send_chain() deducts the DATA length from both the connection-level send window, h2c->send_window, and the stream's send window, stream->send_window.

If the stream is canceled before the DATA is sent, ngx_http_v2_filter_cleanup() removes that stream's remaining DATA frames from the queue and returns the deducted length to the connection-level send window.

nginx deducts credit when it queues DATA, and returns that credit if the stream is canceled before the DATA is sent. Both steps are valid. The problem is what can happen in between. While the DATA is still queued, the client can send a WINDOW_UPDATE that raises the window again. If the stream is then canceled, cleanup adds the returned credit on top of the raised window. Cleanup never checks the result against the HTTP/2 maximum, so h2c->send_window can end up above its permitted upper bound.

According to recent reports, the sequence from the window-accounting error to command execution is summarized below. Subsection (1) covers steps 1–2, subsection (2) covers step 3, and subsection (3) covers steps 4–6 at a high level.

Queue response bodies and deduct their length from the send windows, while preventing the DATA from reaching the client.

Increase the window, return queued credit.

Increase the send window via WINDOW_UPDATE, then cancel the streams so cleanup adds the credit deducted for queued DATA.

Once the shared connection window exceeds its maximum, the remaining-capacity calculation fails and later WINDOW_UPDATE frames remain accepted.

The code interprets the same bits as signed and unsigned values, converting a small negative distance into a very large copy length.

Disclose addresses and corrupt memory.

Position both ends of the copy to return memory pointers in a response, corrupting TLS allocation metadata.

Use the disclosed addresses and corrupted memory to overwrite a cleanup function pointer, then execute an arbitrary command when cleanup calls it.

The first goal is to build up DATA in nginx's output queue that has consumed window credit but has not been sent.

According to recent reports, the client first raises the connection send window to its maximum (Wmax) with a WINDOW_UPDATE on Stream ID 0. The client sets the initial send window for newly introduced streams through SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE in a SETTINGS frame. Setting it to 0 allows nginx to create response HEADERS, but prevents it from sending DATA. This keeps response bodies pending until the client chooses to release them.

It has been revealed that next, the client stops reading and sends a burst of PING frames. nginx places control-frame responses (including PING acknowledgments) ahead of pending DATA, so these acknowledgments fill the TLS and TCP send buffers. The client then sends each stream enough WINDOW_UPDATE credit for its entire response body, causing nginx to queue the DATA and deduct its length from the connection send window. Because the TLS and TCP buffers are already full, this DATA remains queued indefinitely.

Sources indicate that let Q be the total amount of this queued DATA. The client now adds Q back to the h2c window twice. First, it sends a WINDOW_UPDATE on Stream ID 0 that grants Q of credit. Second, it sends RST_STREAM to cancel the streams. Cancellation triggers cleanup, which discards the unsent DATA and returns its credit, adding Q to the h2c window again.

This second addition, shown on the last line above, has no upper-bound check. As a result, the h2c window moves through four values:.

Wmax: the client raises the window to its maximum.

Wmax - Q: queuing the DATA deducts Q.

Wmax: the WINDOW_UPDATE on Stream ID 0 grants Q back.

Wmax + Q: cleanup returns Q a second time, pushing the window past the 31-bit limit.

Recent findings suggest that the exact response sizes and stream count do not matter. What matters is that the same known quantity Q is added back twice, once by the WINDOW_UPDATE and once by cleanup.

ngx_http_v2_state_window_update() calculates the remaining capacity before applying an increment.

This check works only while the shared connection window is at or below Wmax. h2c->send_window has the unsigned type size_t, and the previous step has already changed it to Wmax + Q. The remaining-capacity expression is therefore Wmax - (Wmax + Q), which would be negative as a signed value, but unsigned arithmetic wraps it into a very large positive value.

According to recent reports, nginx treats this value as available capacity and continues accepting connection-level WINDOW_UPDATE frames for h2c. Each increment still complies with the HTTP/2 specification, but the check fails to detect that the current window is already outside its valid range. Repeating this process can increase the send window to any arbitrary 64-bit value.

h2c->send_window has the unsigned type size_t. On 64-bit targets, increasing it to, say, 2^64 - d makes it appear very large as an unsigned value, but casting it to the signed type off_t yields a small negative value -d.

According to recent reports, ngx_http_v2_send_chain() moves this value into the DATA frame size. It first compares the send window with limit, i.e. the maximum amount that the current call may send.

A positive limit is greater than -d, so the condition is true and limit also becomes -d.

The next comparison uses frame_size, the current DATA frame size, and limit.

In a recent development, A positive frame_size is greater than -d, so this condition is also true. Converting -d back to size_t produces 2^64 - d, replacing a normal DATA size with a very large value.

nginx stores the value in rest, which tracks the length not yet attached to a buffer. It then passes this value to ngx_http_v2_filter_get_shadow() to set the buffer's start and end pointers.

According to recent reports, as an off_t, size holds -d, so chunk->last points d bytes before chunk->pos. The TLS output path later uses the difference between these pointers as the copy length.

Industry observers note that last - pos is -d, but the length argument to memcpy() is a size_t. The final conversion turns it back into 2^64 - d, passing in a very large copy length.

In a recent development, A copy of almost 2^64 bytes would normally run past the end of the heap and crash the worker. It does not here, because of how glibc handles large copies. The x86-64 glibc memcpy() path used in our experiment does not copy front to back. It first loads the start and the end of the source, then copies the middle in a loop that walks backward from the end of the destination toward dest.

The end of the destination is dest + size. With size = 2^64 - d, this sum overflows the 64-bit address space and wraps around to dest - d, which is d bytes below dest. Since the end now lies below the start, the backward loop stops after one pass, and the large middle region is never touched. This backward-copy structure, which moves four 32-byte vectors per iteration, has been present in glibc's x86-64 implementation since version 2.24, released in 2016.

A simplified version of the glibc 2.41 AVX2 path is shown below.

align_down(x, 32) rounds x down to a 32-byte boundary. When end is 32-byte aligned, as in the example below, cursor = align_down(end - 129, 32) becomes end - 160. glibc copies 128 bytes from this position and separately copies the final 32 bytes.

Since cursor is already below dest, the loop runs only once. The long middle region is skipped, leaving only the first 128 bytes and the final 160 bytes to be copied.

dest is the next write position in the TLS plaintext buffer, so it falls right after whatever nginx has already written there. Before the response body, nginx writes the acknowledgments for the client's control frames, and the client controls how many of those it sends. In the nginx source, an HTTP/2 frame header is 9 bytes, PING data is 8 bytes, and SETTINGS ACK data is 0 bytes.

A PING without the ACK flag therefore produces a 17-byte PING ACK, while SETTINGS produces a 9-byte SETTINGS ACK. If the client sends p PING frames and s SETTINGS frames, nginx first generates 17p + 9s bytes of responses. Including the 9-byte DATA frame header that follows them gives the start position of the next response body.

The client adjusts the send window with WINDOW_UPDATE so that d = P - 64. The copy end, dest - d, then becomes TLS + 64. The 160-byte region then spans the 96 bytes immediately before the TLS buffer and the first 64 bytes inside it.

The second move copies the 160 bytes just below src - d onto the edge of the TLS buffer. The attacker wants two things in those bytes: a chosen value to overwrite the heap metadata before the TLS buffer, and pointers that land inside the buffer and are sent back in the response. The request pool has both. It holds the request's headers, along with nginx's structures that describe them and point into the nginx image and heap. To move src there, the attacker sends a Range header that asks for several byte ranges. nginx then builds a multipart response that starts with a boundary string allocated in the request pool, so src points there.

This b->pos becomes in->buf->pos as it passes through the output path, so it is the src used by the final memcpy().

If the current request-pool block has enough space, nginx places a newly introduced small allocation immediately after the previous one.

Industry observers note that the first 96 bytes overwrite the size field in the heap area preceding the TLS plaintext buffer. The remaining 64 bytes are sent in the TLS response, disclosing nginx image and heap addresses. A single malformed copy therefore provides both an out-of-bounds write and address disclosure. These can be used to overwrite a cleanup function pointer and execute commands with nginx worker privileges. We omit the detailed function-pointer overwrite procedure.

Sources indicate that using only an externally reachable TLS/HTTP/2 port, we demonstrated unauthenticated remote code execution. The exploit corrupted the send window, disclosed nginx image and heap addresses, and took control of a cleanup function to execute commands with nginx worker privileges.

It has been revealed that the Xint research team confirmed that our exploit works under concurrent normal traffic and across servers with different hardware specifications. On AWS, GCP, and Azure, we verified it from inside the target server, across a private network with separate sender and target hosts, and over a public HTTPS endpoint.

Industry observers note that CVE-2026-123634 is a use-after-free in the nginx DNS resolver logic. A request's handler can free another resolver context that the waiting-list loop has not yet processed, which then continues to use the freed memory.

According to recent reports, nginx can act as a reverse proxy, forwarding client requests to a backend server (called an upstream) to handle them. The proxy_pass config directive specifies the location of the upstream.

In a recent development, an upstream can be fixed in the configuration or chosen from the request. For example, proxy_pass http://$host; uses the request’s hostname in $host as the destination. This value usually comes from the client's Host header. If nginx needs a DNS lookup to obtain the server's IP address, it queries the DNS servers specified by the resolver directive.

In a recent development, because DNS resolution takes time, nginx continues handling other requests while it waits for a DNS answer. Each lookup has a resolver context (ngx_resolver_ctx_t) holding its state, result, and a handler to call when the lookup finishes.

The resolver tracks each domain name in a node. If a lookup for the same name is already in flight, nginx does not send a second query, preferring instead to push the newly introduced context onto the head of that node's waiting list.

Industry observers note that when the answer finally arrives, the resolver detaches the waiting list from the node by setting rn->waiting to NULL. It then walks the list and calls each context's handler, saving the next context in next before each call.

It has been revealed that A handler that frees a later context in the list therefore leaves next dangling. However, separate requests cannot cause this, because terminating a request frees only its own contexts. Hence, this is only a bug if the two contexts come from the same request.

In our testing, we found only one configuration option which creates two contexts attached to the same request. The mirror config directive copies a request to a second location as a background subrequest. It is commonly used to send a copy of live traffic to a test system. If the main request and its mirror use the same upstream name, their contexts can wait for the DNS answer on the same node.

(1) Terminating the Main Request Frees the Mirror's Context.

According to recent reports, if the DNS lookup fails, the main request's ngx_http_upstream_resolve_handler() tries to send a 502 response. If the client has reset the TCP connection, that write can fail, causing ngx_http_terminate_request() to terminate the main request.

The main request’s cleanup list includes the mirror's upstream cleanup, so the cleanup code below also runs for the mirror, even though its DNS result has not yet been processed.

ngx_resolve_name_done() then frees the mirror's context while the resolver loop still holds it in next.

(2) The Resolver Uses the Freed Context.

In a recent development, before the resolver loop reaches it, the mirror's context is still in state NGX_AGAIN. Before freeing a context in this state, ngx_resolve_name_done() tries to unlink it from the node's waiting list. But the loop has already detached that list and set rn->waiting to NULL. The search finds nothing, and the context is freed anyway.

Industry observers note that control then returns to the resolver loop, which advances to the context saved in next, i.e. the mirror's freed context. The loop now triggers the use-after-free by writing ctx->state and ctx->valid, reading ctx->next, and calling ctx->handler(ctx). If another allocation reclaims the freed context’s memory, both next and handler are attacker controlled. As a result, the attacker can redirect the list traversal and the final indirect call, gaining control over the program execution.

Industry observers note that to execute arbitrary code, we first need an address disclosure. Interestingly, this vulnerability can itself be leveraged for the disclosure. glibc's free-list pointer overwrites the context's next field, so the loop's next "context" is a freed array of DNS records whose contents we choose. We then employ a trick: we point the controlled handler at the vsyscall gettimeofday() address (which is fixed on amd64 systems), forging a heap chunk size and placing glibc and heap pointers inside a DNS query that nginx sends to our controlled server.

After the information disclosure, we can chain the loop through that array to a fake context in a pending request body, with its handler set to system() to get arbitrary command execution on the host.

Official nginx:1.31.8 image, with a server block using request-time DNS resolution and mirror added to the stock configuration.

HTTP on port 8080 and DNS answers for the attacker's zone.

nginx's recursive resolver must reach the attacker's authoritative DNS server.

Ubuntu Linux 6.8 (x86-64), with vsyscall=xonly.

Remote code execution with nginx worker privileges.

CVE-2026-123633 is a use-after-free caused by an active HTTP/2 connection remaining eligible for draining. When a request opens an upstream connection, nginx can close the request's own HTTP/2 connection and free its memory while the upstream code continues to access it. This vulnerability requires nginx to open an upstream connection, which is common for production uses of nginx.

Each nginx worker has a fixed number of connection slots, set by worker_connections. Client and upstream connections share these slots. When slots run low, nginx closes idle connections to reclaim them for other purposes. To track which connections can be reclaimed, nginx marks connections as reusable if they meet some protocol-specific conditions, such as idle HTTP/1.1 keep-alive connections or HTTP/2 connections with no active streams. These reusable connections are tracked in a dedicated queue.

Before allocating a slot, ngx_get_connection() calls ngx_drain_connections(). If at most 1/16 of the slots are free and the reusable queue is not empty, it closes connections starting from the oldest entries, a process referred to as “draining”.

Sources indicate that the drain sets c->close and calls each selected connection's read handler directly. These calls are synchronous, and slot allocation resumes only after the handler returns.

(1) An Active HTTP/2 Connection Stays in the Reusable Queue.

ngx_http_v2_handle_connection() queues an HTTP/2 connection as reusable when it has no active streams or pending output frames. If the last read stopped in the middle of a frame, h2c->state.incomplete is set, but the flag is only checked after placing the connection in the queue:.

Normally, an idle connection has its read handler updated to ngx_http_v2_idle_handler(), which takes it off the queue when data arrives. However, when ngx_http_v2_handle_connection returns early because of an incomplete frame, the connection keeps the normal ngx_http_v2_read_handler(), which never removes it from the reusable queue.

The flaw is therefore triggered as follows:.

A client sends the first part of a HEADERS frame, which puts the connection in the reusable queue.

The client then sends the rest, which opens a stream.

If that request opens an upstream connection and triggers a drain, the drain may reclaim the connection the newly opened stream runs on.

In a recent development, to reach the upstream, the request needs another connection slot. ngx_event_connect_peer() calls ngx_get_connection(), which runs the drain if slots are low. The HTTP/2 connection left in the reusable queue can now be selected for closure.

The HTTP/2 read handler sees c->close and tries to send GOAWAY, but if the client has already reset the TCP connection, the write fails and ngx_http_v2_finalize_connection() closes the connection and its streams.

Closing the stream calls ngx_http_free_request(), which destroys the request pool containing both the request r and its upstream structure u.

It has been revealed that when the drain returns, nginx continues running the freed request's upstream code. It connects to the upstream, sends the proxied request, and handles events on that connection, all through the freed r and u.

According to recent reports, with some heap grooming techniques, we arrange for a glibc largebin header to land on top of u and the header's bk_nextsize field to land on u->peer.sockaddr. It then points at bytes we controlled (a sockaddr_in for our own server), causing the upstream connection to actually connect to our own server.

To bypass ASLR, we simply accept the connection and nginx sends the freed request buffer, which now contains a variety of pointer values. The worker then crashes, but its replacement has the same address layout.

To execute commands, we use a different grooming technique to reclaim the freed request with a fake one whose upstream read handler is execv(). When we refuse the connection, epoll reports an error, and nginx calls that handler.

Official nginx:1.31.8 image, with one TLS/HTTP/2 server using proxy_pass added to the stock nginx.conf.

A TLS port with ALPN h2, plus an HTTP/1 port used to occupy connection slots.

nginx can open a TCP connection to the attacker.

Remote code execution with nginx worker privileges.

CVE-2026-121810 is a use-after-free caused by closing a QUIC connection while one of its HTTP/3 requests is still running. During stream creation, the parent QUIC connection is incorrectly made eligible for draining. The request's subsequent upstream connect can then free its own request memory.

The bug is similar to CVE-2026-123633, but it is triggered by a slightly different mechanism, so our writeup will omit some definitions and background we already covered. As a result, we recommend reading Section 5.3 before reading this section.

According to recent reports, HTTP/3 carries multiple request streams over one QUIC connection, but nginx internally allocates one ngx_connection_t for the QUIC connection and an additional one for each stream. All come from the same worker's connection slots, so creating a request stream also requires a free slot. We refer to the QUIC connection containing these streams as the parent connection. Both QUIC connections and HTTP/3 request streams waiting for headers may be eligible for draining.

When an individual stream closes, nginx checks whether the parent connection can also be drained. ngx_quic_can_shutdown() walks the parent's stream tree, and if every remaining stream is cancelable, nginx puts the parent connection in the reusable queue.

(1) Re-Queuing the QUIC Connection During Stream Creation.

Before allocating a connection slot for a new stream, ngx_quic_create_stream() takes the parent connection off the reusable queue, which is meant to prevent ngx_get_connection() from draining the parent during slot allocation.

However, the newly introduced stream only enters the parent's stream tree after the connection slot is allocated.

It has been revealed that suppose the drain closes an existing idle stream on the same parent connection. If both directions of that stream have finished, it can trigger the check that decides whether the parent can be drained, but this check cannot see a stream that is still being created. With no other non-cancelable streams in the tree, nginx puts the parent back in the reusable queue, where it stays even after the upcoming stream has been created.

(2) The Upstream Connect Frees the Request.

In a recent development, when the new stream's request connects upstream, it needs another slot, which can run the drain again and select the parent QUIC connection that was just queued. ngx_quic_close_connection() calls ngx_quic_close_streams() to close the parent's streams, which terminates the request whose upstream connect is still in progress.

Recent findings suggest that ngx_http_free_request() destroys the request pool, including the upstream structure u. Control then returns to ngx_event_connect_peer(), which continues using the freed u->peer and causes a use-after-free.

From here, the ASLR bypass and control-flow hijack paths mirror those in Section 5.3.2, so they are omitted here for brevity.

Official nginx:1.31.8 amd64 image, with an HTTP/3 proxy server added to the stock nginx.conf.

UDP 443 (HTTP/3), TCP 443 (HTTP/2) and TCP 80.

nginx can open a TCP connection to the attacker's listener.

Remote code execution with nginx worker privileges.

It has been revealed that CVE-2026-113425 is a use-after-free in the mail proxy's auth_http authentication path. Closing the client connection frees its session, but the connection to the authentication service remains open. A later event on that connection uses the freed session.

nginx can proxy IMAP, POP3, and SMTP between clients and mail servers. When a client logs in, nginx asks an HTTP service, configured with auth_http, whether the credentials are valid and which backend mail server to use.

During this lookup, nginx maintains two connections: one to the client and one to the HTTP authentication service; the latter is referred to as the auth connection.

Sources indicate that ngx_mail_auth_http_init() creates a lookup context with its own memory pool. However, the auth connection's data and pool fields point to the client's session s and the client connection's pool. That pool must remain allocated while the auth connection uses the session.

It has been revealed that at the start of the lookup, the client's read handler is replaced with ngx_mail_auth_http_block_read(). If re-arming the read event fails, this handler function closes the auth connection, freeing the lookup pool. However, the client's write handler remains ngx_mail_send(), whose error path does not clean up the auth connection. The flaw is that this write handler can close the client connection while the auth connection still points to it.

This path requires the client's write event to be registered beforehand. For example, if the client stops reading replies and fills the socket's send buffer, a send returns EAGAIN. ngx_mail_send() then registers the write event so it can retry.

If the login command and a TCP reset are processed in the same event-loop iteration, nginx handles the socket error reported by epoll by running the active read handler followed by the write handler. The read handler parses the login command, and then starts the auth lookup with a reply still queued in s->out.

ngx_mail_send() then tries to send the queued reply. The write fails on the reset socket, so it closes the client connection and destroys its pool.

It has been revealed that the session s and its module context array were allocated from the now-freed pool. Importantly, the auth connection stays open, with its data field still pointing to s.

The next event (e.g. a connection-completion, response, or timeout) runs a handler on the auth connection. The read and write handlers both take the session pointer from the connection's data field and use it to obtain the lookup context, accessing s->ctx in the freed session. If attacker-controlled data reclaims that memory, s->ctx can point to a fake context. The authentication response path later calls ctx->handler, giving the attacker a control flow hijack.

According to recent reports, to bypass ASLR, we leverage the stale auth connection's timeout. With some heap grooming, the timeout frees memory that now holds a partially received IMAP command from another connection. A later allocation reclaims that memory with heap pointers, and nginx echoes them back to us when it replies to the IMAP command.

To execute commands, we run the trigger again on a fresh worker. Just after the session is freed, an IMAP LOGIN with a controlled password reclaims it with a fake session. Its s->ctx points to a fake lookup context whose handler is system(). When the auth service replies, ngx_mail_auth_http_read_handler() follows the stale session and calls system(s).

Official nginx:1.31.8 image, stock configuration plus a mail block with IMAP, POP3 and SMTP.

IMAP 143, POP3 110, and HTTP 80 served by the same workers.

None. The auth service rejected every login.

Remote code execution with nginx worker privileges.

The nginx vulnerabilities give an attacker code execution with worker privileges. Workers normally run with restricted permissions, so gaining full control of the host additonally requires a privilege escalation bug. We investigated the Linux kernel and found a zero-day vulnerability in its SCTP subsystem. Chaining it with one of the nginx vulnerabilities gave us root privileges on the host. This also worked when nginx ran inside a Docker container.

This section describes the cause of the SCTP vulnerability and our validation results. Until a kernel patch is available, we are withholding most of the details needed to reproduce or exploit it.

SCTP (Stream Control Transmission Protocol) is a transport-layer protocol, like TCP and UDP.

Like TCP, SCTP is connection-oriented. It calls a connection an association. An association can use multiple IP addresses at each endpoint, allowing it to continue over another path if one path fails.

The bug is in the SCTP send path. While a send operation is waiting, its association can be transferred to another socket. The waiting operation can then free the transferred association. Depending on what the other socket does, this leads to a use-after-free or a double free.

On a kernel built with KASAN, the kernel's memory error detector, the double free indicates up like this:.

The bug was introduced in Linux v4.15 in 2018 and has remained in the kernel for more than eight years.

According to recent reports, the use-after-free provides two primitives: a kernel memory disclosure that defeats kernel address space layout randomization (KASLR), and an arbitrary function call in the kernel. Together, they let us control kernel execution and escalate privileges. In our tests, an attacker already running code as an nginx worker could reliably gain root.

We also obtained a root shell on the host in a setup where nginx was running in a Docker container. On many Linux distributions, the SCTP module is installed by default and the kernel loads it automatically the first time a program opens an SCTP socket. Whether SCTP is reachable on a given host still depends on the kernel, the available modules, and the container's restrictions. Where it is reachable, the attacker can take over the host kernel. Since all containers on the host share that kernel, this gives the attacker control of the host and every container on it.

According to recent reports, until a kernel patch is available, hosts that do not use SCTP can block module loading by placing install sctp /bin/false in a .conf file under /etc/modprobe.d/. This only prevents loading through modprobe. It does not unload a module that is already loaded, and it does not disable SCTP compiled into the kernel.

Recent findings suggest that thanks for reading this far. To recap, if you run nginx, upgrade to 1.31.9 as soon as it’s out. If you can’t update right away, apply the mitigations described in Section 3.3. They block the attack paths we know about, but they aren’t a substitute for a patch. Until a kernel fix is available, also block the SCTP module on hosts that don’t need it, as described in Section 6.3.

In a recent development, be careful when checking whether a server is patched. Linux distributions often backport fixes without changing the version that nginx -v demonstrates. Check the full package version against your distribution’s security advisory instead.

According to recent reports, we thank F5 and the nginx team for their cooperation during disclosure and patch validation. We’ll post updates and answers to common questions about nginx2root at nginx2root.com.

According to recent reports, CVE-2026-123007 went unnoticed in nginx for more than ten years, and the SCTP bug has been in the Linux kernel since 2018. Both projects run almost everywhere and have had years of security review, yet these bugs survived until a fully automated Xint scan found them. If you’d like to see what Xint finds in your own code, get in touch.

Breaking: MPS in PyTorch 2.15

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that if you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15! FP8 arrives on MPS, language-model decoding gets faster paths through linear layers and softmax and newly introduced Metal kernels tackle some surprisingly expensive parts of audio, video and training workloads.

A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face. We contribute across PyTorch, and one of our focus areas is the MPS backend, where the goal is to make your Mac a first-class place to run and train PyTorch models. At the start of 2026, running even small models on MPS often meant working around unsupported operations, performance cliffs and unexpected memory growth. So we run real models from the Hugging Face Hub across language, image and video, find where MPS falls short and fix it upstream in PyTorch, more and more often by replacing MPSGraph with dedicated Metal kernels. Much of this post is the result of that work, done together with the PyTorch maintainers and community contributors.

If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:.

Recent findings suggest that you'll need an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 15 or later and Python 3.11 or later (see the 2.15 compatibility matrix). If your OS is too old or no Metal GPU is available, the MPS availability check now tells you why.

To try the release candidate in a separate environment:.

FP8 gives you another way to save memory on your Mac. PyTorch 2.15 adds torch.float8_e4m3fn tensors on MPS: one byte per value, half the storage of FP16 or BF16.

In a recent development, you can multiply these tensors with F.scaled_mm, which supports both tensorwise and rowwise scaling. Here's a small example with one scale per tensor:.

Every LLM has a prefill phase and a decode phase. During decode, each latest token goes through the model as a single row, so the substantial matrix multiplications turn into matrix-vector products. PyTorch 2.15 speeds up both kinds of layers that dominate this step: dense linear layers and mixture-of-experts layers.

In a recent development, MPS has had GEMV kernels for torch.mm since 2.14, but F.linear still went through MPSGraph. PyTorch 2.15 connects them to F.linear, so the common [1, 1, hidden_size] decoding input uses them directly, with eligible bias additions fused in. Across 96 BF16 layer shapes from real models, that's a 1.23× geometric-mean speedup. The biggest wins land on small projections, such as the gates in MoE models, where the old path left most of the memory bandwidth unused. Large layers and LM heads were already close to bandwidth-bound, so they stay near 1×.

Sources indicate that A mixture-of-experts layer sends different numbers of tokens to each expert. Grouped matmul handles those uneven groups in a single operation, and 2.15 gives MPS a native implementation.

It has been revealed that in 2.14, grouped matmul copied the group offsets to the CPU and looped over the groups. The new Metal kernels read the offsets directly on the GPU, using Metal Performance Primitives where available and a separate Metal path elsewhere. Small groups, the common case during decoding, get their own kernel as well.

For example, 64 tokens can be split into groups of 16, 32, and 16:.

Sources indicate that the decoding kernel shows up directly in token throughput. On an M3 Ultra with torch.compile, MoE models generate about 1.3× more tokens per second:.

Working with complex tensors gets easier. complex64 LU factorization, LU solve and triangular solve now run on MPS, which also unlocks the operations and gradients built on them, such as complex determinants. Here's a small system solved directly on the GPU:.

Recent findings suggest that small matrices get fast kernels too. For camera geometry and image transformations, batches of FP32 matrices up to 4 × 4 are inverted in a single Metal kernel that combines factorization and solving. Larger problems get attention as well: QR uses blocked updates, and triangular solves turn much of their work into efficient matrix multiplication.

Gated DeltaNet workloads get a dedicated fast path for batches of 16 × 16, 32 × 32 and 64 × 64 FP32 triangular systems with at least eight right-hand sides.

SVD is also more robust at numerical extremes. It now correctly handles very small singular values, very large or very small input magnitudes and basis completion with full_matrices=True, which in turn makes pseudoinverse and least-squares results more reliable.

Audio models, video decoders and training loops have their own expensive operations. This release gives several of them fresh paths through Metal:.

Industry observers note that token sampling gets faster in 2.15 as well. softmax and log_softmax now run on dedicated Metal kernels, and large vocabularies benefit the most: an FP32 softmax over a [1, 128256] row of logits drops from 57 µs to 7 µs, about 8× faster than the MPSGraph version. The speedup holds across other common vocabulary sizes:.

One of the most striking results in this release comes from the constant-padding change. The VAE decode in Wan-AI/Wan2.2-TI2V-5B-Diffusers makes 8,764 padding calls over a full 28-tile decode. With padding on Metal, peak driver memory drops from about 270 GiB to 8 GiB:.

You can now pick which MPS stream runs your work, directly from Python. torch.mps.Stream and the torch.mps.stream context manager provide the interface, and Tensor.record_stream lets the allocator track a tensor's use on another stream.

Here's a small example that sends work to a separate stream and synchronizes before reading the result:.

It has been revealed that several more operations now run on MPS: torch.frexp, torch.logspace, torch.take and Tensor.put_, torch.heaviside, torch.special.laguerre_polynomial_l and unsigned-integer comparisons. logspace doesn't yet support integer or boolean outputs with more than one element.

Attention gets a correctness fix too: the MPS math implementation of scaled dot-product attention now handles batch and head broadcasting correctly.

Work on 2.16 is already well underway. Some of the changes below have landed on main and are available in the nightlies; others are still in review, so details may change before the release.

Industry observers note that once a model's decode path no longer contains any MPSGraph ops, the GPU only starts on a token after the CPU has finished encoding all of its kernels. PyTorch 2.16 commits the command buffer every 16 kernels, so the GPU gets to work while the CPU is still encoding the rest. For compiled BF16 decoding at a 2048-token context:.

Scaled dot-product attention is dropping MPSGraph completely: every shape will run on Metal kernels, with dedicated vector kernels for decoding and Metal Performance Primitives for half-precision prefill on newer macOS versions. The shapes that used to fall back to MPSGraph benefit the most. On an M5 Pro, decoding with grouped-query attention (32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 80, 4K context) drops from 465 µs to 65 µs, and a 4K × 4K prefill with head dim 40 goes from 42 ms to 6 ms.

The move away from MPSGraph continues. Batch norm forward and backward are in progress, while MSE loss (up to 12× faster on small inputs), std_mean and var_mean (up to 4× faster) and bincount have already landed. bincount is the most dramatic: when most values fall into a single bin, counting 4 million integers used to take 6.8 seconds and now takes half a millisecond.

Industry observers note that bundled shaders will build for Metal 3.1 by default, with Metal 4 versions compiled only for the kernels that need them. That shrinks libtorch_cpu.dylib by about 25%, from 384 MiB to 287 MiB, and lays the groundwork for Metal 4.1 shaders with faster matmuls and native FP8 matrix multiplication.

In a recent development, pyTorch 2.15 brings FP8 to the Mac, faster LLM decoding for dense and MoE models, more linear algebra on the GPU and a long list of operations moved from MPSGraph to dedicated Metal kernels. Give the release candidate a try!

A major thank you to Nikita Shulga, Kurt Mohler and Aaron Gokaslan for reviewing much of this work, and to everyone who contributed to MPS in this release.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Isomorphic Labs revealed on November 19, 2026, a strategic research collaboration with MSD to discover small-molecule oncology drug candidates, combining its AI drug-design engine with selected proprietary datasets and discovery expertise from the pharmaceutical company.

MSD is the trade name used by Merck & Co., Inc., outside the United States and Canada. The partners will work against an oncology target they describe as strategically vital. The announcement concerns early discovery work, rather than an existing candidate entering preclinical or clinical development.

The agreement places a computational design system alongside a pharmaceutical firm’s internal research material. Isomorphic Labs will apply its drug design engine, IsoDDE, which it describes as a computational system composed of foundational AI models. MSD will supply select high-quality proprietary datasets specifically for this collaboration.

Isomorphic Labs will perform in silico, or computational, predictions and deliver molecular designs. The selected MSD data will be incorporated into IsoDDE for the program, giving the engine program-specific inputs from MSD alongside Isomorphic Labs’ modeling and computing capabilities.

Industry observers note that sarah Skerratt, chief research officer at Isomorphic Labs, noted the companies will apply IsoDDE’s generative and predictive capabilities to a challenging program intended to benefit patient populations with unmet needs. Her statement establishes the research objective; the agreement itself begins with molecular design and discovery.

Recent findings suggest that george Addona, senior vice president and head of Discovery, Preclinical Development and Translational Medicine at MSD Research Laboratories, emphasized the operational connection between computational and laboratory work. “The key to successfully leveraging AI/ML for molecular invention lies in close coordination of wet-lab and dry-lab functions,” he noted in the joint press release. The stated aim is to design and create better candidates faster by combining MSD’s internal data and discovery expertise with Isomorphic Labs’ modeling and computing capabilities.

The companies have divided the work between design and downstream execution. Isomorphic Labs handles the computational predictions and molecular designs, while MSD is responsible for preclinical and clinical development, manufacturing, and commercialization of any products derived from the collaboration.

Recent findings suggest that that division puts the AI system at the front end of a longer pharmaceutical development process. A molecular design must still progress through MSD’s preclinical and clinical work before it could become a manufactured and commercialized product.

Sources indicate that isomorphic Labs will receive an upfront payment from MSD. It is also eligible for payments tied to specified research, development, regulatory, and commercial milestones, as well as tiered royalties on net sales. A separate option allows Isomorphic Labs to co-fund development activities in return for elevated royalties.

Recent findings suggest that the economic terms therefore extend beyond the initial design work. Milestone payments depend on progress through successive research and commercial stages, while royalties connect potential returns to product sales. The co-funding option offers Isomorphic Labs a route to contribute development funding in exchange for higher royalties.

According to recent reports, for AI drug discovery, the collaboration’s significance lies in how the pieces are joined: a foundational-model design engine, pharmaceutical datasets, coordinated laboratory research, and an assigned path into development and manufacturing. The open question is whether that integrated workflow can turn molecular designs into oncology candidates that achieve the agreement’s development and regulatory milestones.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last November, we introduced AnyLanguageModel on this blog: a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework that lets you choose the model and provider your app uses. We heard from app developers who were curious about local models but weren't always sure how to get started. They also wanted to avoid the added complexity of supporting multiple inference providers. AnyLanguageModel grew out of that feedback.

In a recent development, local and hosted inference each have their strengths, and both have a role in building this new generation of intelligent apps. A shared API makes it easier to choose the right model for each task.

A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out, along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0.

Here's what changed, and what's next:.

According to recent reports, the core idea of AnyLanguageModel remains the same: use the Foundation Models API with the model that fits your app. To get started, change your import statement:.

The same session code then works with the system model, with open-weight models through llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML, and with the hosted providers below.

Over the past year, we've added several major features:.

On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel also works with any model that conforms to Foundation Models' LanguageModel protocol, including Core AI models.

Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out swift-huggingface and swift-xet to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps.

According to recent reports, support for hosted models expanded this year, too. AnyLanguageModel now supports:.

With Inference Providers, you can use open-weight models that are too major to run on the device with the same session code:.

Hosted providers get the same features as local models: guided generation, tool calling with streaming, and token usage on responses.

It has been revealed that reasoning is now part of the transcript too. When you switch providers, reasoning blocks are automatically omitted from requests if the upcoming provider can't replay them.

API keys come from a closure instead of a string, so your app can fetch short-lived tokens from your own server. The README explains when to let people bring their own keys and when to route requests through a proxy.

AnyLanguageModel also runs on Linux, so the same code can work on a server.

Recent findings suggest that while we've made local models easier to use, the models themselves have become more capable, making the small ones a good place to start. Here are some of the most downloaded models on the Hub right now:.

The first two fit on an iPhone, and Qwen3.8 27B runs on a Mac with 32 GB of memory or more. Selecting the MLX model takes one line:.

Sources indicate that and if you have four maxed-out Mac Studios handy, GLM-5.3 from Z.ai takes about 1.5 TB in BF16. For the rest of us, it's available through Inference Providers.

If you're upgrading an existing app, see the migration guidance in the AnyLanguageModel, swift-huggingface, and swift-xet release notes for help updating your code.

Community feedback and contributions have shaped several of our major features. Thank you to everyone who contributed for helping make AnyLanguageModel more useful to app developers.

Sources indicate that language models have proven to be a powerful tool for building intelligence into products. They're also one of many kinds of models developers can put to work. We're excited to bring the same approach to more capabilities: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of models running on the device. Coming soon: models that decide, and models that listen.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

MegaRobo Technologies announced on November 19, 2026 that it had raised nearly $200 million in newly introduced funding to expand its AI for Science business internationally and build infrastructure connecting AI with laboratory instruments, robotics and other physical systems.

It has been revealed that oman Investment Authority, the sovereign wealth fund of the Sultanate of Oman, joined the round, and CMB International participated as a latest investor. Existing backers Asia Investment Capital, Granite Asia and Sinovation Ventures continued their support. The proceeds also fund continued investment in core technology.

Sources indicate that megaRobo is targeting a limitation in applying AI to science: models can read papers, predict structures or generate molecules, but scientific discovery also requires experiments and observations from physical systems. Its infrastructure is designed to let AI design experiments, execute them in real laboratories and use the results to determine the next step.

It has been revealed that the organization’s One Intelligence Stack combines models and agents, data, workflows, software, scientific instruments, robotics, automation and real-world feedback in a reusable foundation. Its operating loop is think, design, execute, observe and learn. MegaRobo is starting with scientific discovery because that loop must often run without knowing the answer in advance.

Initial scientific and pharmaceutical applications cover early research, target and mechanism discovery, drug screening and candidate optimization. Founder and CEO Daniel Huang said the approach changes AI “from a system that interprets the world into one that can help create latest knowledge, materials, processes and products.”.

MegaRobo reports delivering products and technologies to more than 500 customers, including pharmaceutical companies, drug-discovery organizations, biotechnology companies and research institutions. Megalaxy Lab, its programmable laboratory platform, has served more than 200 customers.

Industry observers note that through Megalaxy Lab, researchers and AI agents can configure experiments, route them to automated laboratory systems, track execution and receive structured, machine-readable results. Those results can feed directly into the next cycle of scientific reasoning, making experimental capacity programmable rather than organizing each laboratory exercise as a standalone project.

According to recent reports, megaRobo has also debuted Poreva Open with partners including Tencent Cloud and Twist Bioscience. The global protein-design challenge is open to all models and technical approaches. MegaRobo claims Megalaxy Lab will validate more than 10,000 protein-design sequences in wet-lab experiments, with the initiative aiming to establish a common benchmark using experimental results. That arrangement connects model assessment to physical evidence: a design can be tested in the laboratory, and the resulting observations can inform subsequent development.

Recent findings suggest that megaRobo reports approximately $600 million raised across multiple financing rounds to date. That history includes a nearly $300 million Series C co-led by Goldman Sachs Alternatives, Asia Investment Capital and Granite Asia, with participation from Pavilion Capital, part of Temasek’s Seviora Group. Earlier industry investors include WuXi AppTec and Bosch Ventures.

According to recent reports, the firm intends further expansion across North America, Europe, the Middle East and Asia. While scientific discovery is the starting market, the same architecture is intended for other settings where AI must interact with instruments, machines, materials, processes and real-world feedback.

Recent findings suggest that the financing therefore supports more than additional laboratory automation. MegaRobo’s wider proposition is that experimental capacity can become a standardized, on-demand resource for scientists, software and AI agents. Its reported customer adoption supplies the current base for that model, while Poreva Open’s planned validation work applies the reasoning-to-experiment loop at a larger scale; international expansion will test how broadly the company can deliver it.
